Honest Review.

So, I dropped PC gaming for nearly 5 years and went to consles.  I am in my mid 30's and have little ones.  For a time this was ok.  Then games like No Man's Sky were previewed.  The first time I saw some of the trailers I knew deep down I would be back someday for PC gaming.  Last year when the first reviews of No Man's Sky came out I was shocked.  Nothing but hate.  So I put off the PC purchase until the holidays.  I bought a top of the line pre built gaming pc from Best Buy ( I know, I was shocked too).  Bought a number of games during the winter sale on steam, but NMS was not one of them.  After weeks of reading the reviews, I purchased the game a few days ago on a whim (having a decent job makes gaming so much easier!). 

Well needless to say I am once again shocked.  I am having a blast in the game.  Like nothing I have ever played before.   As I get older I want less and less action heavy twitch games and more unique exploration and expreiences.  I have to say, this is the most interesting experience I have had just exploring and seeing what is over the next horizon.  Yes, there is no multiplayer, but I dont need it.  I like that there is no tutorial, I like that you have to discover upgrades, I like that everything is so random that sometimes it works great, other times I run away from a planet right after I land.

So, for those of you looking for multiplayer, or a "space" shooter, this is not the game for you.  But for an amazing experience that is beautiful and interesting on many levels above the junk out there, give this game a chance, even at full price I say it is worth it.

BTW, I havent even started building a base or using a freighter yet, so no, it is not because of the 1.1 update.  The core game is actually good!

Reviews.175266:
So I figured I'd type this up, knowing the NMS was probably the biggest game-hype letdown since - maybe ever.

In the beginning, before the release, I didn't know a gamer who wasn't excited for NMS. Every trailer and teaser was littered with comments about excitement and impatience, waiting for this - the ultimate game.
I personally was hyped as well, but knew I wouldn't be able to afford it at launch, so I had pre-set plans to wait a month before buying. $60 is a lot of money when making rent is a strategy game in and of itself.

The release was met with SO MUCH rejoicing. I specifically remember my buddy Chris snapchatting me screenshots of all the witty names for creatures he had come up with. But within only a few days, everything fell from pure elation, to bitter disappointment. 

This was not the game that was promised. This wasn't what HelloGames said it would be. Outcries of anger, demands for refunds, all flooded my social media. 
Personally, I wasn't up to date on what HelloGames had promised. I had - and have - no clue what exactly everyone was upset about, aside from reading a few articles about it not being really multiplayer, and all that. I honestly didn't care to learn, because I didn't want it to spoil my universe exploration experience.
But, the disappointment with the game was rampant, so much so that by the time I had the money to buy, I didn't. I shuffled the money saved back into money for extra groceries, and decided that my universe discovery might have to wait for Star Citizen.

Fast forward to like, November. I was still seeing the occasional article about NMS, and how disappointing it was, but one article got my attention. I was at work, boredly scanning over headlines in the MSN home page, when one about NMS popped up. I don't remember the author, or the entire thing, but that article changed my whole outlook.

The guy recants his excitement, fixing that ship for the first time, new world, new universe, gathering the materials in a strange land. He recalled it being a stressful task, not knowing exactly what he was doing. And when he had finished. When he had hopped in that ship, and launched it for the first time, as he left the atmos, flying into the great abyss... No one was there to greet him. The only fanfare was the small music clip indicating his quest was complete, and that was it. His satisfaction was purely his own. He went into how NMS is a lesson in loneliness. How your accomplishments are your own to celebrate, and how the world around you doesn't give a damn if you live or die. You're not the hero of this story. You're just a dude, with a ship, fucking around on planets.

That was the gist of it, anyway.

So that got me thinking, I want to play this game. But if I'm going to enjoy it, I'm not going to go into it with the expectations that others had. Because that isn't fair to myself. So, I waited, and in late December, I found the game for $32 and purchased it.

No Man's Sky is a solo first person survival game. Think Minecraft but pretty. You gather, you build, you fuel your ship, you fly on. If you take it as anything but that, you'll probably disappoint yourself. If I had paid full price, I might have been disappointed. But honestly, I'm not. It's a beautiful, sometimes silly game, with weird and mysterious history that has a lot of potential. It has quests, albeit they all involve gathering or flying onto the next star system. It has a base system which gives you purpose, as well as the Atlas thing which honestly I haven't gotten far on... It's a big open universe, and it's what you make of it. You give yourself purpose, you give yourself the opportunities you need, the goals you wish to acheive. Because, like in life, the giant-ass universe doesn't give two shits if you feel purposeful, or if your character's existence has meaning. 

That's maybe not how a game should be, maybe lazy of the game's creator, but that's how I look at it.

So there you go. Play the game, don't play full price, but experience it. It was definitely worth the $32.

It's not what people thought it would be, but knowing what it really was before I started playing it, I had a different set of expectations. Here's what it's not:
 - It is not a game based on the sheer wonder of exploring worlds that are varied and unique and all of them look interesting.
 - It is not a game that has a deep story and lore
 - It is not a game that gets everything right (inventory is a giant mess)

Here's what this game IS:
 - It's a mostly relaxing game that you probably won't play for hours on end, but it does scratch a very unique itch when you're in the mood for it.  Even people that seem to talk the most amount of crap about this game will still occasionally be seen logging on to play it.  If it's really that bad, you wouldn't return to it.
 - It's a game that has frustrating combat, annoying inventory, and a lot of things not going well, but for a small independent studio, this is an incredibly ambitious game that does get alot of things right as well.  It's fun to poke fun of the flaws, it's easy comedy.  

Bottom line... if your expectations are low and you just want a moderatly fun space game with some decent freedom and atmosphere, No Man's Sky is a great time killer that certainly justifies the price if it's on sale for $30 or less.  Is it worth the stubborn $60 price tag it still demands?  Absolutely not.  In a game this "big", there's really not enough there to justify the price tag when there are games out there that deserve that price point for both quality and sheer number of hours of enjoyment to be had.

I found out about this game in August of 2016, the week before the (actual) release. Therefore my review isn't influenced by all the hype and anticipation, and thus all the disappointment, from the launch.

I clicked "Yes" that I do recommend it, but I kind of need a neutral. I don't recommend paying $60 for it, but I have recommended the game. It's worth more like $20 in the current state.

There are a lot of bugs: ships falling through launch pads, whenever I teleport back to base I have to restart the game. There are a lot of balance issues: I can't find some resources that I need, but I keep finding traders selling things that are far more rare. And there are interface issues: I can't see below the ship to know where to land, the interface is really clunky and it's easier to press a key to switch inventory views than it is to click and hold for the right amount of time. There's just a lot of things that don't seem to be well-thought.

But with that being said, I continue to play it and I like it. I don't play first person shooters, my game of choice is Minecraft. Of course that makes my opinion less valuable to a lot of gamers, and I'm ok with that. But for what it is, space exploration, time wasting, wander around procedurally generated planets (and my graphics card is not good enough so I had to lower the quality, it's still pretty) ... it's just enjoyable. In normal mode there's some difficulty without having to really try very hard. That's what I prefer out of a game.

So I recommend it, but only if you just want to goof around and only if you get it on sale.
Reviews.175284:
I've waited a while to post a review for this.  Wanted to collect my thoughts on it.  After having watched the drama of this game's release unfold, I'm convinced that there are in fact, [b][i]three[/i][/b] No Man's Skys.

1. The game 'the hype' promised- and never delivered
2. The game that fifty-thousand raging neckbeards can't seem to stop despising
[b]3. The game it actually is.[/b]

As I wasn't on the hype train (I bought the game shortly after the Foundation Update), and I'm not especially prone to groupthink or fits of unreasoning rage either, I'll try to address that third game- because I [i][b]do[/b][/i] think gaming journalism is messed up.

I just happen to [i]also[/i] think that the primary dysfunction has essentially become a difference of extremes.

Which is another way of saying: [i]"trying to buy a game amid all these histrionics is like driving drunk."[/i]

Not- mind you- that I don't think that what happened with 'the hype' isn't reprehensible.  It is.  

On the other hand I also think it's unfortunate in the sense that there [i][b]is[/b][/i] an audience for a game like this.  It's probably a far smaller one than the hype generated, but it's also probably larger than the wave of hate that followed it's release (that [i][b]continues[/b][/i] to follow the release) allows for.


So what is that third game?  Well, it's an atmospheric exploration game with crafting and some survival elements.  

It has some action, but it's not an action-oriented game.
It has some survival elements- but this isn't "hardcore"in that regard and I don't see it ever being.
It's got some crafting elements- but the list ins't tremendously expansive and the flow isn't necessarily... optimized.
It's set in space- replete with different races, lore for those races, factions and so on- but it's not a free-form Mass Effect, no.

What it does well is it's sense of ambience and atmosphere, while giving you a little of all of the above things.  Some might find this boring (and even I tire of it from time to time), but I don't think that the mere fact that you can be bored with a game necessarily makes it a bad game.

This isn't a game for everyone- as I think I said above.  But if you think you might find the idea of exploring a vast-[i]feeling[/i] universe for a bit, while occupying yourself with gathering and cataloguing things, you might enjoy playing this game.

I know I have.

One thing I will absolutely agree with most of this game's detractors on is the price (at least the $60 one used at release).  

[b]This is a $30 game- at most.[/b]  

That puts it in a similar category with a lot of other games like it.

So, if you do get it, wait for a sale- definately.  But again, keep in mind  that there's a lot of nonsense surrounding the game's release.  It's easy to avoid the over-hyping of the game nowadays since it's out and we've got plenty of it's features catalogued and we know what the game is and isn't.

But it's still easy to fall victim to the rage train still following the game.  Make your own decision.  Don't let anyone else (including me) tell you what to buy.

This is a great game.  I was afraid to play this game for so long because I heard so much bad news about it.  But when I looked into the new behind this game I figured why not give this game a try and buy it.  The Foundation update seemed pretty cool and after reading up about the false advertisement claims, I felt pretty confident I was going to be playing a pretty fun game.

Just so people know the false advertisement claims made against Hello Games was really hurtful towards their efforts on this game.  When people saw the things in the ad for this game they thought they would be getting the same expierence as seen in the ad.  Which is wrong  to assume because this game runs on a random generator system.  Which will randomly generate an entire galaxy for you to explore.  So, this means no two play throughs will be the exact same.  I find the false advertisement claim was a big waste of this companies time and really hurt the market for selling this game.  The most I can tell is players thought they would play online with others.  But, later on Hello Games told people you can't.  This helped cover a major false claim perspective players where thinking was an aspect to the game.  This would have been cool don't get me wrong to explore an entire universe with some friends but I personally could care less about it.  I mainly want to play a game which gives me endless hours and a great amount of replay ability.

I looked all that up before I decided to buy and play this game.  Now when I got into playing the game I was overwhelmed.  In a good way mind you.  I couldn't believe how large these planets were and how far I would have to fly to get to other planets.  I have logged 36.5 hours into this game and I'm still not bored with it.  The Foundation update was the best thing for the develpers to add to the game.  It really makes the game worth playing.  The update adds some pretty fun base building and missions to complete to progress further in the game.  Ths games story is way better then I had expected.  You are a stranded human?  I'm not sure since you never get to see your character.  But nevertheless you are a stranded survivor from a crash landing.  You have no clue where you are or who you are exaclty.  All you know is this thing called Atlas is helping you along your journey to other Atlas interfaces.  Though as you continue to play and explore you find out there is something in the center of the galaxy waiting for you?  I'm still figuring out this storyline path.  It seems like you are fallowing the path of Nada and this person's friend.  In short, this game is jam packed with mystery and intrigue.  If you love mysterious stories and endless exploration this is the game for you.

I really feel like you guys should give this game another chance.  This game is meant to be played peacefully and calmly.  Just sit back in your chair and explore all that the galaxy you get generated has to offer.  Yes does the game bug out in weid moments sure, but don't let it stop you.  This games bugs are few to none.  The only way this game bugged out on me was when I landed a ship a little too close to a hill and got teleported into empty game space.  I reloaded the game and the bug was fixed with little harm done to progress.

Hello Games you guys and gals have made a great a game and it is sad to see it be wasted on picky players or players who are afraid due to some terrible unneeded false advertisement.  As an up incoming game artist this game makes me blush with excitement.  I get to see new worlds and levels everytime I play which makes my mind go nuts.  I have even created stories in my head for creatures and aliens I met.  Great job Hello Games!  I would have been honored to work with you guys and gals who created this masterpiece of a game.  It's nice to see new game ideas being made in this copy and paste AAA game world.  Thanks for this amazing gaming experience and I can't wait to see if you have anything else in store for us in No Man's Sky.

Before I go on: 

The reason this game has such poor reviews is really based on three things: 

1. The expectations for this game were made unrealistic by the public

2. The developers greatly contributed to these unrealistic expectations, and

3. The gameplay and content fell far short of what a triple A title should entail.

The negatives in my eyes:

This game costs far too much ($30 or even $40 would be fair) given its current state.

The gameplay is repetitive (not much of a negative though because who else here has hundreds of hundreds of hours in Minecraft or CS?)

The positives:

Regardless of the expectations, this game did something that I haven't experienced in videogames before, the concept is cool, the execution is good, and the gameplay leaves you feeling lost and alone in a universe that really doesn't care about your existence. The atmosphere is eerie yet enjoyable, and the gameplay is elegant and simple

The developers know they messed up, and have been working towards releasing additional content and improving the game. 

Survival mode is painful, and a good challenge for the patient and unwavering.

I have enjoyed the experience so far, and I highly recommend buying this game when the price drops.

[h1][b]No Man's Sky puts the Fun into Space[/b][/h1]

     It is a beautiful game. A wonderful combination of mathematics, art and coding. A game changer, challenging how we might approach and play games of the future. And that's clever. Very clever. It puts Hello Games and Sony in a unique position for its future success.

     To be able to leave the surface of a full size living planet and in 'real time' fly seamlessly to any moon or planet in the sky, indeed across the universe, is an extraordinary achievement.  On the new world, visit new landscapes and life there, then choose any other star in the galaxy and fly back and forth discovering things no one else has. Follow space ships into battle in grand fantastic 'art painted' science fiction encounters on a massive scale, with superb sound design and detail.  With 18,446,744,073,709,551,616 planets to discover there is an impossible lifetime of adventures.

     Accompanying the game is an astonishing sound and musical soundtrack by the award winning band 65 Days of Static, quite out of this world and full of empathy for the design.  Comparable to a mash up of artists like The Orb, Radiohead, Chemical Brothers, Orbital and Air, the band has lovingly created its own defining genre of haunting atmospheric music that mingles in the halcyon days of 90s techno and dance, one of the best of any modern video game.  Arguably worth the price tag of the game alone.

     No Man's Sky despite much discussed promises (and every modern game has flaws), is way ahead of cumbersome games like Elite and Star Citizen which suck all the fun and imagination out of childhood 'B-movie Adventures in Space' leaving just a complicated, text plagued, violent, orange and grey shooters set in a shiny dull tin-can void of padded cupboards and joyless music and design. Science Fiction remember is fiction otherwise we may just as well crowd fund a space tractor simulation in zero gravity for hard core gamers to drool over.  (Yes, tractor simulations do exist).

     NMS pioneering design quirks perhaps leave it suffering from letting us roam in an infinite universe where there really are no rules, asking us to question how we play games as real virtual explorers. Many things could be refined and developed and they will be.  The platform seems ideal for VR development and future improvements to real-time environmental effects would add to the already remarkable experience of setting foot onto an alien surface.  Gravity can be a little silly at times but it can be amusing landing on a tree or destroying objects and realise your starship remains stuck up in the air.  But then you realise you have a jet pack or can blast tunnels through mountains to reach your ship.

     Updates have improved user controls and added an enjoyable well thought out base building and satisfying animated farming experience, without interrupting the flow of the game.  Massive freighters, silent behemoths of the skies, now dwarf planets and moons, giving the player opportunities to win control of and defend your very own Star Wars like the star destroyer, that wowed cinema goers seeing for the first time the opening scenes of A New Hope in 1977.  It’s easy to be awed by the game’s extraordinary work of art on show and forget that the No Man’s Sky universe is at its core procedurally generated by extraordinary mathematics.

     The procedural challenge Hello Games are developing allows you to create your own science fiction adventure without a pre-determined choice of routes.  This is not to say goals are to be ignored in games.  That's the point of a game to take part and reach a satisfying end.  NMS has to decide if there is one goal or infinite goals that can be affected procedurally.  Imagine landing on a planet and being caught up in a war.  Flying to another and having to do search and rescue.  Crash landing and escaping from an alien virus or having to pilot a giant freighter with other players across challenging space and horizons.

     The core procedural planet concept has been realised. Now procedural evolution of storytelling needs refining. It's an enormous undertaking for such a small studio. Procedural animation and emotion might be improved. Sound too, though excellent, might be developed procedurally to define a wider range of birdsong and alien life to captivate the voyager discovering a new horizon.  Animated cinematics revealing story choices might compliment the well written, if slightly obscure, text based story links. Perhaps the game needs some protagonists players call on for help? It would be fun to leave loot or clues or put out distress calls for other players. Maybe even transport alien life from one planet to the other.  The possibilities are infinite.

     The first person approach borrows visual cues for its unique stylised look and procedural concept from all sorts of loved science fiction landmarks like Tron, Forbidden Planet, Hitch Hikers Galaxy, Star Trek, Time Bandits, Star Wars, Alien, Myst, Dr. Who, H.G.Wells, Isaac Asimov, Dune, Star Man, Star Gate, 2001, Moonraker, Natural History documentaries and many, many more. NMS is all the things you want science fiction to be.

     The game is colourful artistic space at last, on a grand, vast scale. Who knows what has yet to be discovered finding that last rewarding creature on a planet? Space is finally fabulous to look at, like all the paperback science fiction covers enticing us to read them. It's fun and serious, it's what YOU want it to be.   With an impossible number of life sized planets to fly to and discover it could be anything you imagine and that is perhaps what challenges us as players to give up an arguably tired, traditional way of playing games that essentially follow a pegged out story mode or 'latest map release' that has become more and more violent.

     Hello Games seems to have angered hard core fans for turning their perceptions of gaming upside down. The goal is discovery and serendipitous adventure. Forget the boring bits of space landing, animated starship steps, over designed sliding doors and fussy spaceships, climbing in and getting out, shopping trolley music and marvelling at what latest fashion to wear in rival space simulators.  Let's go where No Man has gone before... No Man's Sky puts the fun into space.

     Small developers and artists have a passion for their games.  They wouldn't continue to create otherwise.  Hello Games has vision, talent and clearly demonstrated a love and enthusiasm for their science fiction and their artful game.  Something public relations would be wise to handle with care and not stifle.  Despite the bungled early release of the game No Man’s Sky sets a benchmark to be a science fiction dream that appeals to all generations.  Sony will be proud of it.  If not they should be.  It's a great game, flawed perhaps only by its ambition, but a beautiful game none the less set in an astonishing magnificent universe, on an impossible scale, full of ideas that continues to surprise with each update.

     Look back only a few years and compare Tomb Raider for PS1 to today's PS4 franchise.  Look at defining landmark games such as ICO, the early Medal of Honour series and Medal of Honour  Frontline animations, theatre, music and sound, Grand Theft Auto, Deux X and realise how they all changed computer gaming.  There are plenty of classic games which have now become massive franchises but are they as good as when they were creative blocky digital pioneering 3d?  Not really, but great ideas will endure and change.

I've enjoyed my time with No Man's Sky. It's not a product everyone will like, but there's a good amount of content in this game (especially after the first free update came out).

What do I like about the game?

(1) The scope of the game is vast (especially given the small team size) - you'll hop from a space station to battle pirates in space, land on a verdant field, analyze life forms, delve into caverns, and fly back into space - all seamlessly. 

(2) There is a lot to do in the game. Your ship, suit, and multi-tool have a large number of upgrades, and with the update you'll own a large summonable trade freighter, build your own starbase, and generally have a much bigger imprint on the galaxy. 

(3) It's quite cool when you discover something for the first time, whether that's a lovely vista, an alien race in an outpost, or your first visit to one of the Atlas space citadels. Discovery and exploration is the driving force in this game.

Why won't everyone like it?

(1) This isn't an intense space drama or a space strategy game - it's much more low-key and chill than that. Instead of comparing it to Privateer or the (never going to exist) Star Citizen, the best comparison point is actually to MirrorMoon EP.

(2) The game has a storyline with mysteries to uncover, but it's not a story-driven game. Ultimately this is a game about unguided exploration (similar to just exploring in a random Minecraft world).

(3) There are a lot of places to explore, but no pre-designed missions on any planet. So most of your activity in the game is going forward, finding the resources in the game, and going forward some more.

In summary, this is a game that presents a universe to you and basically asks you, "What do you want to do with this game?". I'm personally happy with that. It might be too chill and low-key for you, but that's OK too. If you go into this looking for a game where you can explore a universe, uncover its mysteries, and you're OK without having 15 side quests at a time, this will be a great game for you. 

----------

As for the price, I'm happy to spend $60 on a game that I've played for 30 hours and will continue to play. There are plenty of reviewers with 150+ hours of gametime - for me, that's more than enough return on investment for a $60 game. I personally find it a little disingenuous when a reviewer gives a negative review after 200 hours of play - if you can get that much game time out of a game, maybe it's better than you think.

Reviews.175516:
I rarely write review for games, but No Man's Sky pushed me across the limits that I guess I have to write something about it. I m a big fan of Sandbox survivals or exploration base games, I clocked numerous hours in games like Ark Survival, Terreria(not in my steam),Starbound and Astroneer. I love the genre to death and that what made me so furious at what No Man Sky could have been but didnt.

==============================================
Firstly, Let start with with No Man's Sky Pre-foundation Update
==============================================
1. Game was very pleasing and very fun exploring a single planet.
2. Although gameplay became a pattern, at least there is always a node / new landmark to explore.
3. The game wasnt much about Units(In-game money) and more like exploring and discovering.
4. Speaking with the lifeforms which inhabits the planet is interesting and it feel the planet is alive.
5. The game was chill, key materials like Plutonium and stuff was abundances in certain planets.
6. Very chill but can get boring due to pattern repetition.
7. Goal were simple. Expand Inventory, Ship and Multi Tool. Explore, Relax, Discover. * Find Altas *
8. Checkpoints / Landmarks / New Locations were easy to scan for.  Making good for short term goals.

The game was obviously lacking to some player in terms of things to do, but to me, it was simple and relaxing. You enjoy the sceneries and you gathering around. Hit some jackpot planet and celebrate.
During pre-foundation update, I hardly jump from suns to suns. I spend quite alot of time on one planets before shifting to another. That was probably the simple joy I had with the game. It did get boring, but the game design was solid although little.

=========================================
Post Foundation Update ( Where it went horribly wrong?)
=========================================
Post Foundation update was exciting, I was telling my friend and excitied to jump back into the game to see what cement with the old game design with the new stuff. Nowhere in the patches did they unveil to me, the horror to a certain extent the foundation update had to bring...

1. Key materials start to become sparse in every planet ( I start hoarding plutonium and fearing of losing my stuff )
2. Checkpoints / Landmarks / New Locations become super hard to locate. It came down to a chance system.
3. I cant seem to find anymore Lifeform ( Korvax or Gek ) anywhere in the planets anymore... I only see platnium caches / ruins / drop pods and locations with nothing but a save point.
4. No more signal scanner ( Non-buildable ones) means no more tranmission towers = no chance to find new ships.
5. Base-Building locked behind a very specific questline (making it a wild-goose chase).
6. Freighters and new ships cost a bomb without base building aspect.
7. Planets become more of a resource node than a planet to explore.

The new foundation update threw away alot of what i loved about the game and gave me something wholly new and may not be the best thing. This is because the game has become less of a exploration game and more of a wild goose chase for materials and base building. 

I don't get excited to find new planets to land because landing cost me plutonium and plutonium has become fearfully little on planets. If I dont see a material i want from a planet in the planetary scan, i just turn away and scan another. 

The landmarks have also become so little it scary. Last time, i get annoyed that there was so many landmarks left unchecked on my screen it feels so clustered and annoying. Now I want that back cause I CANT FIND A SINGLE place on the planet. There is probably 1 or 2 markers to lead to me something but usually not something I want.

the Quest line is hilarously stupid. The game tasks the player to find a very very rare and specific resource to unlock more base building. It really pushes the player to view planets more as resource nodes than planets with life to explore.

It seems easier to purchase everything with Units than to do anything else now, cause instead of being fun and relaxing, it starts being tedious and unproductive. Largely, I believe due to the amount you get from mining. It feel like you are getting very little for each rare material you harvest and harvesting an entire rock structure of material can take awhile.

Overall, You guys might feel that I m ranting, and I do feel it too but I have placed so much faith in Hello Games to make things better and right yet to only see it has fall to the ground. I stilll believe this game can get better but if the team stop believing that procedural generating and randomization can prolong this game ( it willl not).  I will still sink hours and hours into the game to complete and max out my spaceship(bag and multitool already max), clear the base building questline and find for all the Altas story. But these Hours will probably not be the same 20+ hours i sank in the pre-foundation update. 

Now, I go on a wild-goose chase for Spadonium, and treat each planet like a resource node. Cause without base-building, I probably can't afford a freighter unless I found a planet which drops ultra rare items.

TL;DR version

Pre-Foundation Update ( Fun but repetitive which leads to being boring but still a chilll game)
Post Foundation Update ( Annoying > fun, Repetitive, Everything is Random, More stuff but no improvement, Planet feels more lifeless )


TO THE DEVELOPERS( IF YOU SEE THIS) :

1. Add mulltiplayer ( this would boost the game so much with base building Ref: Astroneer, Ark Survival)

2. Bring back Pre-Foundation Gameplay cause some of us may not want to spend hours completing base building to gain an income to afford new shiny stuff.

3. Please make scanning for new landmarks easier. The ? marks don't help and are usually disappointment.

A great deal of early reviewers where people who felt disappointed about what the game was in relation to what they expected before it was released. Personally, I strive to always keep my expectations of every new game I play relatively low and go into each new experience with an open mind.  With NMS, I was excited about the uniqueness of concept that this game brought to light.  In that, I was not at all disappointed. It is new and unique.  Sure, they use a proven formula that works well with many MMOs; that is to say you must gather materials and make achievements to upgrade your character and equipment.  To many people, this can be boring, but to millions, this can also be fun because it promotes exploration.

Here's what I love about the game: 1) It is beautiful 2) I love free exploration 3) I can play it how I like and make up my own story as I go 4) I can change how I play the game in a multitude of ways 5) It is unique and different 6) I can pick it up and play it for any amount of time and put it down in a moment's notice without feeling like I'm interrupting my game... it is fun to play if even for just a few minutes 7) like in Minecraft, I'm in it for the long haul and excited about what the developers are planning. Each update and new release (like with the foundation update) will only draw me back in and let me play the game just a little differently so I really don't mind waiting for them 8) finally, I love that the developers seem to embrace the modding community.  There are many mods that change the look, feel, and/or experience of the game so if you get bored or frustrated with something, you might just be able to change it with a mod.

If you like a baked-in story and want clear instruction on what you're "supposed to do" in a game, this is not for you.  If you want weekly content updates, this game is not for you. If you want action-packed multiplayer battles, this game is not (at least yet) for you. If you can't get past what you expected the game to be so you can appreciate what it actually is, this game is not for you.

Personally, this game is one of my three favorite casual games, right along with Farming Simulator and Minecraft.  I love shooters, adventure games, MMOs, and traditional RPGs also, but when it comes to relaxing, simple fun, I love this title.

Where to start? I am giving it a thumbs up as it has the most played time in my Steam library presently, above Skyrim and Borderlands 2, even though it is definately not as good a game, and I am not the type of person to play something for that long and then eventually give it a thumbs down. The more you play, the more you see little things that seem so obvious to have been included, but are not. The developers, seem to be patching the game and adding content, but it is slow. Hopefully with further patches it will be worth the price.

The game is polished, in that it never once crashed on me, and I only encountered small glitches, most that benefited you, such as removing a hydroponics tray in your base after adding a plant, and having the plant still grow fine, and being able to hit the melee button followed by the jetpack and moving a lot faster than sprinting allows.

Some of the things that are the most frustrating about the game include:

- Even though animals and plants are procedurally generated, the majority of land animals are either two or four legs, with various random features. But other than this the only "alien" type creates that I have discovered are ones that look like plants, that mostly jump. Where are the six, eight or more legged creatures? Snakelike ones? Blobs? Surely alien life would be a LOT more varied than this? In regards to swimming and flying animals, they seem even less varied, and in all my time playing, I only really encountered 3 different types of flying animals, with small batlike ones, and large phallic looking ones the most common.

- Although the planets are procedurally generated, everything still looks the same. It feels like every planet is the same size, there is no change in gravity (surely this is a variable in the code, as the gravity doesn't work until you are close to the planets surface so should be easy to randomise?), and it seems like each planet is created by randimising the terrain, colouring this with a two or three different colours then adding features specific to that planet, like floating half domes, spires, craters or other rock features, and then dotting these across the landscape, interspersed with discoverable features like camps and buildings. In the end it feels like each planet you go to is just different coloured rolling hills, with features dotted in every 500m or so. Once you have first landed and looked around, you have really seen everything, as flying halfway around the world to land again, you will feel like you have landed in the same spot. I have never encountered, forests, jungles, plains, swamps, large lakes, running water, rivers, waterfalls, large cliffs in all my play time.
Worse than this though is the caves. Once you have seen one you HAVE seen them all. Where is the randomness in this? Where is the discovering that amazing spot or feature in the game?

- The combat in the game is awful, with no real purpose. they could have just left this out of the game entirely and it would be much the same. The sentinels that are your only real "enemies" besides the odd hostile creature, and they are more annoying than anything else. Space combat is okay for the first couple of times, then it is just tedious, really just being, turn, shoot, turn, shoot. The HUD doesn't accurately tell you where enemies are located, so to find them, you really just scroll the mouse around searching till you find it. Where is the hostile aliens? The big hostile creatures that are hard to kill? The hostile packs of animals?

- Even though for the first couple of hours the scanning feature gets you into scanning and looking for wildlife, after a while there is no real reason to do it beyond getting the achievements. The game is really about exploration and discovery, but most of the time you are just collecting materials to make Warp Cells, warping into systems, and then warping again. 90% of the systems I visited I was there for 10 secs, before warping again, without landing on or exploring any planets at all. Why not reduce the distance to the galactic centre, and everytime you warp into a system, you need to explore to find something that is stopping your warp drive from working. Maybe an artifiact, animal, plant, landscape item?

- There REALLY needs to be some sort of bad luck protection when getting blueprints for things. Over 230 hrs of playtime as of writing this, and still don't have the blueprints for 2 of the Warp Drive Upgrades, Photonix Core, or the Atlas Pass V2. Only got the Atlas Pass V3 after 125hrs or so. You just get the same blueprints over and over aagin, and after a while you just give up.

Some of the things I think this game just needs (which may come in future patches) include:

- Spaceship building. It is clear that there are base ships with different decorations applied from the varied ships you see land at space stations, so all these are in the game. Why not after buying a certian type of base ship you can then customise it with your own colours, decorations and accoutrements?

- Really needs to have more things that people can add through the Workshop. The basis is there for truly random stuff, but allow others to create different things for animals, plants, landscape features, spaceship items, base items, spacestation items etc.

- Why not have procedurally generated instanced caves, buildings, space stations, carriers etc, with decent combat to get rewards at the end. I know the game was meant to be massive with no loading screens (but the warp animations, black hole animations, and teleport animations ARE loading screens, they just don't say that), but instanced areas that are randomised wouldn't hurt this idea too much. This could be tied in with warping into a system and having to explore to find what is interupting your Warp Drive, with an animal or plant deep in an instanced cave doing this, requiring you to kill  or scan it to be able to warp again. Have random "stories" for each system leading to you to this end. Shouldn't be too hard to add random story to the game, so that you warp into a system, have some various quests (scan a specific animal, scan 5 plants, collect some of this, kill this, kill that, find this etc) which lead you through the planets in the system and allow you to explore more, which is what the game is about. Allowing people to make workshop content for this also, so unlike the carriers and space stations in game presently, they are actually different and random.

- Needs more randomised content, so some of the items I mentioned above will appear in game (jungles, forests, plains, cities etc.

In the end, if this game actually had a bit more randomness to the landscape, making it feel rewarding to actually explore, and more story to encourage you to explore each system you landed into it would be amazing. Learning a bit more about the races of the system, rather than just that Gek's are traders, Vykeen are warriors, and Korvax are hive entities would have been great. Being able to sit at a waterfall that you have found, explore everything in an abandoned carrier, fighting your way into a space station or city/town, piecing together lore etc......

Each system you landed in would be truly random, with you having to do truly random things to get you Warp Drive working, and exploring more, which is what it is meant to be all about.

While giving a thumbs up, I still have missgivings, mostly tied to frustration on what this game could have been.

I don't leave reviews very often, but I felt that I needed to for this game.

At the moment, I'm 4 hours into it. Impossibly, until today I not only had not played No Man's Sky, but I had also managed to avoid any spoilers or gameplay videos. Like everyone else, I was hyped for its release, and I didn't want anything to possibly risk my pristine experience of this game. Of course, I couldn't avoid hearing about the massive disappointments, but that's it. Though I preordered it, I was stuck having to wait until I got a computer that could handle it, and that finally happened today. In a sense, I'm glad I waited, because it's no longer at the center of so much media attention, and I feel I can be a bit more objective as I go into it. Also, my first experience will be with whatever updates they've released for it, so at least I'll get to experience a later version.

Though I'm not at all far in the game at all, I just want to share what my first 4 hours have been like. In summary, they've consisted of dying, dying, and some more dying. I started on survival mode and the game dropped me smack dab in the middle of a frozen planet. As I figured out the controls and the way the different parts of the game worked, both my hazard suit and life-support system depleted pretty quickly, and I died and had no resources with which to get back on my feet. I had no idea what to do, and I didn't want to search for help online, or restart my game to hope for a better planet. I wanted to survive here, and I wanted to succeed.

The next 4 hours after that consisted of little tiny attempts to run in each direction, to plot out as much of the area as I could before dying. Little by litle I learned, and got better. I figured out what sparse materials I needed to prioritize to recharge and repair my equipment, and managed to survive a little bit longer each time. Just now, I finally finished the longest of these excursions - the one that finally got me to my ship - and let me tell you, my heart is still beating. Never before has a game given me such an experience. I feel like I just came out on top of some major life challenge, that I would tell friends and family about for years.

Very few games have ever managed to give me an experience like this, and that's why I needed to come straight here and give it some credit. True, I haven't even touched space travel and apparently that's where people's criticisms really come into play - but such an incredible experience over the course of 4 hours? I've bought and played indie games that run about the same length, so if this was the entire game I would be cool. BUT IT'S NOT THE ENTIRE GAME, AND THERE'S MORE.

No matter how disappointing the rest is, the fact that it was already amazing, and still has more to offer, at the very least puts it towards the top of the most memorable games I've ever played. I look forward to continuing, and playing resource management/survival in real life as I balance my NMS levels and my grad school grades.

This is a complicated game.

When I heard about this game coming out, I was completely psyched and ready for it, but it was years before it was planned to be released.

They later gave a release date and I was excited for it alllll over again. 

They announced the game on steam and put it up for early purchase, and I purchased it. 

The game was released while I wasn't home, and I kept hearing about all sorts of people were crashing or couldn't play the game, but I found out it was because their rigs couldn't handle it, which mine could. I got home, and began playing the game.

The tutorial had me scared out of my mind, stranded on the planet running out of life support and struggling with radioactivity. I didn't wanna go anywhere that I wouldn't be able to see my ship in fear of being eaten by a giant space worm or being attacked by a giant robot or something, but I got my ship into the air. I've now been to tons of planets, tons of galaxies and have a bit over 1 million credits, and I still use the beta ship. 

To be completely honest: I enjoyed this game, I enjoy this game, and I will continue to enjoy this game. I played it a ton when it was first released, and I started playing it again about a month ago because of the new release. 

True, it would be much better and I would enjoy it a lot more if I could have my friend flying through space with me,  but that doesn't make it so I stop playing. 

True, I felt like I was running out of ideas, doing the same thing over and over again, but the new update changed everything.

I now have a new purpose for playing this game, a reason to keep going. Sure, there's always the end goal of reaching the center (and the goal of avoiding spoilers for those who actually TRIED reaching it, instead of following the atlas storyline like I have been. Before the update, there was always the goal of collecting all the resources I needed from a planet by landing on it once at a random station, and items marked as "rare" were found everywhere, such as plutonium, so I could waste whatever I wanted on whatever I wanted to do because I could just land at any planet and collect 200 plutonium in about 12 seconds. After that, I would craft a few warp thingies and started off towards the next atlas objective.

Now, after playing the new update for a bit, I still haven't chosen a planet for a house. I now have the goal of finding the perfect planet with all the materials that I want in the right galaxy that has no atmospheric issues, other than life support dropping but that happens anyway. 

I've also been collecting more money, as I've found the type of ship that I want that usually has the same specific price. Every now and then when I think I have enough money I'll wait at a station for a bit, but realize I either don't have enough for the perfect ship or that I'm in an empty galaxy with not too much commotion, which is perfectly fine with me because it means less pirates.

There's also the endgoal of getting a frigate. That is going to come much later for me and once I get my perfect ship and find a home, I can start grinding for money for a frigate, which I will take with me to the center of the galaxy (assuming I ever finish the atlas storyline).

After all this ranting and my story, if you're still here, well, yes. I would recommend this game.

The game was released as a sort of "pre-release", almost enough to the point where it could have been an early access game and no one would hate on it constantly, but there is more coming. I almost gave up on it but eventually went back when the new update came because I knew it meant they were still going, still working on it.

Sure, maybe they'll even make a way for multiplayer to work.

TL:DR = If you're fine with grinding for stuff, then you'll have fun. The way you have to look at this game though, is a game about exploration. Sure, grinding is a big part of it, but if you look at it in the sense that you're looking for some cool, new planets and cool new creatures (although a lot of them look like demented kangoroos), you won't really run out of excitement. Most of the planets before the update were just either deserts or snowstorms, but I believe the update contained something about terrain reformations, and there seem to be different types of planets now.

Anyway, I enjoyed the game but don't have very many hours into it because I've been busy a lot, but making this review made me remember what I enjoyed about this game.

If you do purchase it, congratulations, there's more to come and you could really enjoy it. If you don't decide to purchase it, maybe check back on it in a while, they might've added another update.

Starbound + Elite 3 + Noctis (whatever version was the last version) == No Man's Sky.  If you want more than that then you will be disappointed.  This, however, was exactly what I wanted it to be.  
This is not a space battle sim, it's more like an intergalatic walking sim; you're dropped randomly into the universe on a planet and just told to fix your ship and then go see what's out there.  The planets are all fairly similiar out of necessity (otherwise only about 1/10000 start points would allow you to get off world), the plants and animals all do seem to run together, but dispite that it's still a wonderful game.  
It's the only surface-to-sky space sim I've seen that actually works.  Many attempts at this have been made and all of them have failed in some vital way.  This succeeds.  
The hatred seems to mostly come from early adopters, backers, and others whose expectations could never, ever have been met any ways.  Maybe that's the fault of the developer, I don't care at all about that.  It's fun, thoughtful, immersive, huge, stunning, lonely, all the things it should be.  It's also sort of over priced.  
If you go into it knowing what you're getting you'll enjoy it.  If you go into it thinking you're getting the last game you'll ever want to play, you won't.
Get it on sale if you can, but certainly get it.
9/10.  A standout game on Steam.

I bought in early, and despite the known problems with the game, I have enjoyed it a lot.   The planets do have commonality and look the same -- until they don't.   The animals are all the sameish -- until they aren't.   The three species of sentients are all a little clone-ish, until one of them looks at you and you just have to laugh,  and the game is visual, fun and usually relaxing.

With the update, No Man's Sky has taken on new fun and dimension, but I'm at a standstill with some aspects.  I haven't gotten past Atlas 1 Pass, and I don't CARE if it won't get me much of anything; at this point I just want to get it!  So there are some challenges to pursue.

Your mindset is the only thing that will make or break the game.  The graphics are exceptional, and some planets turn out being a delightful place to take a stroll and gather resources.  Befriend an animal or 2, and they may accompany you on the jaunt like puppies on a walk.  Set your own goals for the best experience:  on this planet I will gather all the species; in this star system I will visit every satellite and planet; I will do nothing until I find and mine 100 units of aluminum.  etc  

As for the negatives:  no one seems to have consulted a botanist, zoologist, geologist, astronomer. . . it is sad to think of the missed opportunities because the science that was mangled.  

The premise of travellng a galaxy and seeing strange new things was a huge overreach by Hello Games.  If it was repackaged as exploring  expanses and ecologies of one world  it would have been more reasonable, logical, and would have a far better storyline.   So if you have the imagination to make your own game of it, No Man's Sky is worth it.

I've waited a long time to give a review. I knew of this game fom the first major announcment years ago, Pre-Ordered It and was caught up in the hype along with everybody else. And in hindsight those expectations we all set were ridiculous. But we do have high expectations for games nowadays, we've had such great games over the past decade If we try and compare it to the 90's and early 2000's, at least in terms of size/scale, depth of stories and graphics quality. The rate of growth has been incredibly fast, and with stuff like VR a complete possibility now which we dreamed of as kids, it seems like anything should be possible...

And this is where No Man's Sky comes in. I know that I have always wanted a game like this, planet and space exploration, traveling farther than anyone else, seeing what no one else has ever seen before, surviving in unknown hostile environments, finding aliens and lost technology, dinosaurs and sky sharks, space wars between factions... The list could go on. We thought we finally had the ultimate game, we all over-hyped each other thinking we might be able find the "Space Whale" in the never-ending black abyss of this procedurally generated universe.

Right before the game finally launched, amidst all the videos and game predictions/possibilities, I heard something inspiring. Someone said that we are all going to end up hating this game because the hype we built up for it. That it could never live up to the expectations we have. And the best way to calm down the expectations for this game and all games that get over-hyped before release. Is to imagine the game to have come out 10 years ago or even 20. What would people have thought of the game then... 10 years ago this Game would have been in to the top 5 for sure. But 20 years ago, when one of the best games that everyone knew and talked about was let's say Super Mario 64. If we could've had No Man's Sky launch back then, It would've been the best thing ever.

So I put myself in this mindset. Ignored what everyone else was saying about it, good or bad. I calmed down, and waited for the game to release. And of course downloaded it within seconds of it finally coming out. I had days scheduled off work and everything, I was ready to devote as much time as I could to this new universe. I played for hours, and then more hours, before I knew it I had over 190 hours in the game. This rarely happens for me, I get bored with most games after a while, but I kept coming back to NMS. Eventually I had to take a break, I did get a little burnt out on it after a while, but I found it no more repetitious than any other game, there was enough new stuff for me to find or explore that I was sufficed. So in between my busy schedule, full-time job, family, and school. I do find myself still playing NMS.

And my favorite part is seeing what is to come. Hello Games told us from the beginning that there would be updates, game-changing updates at that. NMS was and still is a huge revolution for the game industry in my opinion. I like to think of it as the blueprint or "foundation" to what could be... I believe that with time this game has the opportunity to become what we all wanted it to be, it has gotten better and will get better, either from the dev's or the modding community. And if nothing else it will be the inspiration for someone else to improve upon, and to create this ultimate game that we all want, that we know eventually we will have...

No Man’s Sky, at it’s core, just wants you to walk around it’s planets, say “oooh” and head off. It wants to simulate the feeling of finding something unknown, something mysterious and understanding it a tiny bit. It wants to let you jump into a sci-fi novel’s cover and not come back.

Instead, No Man’s Sky’s curve is so gentle, so obviously pushing you in the direction of “existing slightly better than you did before” instead of “upgrading until you can’t upgrade no-more, congratulations you rule over man, sky, and weird little crab creatures, you have won the game.”

I mean, sure, you can try doing that, and it is possible to get a Very Good Ship™, but this is not the way No Mans Sky wants you to play, despite the triple-A nature of the marketing.

No Man’s Sky, just wants you to walk.

No Mans Sky is an over-promised and under-delivered game. We must never forget that and always acknowledge it. 

But it's also fun and I've clocked up quite a few hours and haven't lost interest yet.

Let me say first that the procedurally generated galaxy is amazing, but alone would not have been enough to keep me interested - it's very clever what they've done, but things really do start to look the same after a while - after a couple of galaxies you've seen probably 98% of what there is to offer. That, and the  modding community have really brought to light the shortcomings of the vanilla game, if you care to look into it. 

Having said that I am still finding surprises as I play on (not big surprises, but surprises nonetheless). Like last night I was attacked by a man-eating gopher with headlights. 

But the thing that really draws me back is the gameplay - there's a lot of fun challenges in making it to the center of the galaxy, searching for resources, managing inventories, finding/upgrading tech etc. So really (for me) that is the saving grace, even though IMO it would probably been second to the procedural universe development in Sean Murray's eyes. 

And lets admin it - Hello Games have really set somewhat of a bar here. Space games can only get (procedurally) better from this point. 

So, GG Hello Games. Let's hope you keep fulfilling your promises. 

And yes I can recommend the game as it is now, It's fun, and I do have faith HG will finish what they've started. You should probably wait for a sale though :)

With the limited experience I have with this game I can say with confidence this:

-If you are coming here looking for a multiplayer experience, you will be disappointed.
-If you are coming here looking for a cohesive story line or enriching campaign, you will be disappointed.
-If you are coming here looking for a game that will make you say "Woah, how the f*ck did they make something of this    scale and with these graphics", you will be VERY VERY HAPPY.

This game does have some downfalls, such as repetitive gameplay, tough progression, constantly gathering resources to fuel your ship, etc. However, this game is much more playable than I originally anticipated. I purchased this game over the winter sale, simply because I thought it looked amazing, even with the poor reviews. I can happily tell you that I am not at all upset about my purchase. This game has given me several moments where I fly out of the vast planet that I was gathering resources from into space, look around, and just say "Holy sh*t. This place is huge." This feeling is exactly what Hello Games wanted each and every buyer to feel, and so, in this way, I feel they accomplished their goal.

For those of you looking for an analogy, this game feels as if you are put in first person perspective in the space stage of Spore. I'm pretty sure I even recognize some sounds (not really but you can imagine some). Establishing multiple bases, buying freighters to ship goods to other systems to get the best price, etc. all have parallels to Spore, but this game goes one step further, allowing the player to hop out of their spaceship at any time in order to actually explore the planets they visit. 

In conclusion, if you purchase this game with the intent of it filling your certain niche of games and providing you with everything you've ever wanted, you will be sorely disappointed and will miss out on an opportunity to enjoy a fantastic game. With that in mind, my advice to everyone that purchases this game is to throw away your pre-conceived notions about the game and just simply sit down and try it out. If you enter this game throwing away all of the negative reviews you have read and all the criticisms that you will subconciously be looking for throughout playing, you are left with what the developers truly wanted: A game that makes you sit back, look at all of the stars around you, and say, "Holy sh*t. Where do I start."

tl/dr : This game is comparable to Spore if you were put in first person on the Space Stage. While it has flaws, drop the negative reviews you have read, buy this on sale, and try it for yourself. It is truly an awe inspiring game.

Haters gonna hate. A lot of people are still holding a huge grudge against this game for reasons that, in my opinion, have very little to do with the game at hand and lot more to do with all of Hello Games' pre-release tomfoolery. People are also expressing a lot of dissapointment with the game's lack of adherence to rigidly defined categories, which I actually see as a big plus. If you're going to break new ground and blur old categories together, you have to expect that there's going to be some misses with the hits. That's just the downside of taking risks, something that I think the makers have done admirably.

With over 100 hours played, and a huge resurgence of interest since the game-changing foundation update, here are what I see as some key pros/cons:

CONS:
- god awful navigation of your ship near planet surfaces, still - it floats, speeds up, and slows down based on unclear obstacles and/or altitude factors
- massive, but meaningless space stations - you spend far more time walking around than doing anything in these, and all traders have more or less the exact same thing - the teleporter has added some use to these, but IMo the expereince still needs to be tightened up a lot
- clunky interstellar navigation - again, it feels very floaty - I feel like they sacrificed perofrmance for a sense of vastness

PROS: 
- a truly brutal surival mode (post-foundation) with vicious enemies both on- and off-world, constant resource management, cruel planets, and just lots of general carnage. I've died 30+ times in 20 hours, compared to 7 in 80 pre-foundation.
- multi-system resource gathering - If you want to build up a base, you're going to have to travel far and wide looking for the elements you need. Even when you find a planet with the resource you need, you may have to do a lot of hunting.
- a promising, nascent mission system - as you hire underlings for your base, they send you on wild goose chases to upgrade technologies and base components. I find these fun, and providing a bit of structure that the earlier versions of the game lacked, when I want it
- a very slow upgrade system - I don't want to be murdering everything in two hours. I like that things take a while.
- related to the last point, the opportunity to ramp up personal challenges over time - I tried attacking a fugutive ship on survival mode early on, and promptly had my ass handed to me. That was a 1-star enemy, labelled "mostly harmless." I don't know how high they go, but I'm looking forward to finding out.
 
There are obviously a ton of other things people comment on, such as the tediousness of resource gathering (con) or the game's general beauty (pro). I just wanted to comment on a few things that have kept me interested in the game. All I would say if you're considering buying it, is disregard the extracurricular hype, and see if the features of the game itself are appealing to you (it's only going to get better with future patches).

The foundation update was a step in the right direction. Looking forward to future updates. Really hoping to see freighter/starship construction soon. However, even that would not be enough, at the very least there needs to be conflict.

I would recommend randomly spawning "strategic points" that signal players within a reasonable distance, causing a "capture-the-flag/base" style combat with a hefty reward or prestige for the victors. Preferrably with faction vs faction ad infinitum, or species vs species vs species with all players proportionally assigned to each species.

Another idea is to have the sentinels play a more fundamental role. Instead of simply throwing drones around to keep tourists from picking all the flowers, try turning them into a full blown existential threat. Give them bases, home-planets, give them bigger, badder drones. Set them out to conquer the galaxy, let player's reconquer systems from the sentinels.

All in all, I've found sentinel hunting and pirating to be the funnest part of the game, as they are the only real challenges to the game so far. However, I will admit the outpost puzzles can be fun too. Now, I've gotten to the point where I can take down sentinel starships incredibly easily. The game gets rather boring at that point. 

Sentinel starships need better flight patterns, their turns are unnecessarily wide. Also, please remove the speed limit zones during space battles and around space stations, I would rather die a hundred times learning not to fly into objects rather than wait two minutes trying to dock at a space station, or four minutes trying to save a freighter from pirates on the other side of the system.

The speed limits within a planet's atmosphere are understandable. However, I have noticed a few bugs after the update, when entering a planet at max speed (when the atmosphere around the hull ionizes) and upon getting as close as possible to the ground, my starship begins moving incredibly slow, almost coming to a stop with no ability to turn due to the ionization-effect continuing longer than it should. Essentially, it looks like I'm a meteor hanging above the ground not moving. Also, there have been times when I have landed my starship and I have been thrown out of it rather than placed on the ground in front of it.

All in all, this game still has great potential. I recently saw the inside of an Atlas Pass v3 locked room and was sorely disappointed to see nothing of import. However, recongizing in-game structures, I saw the capacity to add more rooms, keeping my fingers crossed for now.

Reviews.175860:
Bought this game as part of the Winter Sale. I'd been leery, because of all the negative reviews. However, it was on sale, had updated, and I'd really wanted this game before reading the reviews.

It took me awhile to get into the groove. Heck, it took me a half an hour to realize how to even enter the game. Had to read a discussion board to realize what I was doing wrong. But once I was in, oh...

Oh this was what I was looking for. 

Maybe not the attack by the ferocious winter weather dinos or the eerie looking brain crab. But walking along, seeing the animals, trying to feed them or scare them off, discovering new plants, rocks, trees, mining for gold and iridium, looting jettisoned drop boxes, investigating abandoned outposts, investigating unabandoned outposts, slowly (oh god, so slowly) learning new words, navigating how to fight pirates (why are they shooting at me?! I got nothing in the hulll... Oh, right, I just mined a lot of asteroids...). And that was just in the one system. Then once I got out there, there was more.

Now, is it perfect? Oh no. I'm terrible at this. I get lost. I get confused in the caves. I manage to bypass the starbases. Personally, I'm glad I got a base way the heck back near the start, because I'm still fumbling through on the way out there. I'll probably move it forward when I have a few more skills under my belt. 

Gotta mention, love the bases, the freighters, the added storage. I mean, it's all new to me, but given how much difference it makes to me, a new player, I can only imagine how much it means to those who are old hands at it.

As for mods.... yes, I wish this had more mod features. One of the things I love about steam is how easy it makes to add and delete mods. I love seeing the brilliance of other people. And this game could use people who love making new things, new trees, new plants, new ruins, etc. I mean, there are mods out there and I intend to try them. But for now it's been fun.

I will mention here that this game reminds of a roguelike space merchant game called Prospector. It's got similarities in the option to visit new systems with loads of planets (some of which might kill you) and (except the universe there is randomly generated through seed numbers). It's got differences - and not just in the visuals. But I can see where the inspiration for this game grew from similar games previous to it and it's really kind of awesome.

As for multiplayer? Personally, I can live without it, especially if its the kind of PvP thing that I know some would want. I'm not interested in PvP at all. At all. But I'd love to see the opportunity to build merchant fleets, maybe patrol fleets, or exploratory fleets. Or even just bars and stores and bases where friends could hang out. There is a ton of potential here. I mean, just an amazing amount. But given how antisocial I am, I'd like to be able to toggle the multiplayer off or select the options of how I want to run it for myself. Not that this is in the future per se, but the potential might be there.

I say this because Hello games has apparently been updating like mad and I anticipate we'll continue to see an expansion of what is already a vast universe - either through updates or DLC. I look forward to it. I also look forward to the possible evolutions in gaming this might inspire. 

So, down to the nitty gritty, would I recommend this game? Yes. Absollutely. I would recommend it for patient and mature people interested in exploration, soft puzzle solving, alien interactions, base building and sundry other possible experiences. I would not necessarily recommend this for those more interested in super fast paced games with lots of shooting and mayhem. 

Though, given the pirates and the wild animals, who knows...

Personally I love this game. I hope others will also enjoy it.

I didn't buy it when it released. I rarely purchase a game when it is new. Since I play games on a PC, instead of a console, I get most of my games through online retailers such as Steam. I am glad I waited. The frustration of those who were early "investors" put me on guard.  When I read the reviews and articles about the problems, I was content to wait. So when the winter sales of 2016 arrived, I added No Man's Sky to my collection.

As of today, I am 26 hours into the game. I have started two games with slightly different play styles. The first game was about getting off of the starting planet as quickly as possible and experience multiple planets. The second game was slower paced and I have stuck around on each planet longer to see what it has to offer.

No Man's Sky is not a game that holds your hand and tells you how to play. You are free to go about the storyline. So far, I haven't found much of a plot to the story. There are some threads you can follow. As I explore more, I may find more substance. At this point, though, it is an open ranging experience. For people who like a solid story to carry you through a game, don't start looking here. I like open world experiences, though. I have enjoyed both styles of game play. And spent too many hours at one time playing through the slower paced style.

It is a pretty game. The planets are nicely rendered. The plant and animal life get a little redundant (at the "level" I am playing). There are some hard to achieve objectives. And there is a LOT to see. The planets are huge. And then the galaxy is expansive. The core "goal" of the game is to reach the galactic core. For people who have to reach the finish line, it is possible to do it quickly. At least I have heard of people doing it quickly. But this game is meant to be taken at a slower pace. The universe is meant to be explored.

No Man's Sky is solitary. You character interacts with other species of intelligent life. But there is extremely limited multi-player interaction. This is not a game for the social gamer. If you want to squad up with 3 of your buds and take on space pirates, you need to check out a different game. This is an introverts dream, though. You can explore peacefully without the constant chatter of a chat stream. You can interact with programmed bots that allow you to choose how you will respond. You have little markers that let you know that someone else was here before you. You leave little markers that let others know you have been here. But there is no real social interaction with another living soul.

This is a Trekkers game, not a galaxy far, far away. This is not a game of exciting twists and turns. It plays out slowly. It is more exploration than adventure. This is Star Trek: The Next Generation at its purest (without the need to inject romance/intrigue/action). This is an effort to go where no one has gone before. It is a mind game more than a button mashing game. You cannot experience this game waiting for the next bad guy to pop up. You can experience this game anticipating what is over the horizon or when you break through the atmosphere.

Hello Games took a beating in reviews because they didn't deliver the game that gamers were expecting. I sort of let my expectations go away. I entered the game with a bit of trepidation that it would be a waste of time. But I have enjoyed it. It has turned into one of those "just 10 more minutes" kind of games. My wife is probably a little miffed that it consumed as much time as it did. And I will be backing off of it now that the extraordinary schedule of the holidays are passed. But I will be coming back to it again and again.
Reviews.175878:
An honest, hype/hate free review:

Let me preface this by first saying that A: I got this game at a *steep* discount, and B: I use a whole suite of mods. 
That being said, I like this game. A lot. I recommend it, but not for $60. And the mods I use are mostly for graphical performance optimization that don't affect the core game-play experience. That part came later, as you'll see. I didn't get No Man's Sky until after the Foundations update. By then the over-hype, and ensuing backlash had (mostly) passed. I had watched a few Let's Plays, and I felt like I was ready. (read: I had low expectations.)

First, the bad:

The first time I started a new vanilla game, it took nearly 3 minutes to load, and the low FPS made the game nearly unplayable. I have a very good gaming PC, so this was new in my experience. This is where most people would have stopped and got a refund. To be fair, I spent most of the first day testing different mods to see what worked, or broke the game. (I highly recommend looking at Nexusmods.com) The optimization mods helped keep the game looking good, but brought the load time down from 3 minutes to 38 seconds. Tolerable at least.

My (good) Experience:

Once I got the game running smooth like butter, I did what any good tester would do, and tried my best to break it. You see, I had heard that most of the game-play was grinding. Grinding for money, resources for upgrades, for inventory expansions, etc. So the first thing I did was eliminate all of that to see if there was still a game left. After a bit of hacking, I started a new game with all inventor slots unlocked, all crafting recipes known, and 100 million units (money). Now you might say that it made the game stupid-easy, but I still had to find and collect the resources I needed. This way, I was still forced to explore. And I'm glad I did. You see, I could have just given myself unlimited warp fuel, and high-tailed it for the galactic center (the 'end' of the game) but I had already watched a video of 'the end' of the game and I wasn't in a hurry to reach it.

No. The hidden gem of this game is in the exploring. Once you've gotten the hang of surviving the basic elements of the weather, and the knack of dealing with the odd pirate attack, it's less about the pitched excitement of danger and combat, and more about seeing the sights, making discoveries, meeting aliens, and learning about the alien backstories and language, which is my favorite part. I like the varying pace of the game. Mostly peaceful, with excitement sprinkled in when you least expect it. Like going for a bike ride in the park, and then every so often the bike briefly turns into a bear.

I was able to get to, and focus on this aspect of the game quickly (within a couple hours) by eliminating the busywork of grinding. (And I won't sugarcoat it, the grind is real.) The grind serves to pad gameplay time, but I don't feel it adds to the experience in a meaningful way. BUT! you can still enjoy the game with the grind, just at a slower pace.

I was trying to see how fast I could get to the point where the -core- gameplay stopped being fun. But after over 25 hours (at time of writing) in a couple marathon sessions, I haven't found it. Sure, a lot of the locations have that copy-pasta feel to them, but it never stopped being engaging for me. Even if I started the game with the best ship and weapon, and all the upgrades from the word go, already knowing how the game 'ends', I would still have a blast jet-setting around and meeting people, and seeing things, claiming a home planet and building a base. (The last part, coming with the new update, bringing a whole other new, good, dimension to the game.)

Ultimately, I like the game. A lot! But I had to do a TON of exceptional things to get there, and that shouldn't be required of the average player. Which is a shame. Because at it's heart NMS is a fantastic gem. But it's mired by a lot of rough that you have to get through to see it. I can only hope that with future updates, these core problems may get addressed. As it is, my review is, like it's current rating, Mixed. But I still recommend it because I think it's worth a chance. This game needs more positive reviews to off-set the negative, vocal minority.


TL;DR: Good game at heart. Has (fixable) technical issues. KNOW what kind of game you're getting into. Don't pay full price ($60).

Do not buy this game if you want a high intensity, "shoot em up," competitive, action game.  You will not like it.
