I work in an Emergency Room and I find the game play an immersing and relaxing break from my work place.  I also enjoy trekking, travel, science, and reading about the same. Multiplayer would be nice, or at least the ability to meet up and track a friend so you both explore together like co-op play. But in regards to the game overall, well... here we go. Was it "the marketing team that screwed up"? No. Let's be honest... It's a small shop, like REALLY small. Or at least it was at the time of release. There was no marketing "team" like there would be at EA Games, Ubisoft, Sony, or any other large corporation. This was a handful of guys that came together to create and release a video game. So all these claims that it was anyone else's fault is just people grasping at straws trying to ignore the ugly truth. Every video that I watched leading up to the release of this game involved Sean Murray, and Sean Murray ONLY. There was no commercial on TV that showed false gameplay footage, and there were no misleading posters or ads. Sean went on small interviews, talk shows, etc. and discussed the game. "Sean, will I be able to ______" and he answered "yes". That's what truly bothers me. The game was released and we found that all those claims were actually false. I even scheduled time off from work months in advance, just so I could play this when it was released. I was expecting missions/quests, stealing or interacting with freighters, and earning some type of good standing with an alien race, just like Sean said I'd be able to do. But somehow that wasn't possible, the game simply didn't line up with what I was told. By the end of that first day I felt like I was playing a game still in beta. Think about it. Most of us have played games still in Alpha/Beta and that's exactly how it works: you pay full price, play the game as-is, and then you wait for the full content to be added later on down the road. Many times that content completely changes the game in a good way, allowing you to do things that you couldn't before. Well... that's No Man's Sky. The game was released and I could fly around, collect resources and... actually that's it. Now there's a "Foundation Update" where they added content in which you can interact with freighters, build a small base, and a few other things. Great! But... this game came out 4 months ago, why wasn't this in the initial release? That's because the game is in Beta. Wait, it's not? It sure feels like it.

At the end of my first day of playing, I had a moment of reflection. I stopped for a second and thought to myself, I just spent $60 on this. I had also just wasted a perfectly good vacation day. Did I feel enlightened? Did I feel like I had just played the greatest game of 2016? No, no, no, and... no. My only consolation was when I checked the reviews on Steam, just to see if maybe I was missing something. Maybe I just didn't play enough yet, or maybe I was doing something wrong? Boy was I not alone... Not only was I not alone, there were THOUSANDS of others that shared my same frustration and disappointment. Sure, there were a few thumbs up reviews and the "I think the game is great" kind of posts, but they were vastly outnumbered. VASTLY. Even to this day, almost 5 months after, the game is still "Overwhelmingly Negative" on Steam. If you're thinking of buying a game, terms such as "overwhelmingly negative" isn't what you want to see. But that's No Man's Sky. Go ahead, scroll through the other reviews. It's OK. You'll find long rants of dislike, moments of sorrow, and claims of regret from thousands of fellow gamers, much like this one. Click the "buy" button if you dare, and join the community of Beta testers.

Purchased on sale after the 1.1 update without having read the hype and found a fun, survival game. Exploring planets for resources is the core of the game and the planets have a fair degree of variability and there is plenty to build and construct with resources although continually having to find resources for ship engines, guns an life support gets a bit tiring.

While the game is fun it lacks depth and realism. Each system has a single, very simplistic space port and trading is extremely limited. The galaxy to all intents and purposes does not exist because you can only see a handful of stars close to you and navigating large distances is utterly impossible. This would make a base useless but to fix this they added a magical teleporter to allow you to move from whichever spaceport you are at to your base (and your ship teleports too!).

This game is in a similar vein to Astroneer and Kerbal Space program but whereas these make fun of their inconsistencies and cartoon-like nature, No Man's Sky takes it all seriously which unfortunately does not work too well when the game is so unrealistic and inconsistent. Hopefully things will improve in future updates, the game has a lot of promise, but at the moment it is very clearly an early release game which should be priced as such but which may turn out to be something great if it can add more depth and realism.

I will say that post "The Foundation Update" No Man's Sky is well worth it's cost. It can never live up to the hype and the lies that were spread about it by it's creator, but in it's current state it is a great game. Sure, if you don't get it on sale (near impossible) it seems expensive. People say you can buy three survival games for the same price. Really though, you can't buy anything that does it it does. It provides you with endless procedurally generated worlds full of weird creatures and interesting landscapes. The lore of the world is deep and interesting. It calls back to the weird cosmic new age philosophies that inspired me as a kid. The visuals are amazing.
I think the problem people have now is they do not know what the game is. They claim they don't like the end. Well the end is the same end that minecraft gave you. It's more of a meta self reflective journey that a lot of people don't like. Neither of these games is made to be beaten though. The genre almost never produces a story or an ending in the first place. Notch only really added the ending of minecraft to quiet down some of it's detractors.
These games are made to be experienced and that is pretty much it. The motivation behind sandbox games belongs to the player. Some people will play the game in order to max out their gear. Some people will try to build the best base, or fully explore a single planet. A few will go on to finish the game and wonder why they feel so unfulfilled. The answer is simple, in a sandbox style game the answer to the question "how do I win?" is "by having the most fun while playing," it is not a race to the finish like most other genres.
It still has a few bugs. On one of the planets I landed it there was really bad texture flickering, you still get annoying milestones every few minutes that seem more like a punishment than a reward, and your ship still auto ejects you when you land which can be deadly if you are not careful.
This is not a run and gun shooter, it's a very chill sandbox exploration and survival game with base building.
TLDR; Strip away the hype and the hate and the current state of the game is amazing. Great visuals, a relaxed world to explore, and amazing music.

Having played Elite, Frontier and First Encounters I always wished that there was more to explore - in this game there is. My experience has not been without its niggles. Exploring some of the question markers on planetary surfaces it soon becomes apparent that they are often generated 2 mins flight/walk time away and will disappear even if you revisit the location. It seems that control of thrust disappears during space flight - it is clear that to make the game more accessible there is heavy intervention in the flight controls during battles and near planetary surfaces.

I approached the game with low expectations  but I am really enjoying this game and I recommend it.

No Man's Sky is a game the majority shunned soon after release due to the lacking of teased gameplay options, at first putting me off purchasing NMS. No Man's Sky isn't for everyone, but it's fast becoming my 2nd place GOTY (sorry NMS--nothing will top Overwatch).  Does that mean it will win anyone of consequence's GOTY?  No.  It's not a perfect game.  Heck, it's not even a well-made or even finished game.  Some people might not even call it a game.  

But if you are the type of person who has dreamt of walking on exoplanets his whole life and exploring the vastness of space, then this game might fit you like a glove.

I didn't review the game the first chance I was able, because this really isn't a game you can get a sense of after 10 hours, maybe not even after 100 hours.  That isn't to say that you'll see all this new and exciting stuff 100 hours in, but you will feel a definite sense of progression--you little tiny ship that you started with is now a behemoth anchored with your freighter (an addition in the "foundation" update).  Survival is tough at first in, well, Survival mode, but now you know how to survive on the most unwelcoming heat-scorched or frozen worlds.

Many people have compared No Man's Sky to a puddle that stretches for miles (not deep, but very big), and there's a lot of truth in that.  If you don't like the first few hours, this game might not be for you--don't expect it to suddenly get better, though HG has done a LOT in the "foundations" update.  I think it's no conincidence the update is called "foundations", and you can't help but wonder how rushed the devs must have been to release the product in the state it was in, which is unfortunate.

That said, the update to me holds vast promise and potential, and as I currently like the game as stands, I can only be excited for the future.

No multiplayer?  I don't care.  I wouldn't want any, to be honest, the game doesn't need it--what, are you going to mine Emeril together?--but with the foundations update, we are starting to see the building blocks upon which the game will eventually be built.

This ABSOLUTELY should have been an early-alpha and NOT priced at triple AAA.  It's clearly not finished, but I am enjoying it immensely for what is already there, and look forward to what is to come.

Having played this game since day 1, I forced to keep myself being quiet about the game unless friends are asking me about it. It's very clear that HG did not deliver the game we all wanted to have and thought we would get after seeing the trailers, presentations etc.

Now, half a year later, we received a big fresh update and I tried as much as possible to mentally restart the game for me. This review is trying to give you a feeling of someone who enjoys video games, exploration and astronomy as the background layer for it.

If you expect competitive gameplay, don't buy it. If you are in for a long, dedicated quest line - don't buy this game.
If you need multiplayer to enjoy a game, please step away. Close this tab and move on.

If you are still here, you probably are a bit like me. I DO enjoy multiplayer, huge quest lines and competitive gameplay, but hell, I don't *need* it to enjoy playing a game. 
I expected long evenings in my space ship, freedom of exploring wild and rough planets and a grind-n-craft system to lead me to having a nice ship, base and gear. And this is what no man's sky offers, no more and no less.  
The game is far from being perfect and it's still only a good chunk of what we all want this to be, but from my perspective, the game is worth an upvote and will be even more on the future.
Don't let yourself be fooled by earlier votes. If you don't want to to spend your money here, it's perfectly okay. 
But if you spend 60$ on a battlefield or doom and play through the campaign in 12 hours to regret your spending, no man's sky offers a better money/time value.

I like this game, and I expect to love it in the future.

[h1] A lot of hate for a niche title.	[/h1]

Obviously this game is not for every buyer, but anyone who did a little bit of research beforehand should have known that going in. Yes, it was overhyped. Yes, it seemed far grander in the trailers than the player's first impression. Yes, the PC-port fiasco was a fiasco. But all of the 'lies' and 'broken promises' can really be tied to angry customers who shouldn't have purchased the game to begin with, and all of the supposed shotcomings of the game were well-stated pre-launch. I'm not mad at Hello Games for this game. I'm not even disappointed. I'm just incredulous at the general opinion of this game. All the anger and uproar really was not well-founded. I bought this game fully aware of what I was buying, and for the folks who can't say the same and pointed the finger of blame at HG, shame on you. If you're not responsible enough to manage your own expectations, you're setting yourself up for disappointment again and again. I'm relieved you got your money back.

Now, if you are easily immersed in a nonspecific, nonlinear storyline, enjoy casual, nondemanding gameplay, and enjoy working for occasionally really very rewarding exploration situations, look into this game. Don't buy it expecting visceral combat or endless excitement or a highly polished experience. This is a small-studio game with definite limitations. Occasionally, though, you find something truly breathtaking. And along the way you're bound to discover new and exciting situations. I wish it had broader appeal, but a game like this just can't possibly satisfy everybody's expectations.

I do still commend the team behind No Man's Sky. They really have done a fine job, regardless of how their dissatisfied consumer base feels. I wish, for the record, that there was a "Yes, I recommend this IF..." option. It's just not for everyone.

Reviews.176269:
I bought No Man's Sky just after its first major update, and have been playing it - a lot - while recovering from major surgery.  I'm really bored, but compelled, too. I'm compelled partly because I'm a game dev major and it's fascinating trying to figure out what went right, and what went wrong (so far) with this game.

There's so much potential to this game. It could be epic. But it's not because, at its core, the game is out of balance. The content provided by the devs in no way matches the vastness of the game universe and the potential for discovery. What is the point, I wonder, of providing a seemingly endless galaxy to explore, if you only provide enough unique dialogue, equipment upgrade, etc., for a much more limited game? In a word, this game lacks an overall story arc; it lacks game design. It's fun to be lost or aimless in space for a little while; but it's more fun when you get your bearings. By that time, though, boredom will have begun creeping in.

Positives:

*  It's a beautiful game a lot of the time. Kudos to the color theory expert on the team.

* The sound is good, although I find the Gek alien voices annoying.

* Scanning life forms on planets is a cool and fun idea. The game is not based soley on survival and crafting. Exploration has a purpose. That said, it's more of an inferred purpose; there seems to be no concrete objective related to it other than impressing Polo and getting units for everything you scan.

*  Being able to fly through space and land directly on planets is a lot of fun.  

* Base building is fun, but why can we have only one base? Why are the base sizes so limited?

* Being able to explore endless planets is a lot of fun, but just try getting back to a planet you like once you've strayed too far from it.

* Building up your vocabulary for the alien races you encounter is a very unique idea, but again, it's out of balance. By the time you build up even a small vocabulary, the game will have started repeating itself in every respect, so you'll be bored, and there's no real purpose that one can ascertain.

* The little number sequence puzzles are nice; sometimes overly simple, but that's okay. 

* The animal life is sometimes quite enchanting. Sometimes it seems as if Hieronymous Bosch meets Keith Haring



Negatives:

* There is no story whatsoever. There's no sense of what you're doing in this universe, who you are, why you're there, what you want. You play as an inferior being, apparently. One gets the sense, slowly, that he/she is chosen to fullfil some electro-spiritual quest for oneness in a sea of unbridled capitalism...  

* On every planet, regardless of the star system, everything is the same. The flora and fauna may be different, but the buildings, the dialogues, et al, all the same. There are no cities to encounter, which is really weird, and a huge oversight as far as I'm concerned. Cities or other gathering places (besides space stations) would add a whole new layer of depth to the game. Cities with people who might need help performing tasks. Give me a reason to seek out specific planets. Maybe this notion wouldn't work with the procedurally generated monotony.

* The Foundation update provided some goals for the player. But alas, these end all too soon. Your hirelings will, one by one, announce they've got nothing left to teach you. At this point the game becomes purely economic in scope. It's a really good start, though. It's hard to imagine playing this game without at least that.

* My status with the various races is endlessly increasing, but to no apparent end. Once I reached certain levels, there seems to be no higher I can go, and there are few, if any, benefits to my increasing status. The sad thing about this is that it remains one of the few goals left in the game after you've acquired all the blue prints and all of the formulas, and once you've exhausted all of the unique dialogue. The thing is, you get all of this stuff before you've even gotten to the blue or violet star systems, probably. You can look forward to those systems, but if they are anything like th Red and Green and Yellow star systems, they will only offer more identical experiences. The ships with Theta warp drives installed are really expensive if they have a reasonable number of storage slots. Even with a prettye big farming operation, it will take a while to raise the many millions one will need to buy a good ship. 

* The Atlas passes are too damn hard to find, and no clue is provided in the game as to how one might locate them. 

*Once you get the Atlas passes, after way, way too much effort, the reward is...voila!...more of the same stuff you find everywhere. The Atlas passes do not unlock any mysteries, any levels, any extra cool gear, or whatever else might be worthy of such a tedious and mysterious route to gaining the passes in the first place. 

* The UI is seriously slow and intrusive. It takes over the screen, and removes player control while the cinematic UI scenes are unfolding. However, drones can still attack you while you're trapped in a UI vortex from which there is no fast escape. Also, what is with the blinding white screen everytime we save a new location? Are we not doing enough damage to our vision by staring at the game screen so long in the first place? Everything UI and HUD needs to happen a lot faster. 


BUGS:

* When I teleport to my base, game play drags for several minutes. Same can happen if I load a former save from any location. My PC is a fairly powerful MSI gaming device wtih an i7 and lots of RAM, so it's hard to imagine that it's my machine causing the problem.

* When I return to my home planet and base, one of the ladders I placed to reach a second floor is always closed at the top. The only way I can deal with it is to delete and rebuild the ladder. Every time. 



All of the above notwithstanding, this is a really GREAT foundation for an epic game. I hope the developers will continue crafting this. They need to expand content and get a few quest lines in the game pronto. Adding these features will only enhance one's rambling and haphazard journey toward convergence. I haven't reached the end yet. Maybe it all becomes clear by that time. But there's a great danger I'll simply get too bored with the monotony of the game to ever get that far.

To begin, I'd like to make known that I played the game only after the 1.1 update, so my views might be slightly biased. That being said, I think the game was much better than people here have said. There are space battles (albeit, not huge, but large enough to have a reasonable risk of dying), options to either help or steal from freighters during battles, plenty of places to explore, and different options to play how you want to play. You can greatly improve a home base by collecting/building things for your team (which you create by exploring and meeting life forms), you can focus solely on exploring and mining, and/or get involved in pirating goods from other ships.

I view this kind of like a new Minecraft: you do what you want, you can build and explore, but there isn't necessarily a moment where you feel like you've beaten the game or in-depth quests. Going by this standard, I think the dev team did a great job. Many of the people here seem to have wanted a completely solid game that would remove the need to buy any other space game in the future, and that will obviously make the reviews more negative than they should be. For all intents and purposes, I enjoyed this more than Minecraft but less than Skyrim.

I will recommend this game as long as the dev team keeps pushing free, substantial updates, especially since they did promise a lot for the launch that wasn't present initially.

Things I think should be added (that are hopefully in the process of development now):
~More in-depth space battles
~Factions of space pirates to join that result in quests to attack/invade/sneak into other pirates' bases.
~Big cities on some planets that have many, many life forms to interact with/get quests from (other than just searching for certain minerals).

I bought this game on a sale after the foundation update came out so my review is based on how the game is after that update. I like this game, it looks good, plays decently and I've not encountered many bugs. This is a SINGLE-PLAYER space exploration game, so I don't recommend this if you're looking for multiplayer or action driven gameplay.
Even after over 30 hours of gameplay on Normal mode (got roasted when trying out survival - will try that again later), there's still so much to do. You can follow this Atlas path, or you can just wander around exploring new systems and their various planets, environments, plants and animals. You can hunt for riches by grinding materials and trading them and you can build your own bases with alien workers to further your income. The workers give you quests that unlock more builds or upgrades. If you like exloding or killing things then you can do that as well, sentinels and space pirates can be challenging, specially in numbers. So, you can basically do what ever you want in an endlessly big world.
There are of course some cons I need to mention even though the pros outweigh them for me.
For starters, the handling of spacecraft is annoying and when flying over planets there's some kind of a "safety cushion" that makes you unable to land or crash yourself. Instead you'll just hover over the ground and press the landing button for auto landing. This is specially annoying since you can't see below your craft, so controlling on what spot you land is very hard (like trying to land on a landing pad or next to a base, instead of randomly landing some 100 meters or more away from it). The crafting system might also need some overhaul, since you'll need an empty slot in your inventory when making an item, even though you're emptying 2-3 slots in the process. There are a few minor complaints here and there also but for the most part I can look past it because other aspects of the game are enjoyable to me and I'm optimistic that the devs will add more features in the future to expand this world even further as well as addressing the issues most complained about.

Reviews.176487:
Pros:
[list]
 [*]The procedural generation of planets gives countless hours of gameplay and free-roam. The urge to explore the unknown is real and is what makes me want to constatly play more of this game.
 [*]Graphics are beautiful. You often stop in your tracks just to enjoy the stunning scenery and to take screenshots
 [*]Exploration is really immersive and unlike any other released game in its class. You explore the world based on what you can see, not based on icons on a map
 [*]The procedural generation of animals will make you gasp, laugh and sometimes shock you. 
 [*]Survival mode really makes the game more interesting and more of a challenge. Initially it is a real challenge to survive.
 [*]Base building is enjoyable, although some resources are quite difficult, or take time to find and grind.
 [*]Upgrades to your spaceship, space suit and multi-tool give countless hours of gameplay and a goal to acomplish
 [*]Space combat and freighters are fun.
 [*]Space is massive!!
 [*]Third party mods do work, but are not officially supported. 

Many of the above are pros, but can be improved massively by future updates. 
I mainly play the game with TV shows in the background. They work well together.

[/list]

Cons:
 [list]
 [*]Repetitiveness! Structures, some plants and planets look quite similar to each other. The procedural engine needs updating and improving. The repetitiveness makes you want to leave planets once you have explored them a bit.
 [*]The space ship controls work well, but lack complete control. The game prevents you crashing into planets and prevents you from falling below a certain altitude when flying on the surface. You can still crash into asteroids, other ships and freighters, etc.
 [*]Scanning for animals can be fustrating on some planets and you could find yourself looking for hours. I strangely do enjoy this though.
[/list]
 [*]Space travel between star systems need to be improved. The current system works, but is far from optimal.
 [*]No Multiplayer, except for being able to see other peoples discovered planets and systems. 
 [*]You can't sell your ship when you upgrade it. You seem to just leave it to rust.
 [*]The many lies that Sean Murray told to market this game.
 [*]The developer is silent about future updates and progress. I really hate this! They are still working on the game though and the developer branch steam client is getting constant updates. We just don't know what they are planning!
Example: https://steamdb.info/app/275850/history/
 [*]Mods are not officially supported!

Despite its faults, I really do love the game.

Review written after 132 hours of gameplay.

I purchased this game on a Steam sale for ~$35.

I've had a lot of fun playing No Man's Sky, but I had low expectations going in and did not play prior to the Foundations update. There's not a ton of depth with what is presently available; the game is predominantly about exploring a procedurally generated universe and scavenging the necessary resources to do so. I find it a relaxing exercise in wandering and poking my nose around in new locations.

To characterize the game overall I'd describe it as broad, but shallow. There's a lot of planets to explore, but they have a relatively small number of themes to draw from. There's crafting systems with discoverable recipes for many gameplay mechanics, but the recipes for any individual mechanic have 4 or 5 elements. Xenobiology produces some interesting looking races, but they generally fall into one of three or four distinct types. More depth in each of these dimensions will make them feel more substantial and the universe less samey-feeling.

The idea is interesting and should be rewarding to play for people who can appreciate slower paced games and a focus on explorative gameplay.

Blah blah blah I was mad too. Looking at this whole debaccle, you can gleam that Sean and his team handled the PR front like a bunch of monkeys throwing their feces at each other.

It's an unacceptable business practice, and should not be encouraged. This review is an objective review on the product itself however, so I will try to include as little bias about the whole scandal as I can.

~16 quintillion "procedurally generated" planets. That's a fucking lot. You see negative reviews complaiining about the lack of diversity in the planets, and to them I say you either haven't played enough of the game, or you're missing the whole point of the experience.

At it's core, No Man's Sky is less of a game and more a sandbox with the potential for unlimited exploration. Many gamers, including myself see this as nothing but a boring simulated nature walk with the same assets reused in different combinations throughout each planet.

But holy shit, when you *do* find that planet that just makes your jaw drop, you realize that the last 16 hours of hopping across barren hellscapes was totally worth it. No Man's Sky isn't a game that's meant to take you on a fun ride and keep you going with the same momentum throughout like most games. This game is about those short moments of awe that you experience when you see something you never thought the game would churn out. Those rare beautiful worlds that fill you with a sense of true zen and tranquility are, what I believe, to be the meat and bones of this game.

In short, you will spend a lot of time being bored with the mechanics and a lot of time dicking around looking for cool shit. That's pretty much what the game's meant to be! If you're the type of person that needs a complex gameplay experience to keep them engaged, stay away. If you're just looking for something to wind down with at the end of the day, or something to play inebriated (lol me), this game is perfect for you :)

I am admittedly one of the few that enjoyed the game as it was released. I don't really care about the PR nightmare that surrounded the game when it released. I enjoyed it and have been playing it casually to unwind since it launched.

That being said, the Foundation Update is truly a breath of fresh air. 

I'm not going to go through the entire patch notes to tell you what they added, but here is a short list of the best additions/improvements from the perspective of a player who enjoyed the game in the first place:

-*-*-Construction-*-*-
This is huge. It increases the demand on resources and allows us to finally make our mark on a planet. It cannot be overstated how much this enhances the game experience. I feel that the construction interface is about 80-90% efficient. Using the Q and E buttons to cycle through items feels a bit strange, but maybe I just have small fingers. 

-*-*-Freighters and Space Events-*-*-
Answering a distress call in game is more rewarding now that you can board the freighter you saved and speak with the commander and possibly buy his services. I haven't accumulated enough wealth to buy one yet (they seem to initially cost around 7 mil units), so I cannot yet comment on construction on the freighters, but it's nice to be able to land on them and interact in a somewhat meaningful way.

-*-*-Scan from Space-*-*-
Such a simple change that drastically reduces the mundanity of trying to locate a particular element. Every planet seems to contain some amount of Iron, Carbon, Plutonium, but now you can scan for harder to find resources from your ship at range. If you can see the planet, you can scan it. I have not experienced any kind of distance limitation as of yet.

-*-*-New Elements-*-*-
More elements competing for space in your inventory, and now you need technology other than your multi-tool to harvest them, which adds a great 'element' to the gameplay. ;-)


I know many players were outraged about the game when it launched, if you didn't get a refund, launch the game again and check out the improvements. I personally think it's worth it. Happy Gaming!

1. First things first: it's massively videocard demanding. I mean, my VC is not exactly a must, but it runs games like Fallout 4 or GTA V at their highest config with no problem at all.

2. It demands lots of processing, too. That said, if you don't own a decent PC, with SSD disk and, at least, an i7 processor, quit it before you cry. I do have one. And I cried.

3. Let's forget about the hardware hunger. Let's focus on the gameplay (or the lack of it). The game gives you no macro objective at all. If freedom's what they meant, failed miserably towards engaging people to play more than a few minutes. The micro-objectives (like improving the gun/ship or discovering new planets and species) keeps you entertained for a few hours, and that's it. I'll not be dishonest: you'll play 4 hours thrilled, at most. Then, you'll start to think "how did I spend my money in this $&it?"

4. The repeatability. Oh, man... "Craft an X number of ore due to improve your item to level Y". Once there, guess what? Start over again, to improve it even more. Lame.

5. The space combat is infamous. I truly missed my old DOS Tie-Fighter game.

6. Multiplayer. None. Next.

7. The creatures. Remember those big fellas you saw on teasers/trailers before the launch? Well, the in-game ones don't consider minimal evolutionary conditions/rules. All the big fellas I found on my way were "Quaker Oats" raised version of the smaller ones, and that's... Pure crap.

When NMS first came out I played for about 30 hours, like most people's experience the first dozen hours were the most fun, fixing up your ship, discovering a new planet, starting the atlas path etc. it was hugely disappointing when it turned out there wasn't anything at the centre (I never got there, but read about it), and finishing the atlas path didn't really seem worth it, however I still enjoyed most of my time with the game, so I put it down and waited. 

HG had talked about free dlc and it definately felt like they had been a little rushed to get the game out. 
There was stuff that I thought would be in the game that wasn't (quite a lot), but I am pretty used to that by now, so many games have had reveal trailers that make them seem to be something other than the final game you end up playing. Still I had confidence in HG adding those things in over time.

The silence was a bit annoying but I think a lot of people vastly overeacted. For such a small team the reception and hounding from certain communities online must have been crushing, they poured heart and soul into this game, even lacking much that was hinted at, it is quite unique and I think there only option was keep quiet and work hard to deliver updates that realised it's potential, the last thing they needed was to make promises they may not be able to keep. 
The game suffered because of monumental hype and it obviously was too much for some people when it didn't fully deliver ever single thing they expected.

The Foundation update has made me love this game again. I started a survival mode game and it's so much more rewarding than the normal mode, even though I must have died about 12 times so far. 

It forces you to plan ahead, I won't go to a new planet without enough plutonium to take off again (often hanging around in the station hanger bay buying small amounts off each ship that comes in). 

I also make sure I had enough power to recharge my exosuit systems incase I end up in an extreme enviroment. 

That said, I have still had at least three occasons where I have been pretty much resigned to my fate, seeing no way out other than starting a new game; stuck on an extreme planet with no way to recharge my suit and only small pockets of plutonium at distances too far to gather and return. 

Somehow I have always eventually found a way to continue, even if that required gathering tiny amounts of plutonium, with just enough time to transfer to my ship before death, rinse and repeat, enough to get back to a station and stock up again.

I have now built my frst base and am doing missions for the staff I have hired. The update seems to have massively improved the diversity of planet generation, my home planet has vast deep gorges, sprawling cave networks and is a joy to explore.

I have seen planet's with huge mountains far bigger than anything I saw previously, and resource and flora placement gives the impression of different planet biome's as you explore. A lot is familiar but it always seems an improvement on how it was previously generated.

I am really looking forward to what the next updates bring, and hope HG can regain trust in those people that are cleary currently unable to forgive the past mistakes.

I preordered No man's sky earlier this year. It kept getting pushed back due to delays, but I can appreciate a game company allowing their work to "cook" a little longer. After waiting a couple days for Hello Games to work out the kinks, I was able to finally play the game. My excitement for game dwindled the more I played it, and at the 20 hour mark, I realized that the infinite game that was advertised was quite limited.

Several months went by and I had pretty much forgotten about NMS until I heard a blurb on Kotaku that an update was about to be released. I was completely surprised because I thought it was a dead game and Hello Games had pretty much just cut their "losses" on it. However, after watching the new gameplay video, the interest that I had for this game several years ago when I first heard about it came back.

All I can say at this point is, "Thank you Hello Games for continuing to support this game." A lot of folks are going to hate on it regardless of how many updates get released for it. The initial disappointment has left a bad taste that may never go away for some. I personally think that this "Foundation" update is a huge step in the right direction. The biggest thing it has to offer is that it actually gives the game some direction. Adding a kind of questing system to the gameplay gives some purpose that ultimately makes it a more satisfying play. The base building adds a whole new dynamic to the game that gives you a zero point in which you can stretch out from, and continue to explore. While there are still some bugs, they are minor, and I can send an error report and move on. What games out there don't have their fair share of bugs?

Anyways, this review would have been a whole different story a couple months ago, but now, I can recommend it. I have considered this game an early access title from day one and will continue to consider it that for some time to come. It's still a work in progress, but it's great to see that Hello Games has not given up on the small fan base they still have. First, I want to let readers of this to know that the hate over this game has been overhyped by internet bullies and trolls. The ASA cleared Hello Games and Valve of false advertising, and nothing you've heard about this game from a comment section is true. Ignore the bandwagon bullying and decide for yourself what kind of gamer you want to be. 
 
Overall, I'd describe this game as a relaxing and wondrous experience. It is the MOST immersive game I've ever played. The fact that Hello Games is going to be releasing more and more content over time is incredibly exciting, because the content as it stands provides an incredibly setting and canvas for them to build upon with a diversity of features, especially the rumoured planetary "buggy" vehicles. Maybe there will be some kind of settlement building feature in the future, to expand on the base-building?

The diversity of the planets and the creatures is incredible, and it is a really nice place to retreat to after hours of working or studying. There's a little bit of action, a lot of clever design, all kinds of things to do, and a lot of beauty in the kinds of planets you can visit.

In terms of games I would compare it to, I would say the liesure and genre of Portal 2, with the gameplay objectives of Minecraft, and the setting and wonder of Destiny. 

There are so much to see, you'll end up torn between spending hours on every planet and moon you visit, naming all the species and exploring, and hours flying between planets and solar systems, in search of something new. 

TL;DR - The trolls are lying to you, and this is an amazing place to spend time. They're just mad because in this game, you can't pwn noobz and yell "BOOM, HEADSHOT!" at the tv in your mom's basement. This is a game for grown-ups who enjoy thoughtful, innovative design and a creative, liesurely sense of discovery.

Reviews.176769:
At release this was a very good basis for a game, it had some content, a good premise, a unique gimic, and great graphics, but as for actual playability the game was somewhat empty, the only goal was to try to make it to the centre of the galaxy with very little reason to do so.

In my opinion what the game needed to round it out into an amazing gaming experience was plentiful, but did not include removing or redoing what was already there, essentially, all they needed to do was realise they had made an incomplete product and then finish it, as for finishing it, I would say the key features they needed to add were the following:

Game Mechanics:
1) Some sort of base-building ability
2) The ability to purchase capital ships and modify them in the same way you do your smaller craft
3) A far more advanced stellar mapping system that allows you to see the galaxy as a whole and plot your own courses, allowing meet-ups with friends (though this may still take weeks to reach an agreed destination) and for you to keep track of visited worlds
4) Some sort of faction system allowing bases to be shared between other faction members and allowing you to recruit NPCs, maybe even claim territory which can be taken by other players and vice versa

Fixes:
1) A few fixes to stop exploits which allow infinite crashed ship spawns on 1 planet
2) True Multiplayer (the fact that you could never actually interract with another player in the same map was disappointing
3) More difficult survival

The fact that they have released a new update is encouraging especially since they have intrudocued several of the features that I stated above would complete the game, namely more difficult survival, base building and capital ship purchasing, thats actually almost half the list checked off.

The main problem with this game though is that a game can either focus on giving the player something complicated to do or letting multiple players make something to do for themselves, but this game seemed to try to do both without actually giving a multiplayer.

I think that if they continue to develop the game and listen to the more constructive criticism without completely compromising the game's original concept, this could still turn into a real winner of a game, however, they have some serious credit to win back with the playerbase, so its an uphill battle for them, I just hope they can make it, because before I ran out of things to do (which admittedly took way too little time) this game was actually quite fun.

For now I dont recommend this game, however I do recommend you keep an eye on it because there is a chance, however small, that this game could still turn out to be a real winner in the future.

"Sean lied", "refund button works" and other negative reviews filled this game. However, there are not so many reviews about the ACTUAL game. Everybody talks about what is it supposed to be but nobody thinks about what is it at the moment or can become. 

 So this review is for those people who don't care about all that "omg he lied/bad ending/game sucks/I expected more". 

 [b]First of all, I need to say - at the moment this game doesn't worth that much money. Yet it doesn't mean that No Man's Sky is a bad game. It's more like an Early Access game.[/b]
 This game is not for everybody. Literally. You can compare it to walking in the park. Some people enjoy looking around, exploring, searching for new stuff without any point or actual end. Some people don't. Same is with this game. It's all about exploring, walking, listening and such stuff. It's an awesome game for taking epic and awesome screenshots. It's a nice game to chill after a hard day. It's a perfect game for dreamers. And it's a terrible game for those who are waiting for action all the way, storyline and the gameplay like in CoD. 
 You have a freedom to explore all the planets, all species. Some people say that random makes animals to look ugly, unreal, stupid. However, we can't know for sure if those creations can't be real. Moreover, random doesn't always make them that unlucky. Sometimes you can find something really nice looking. 
 Another problem that everybody complains about is that there are no those super epic space battles. Again, this game wasn't made for action. The main point of it is a calm exploration. Not the destruction of everything, killing the evil guy and living happily with a lady. In this game you have your own adventure and only you decide what do you want to do. 

So fast cons and pros:

+ Nice graphics (not for everybody but really unusual)
+ Really a lot of stuff to explore. (if you are not looking for fast running point-to-point)
+ Epic space
+ You can be first to discover one of the best planets
+ There are probably going to be some updates to this game 
+ Lots of freedom for modding.
+ Awesome ambient.

- Mostly all animals have a same colour
- Animal's sounds may become annoying
- Some colours are too toxic. 
- Can be a bit too grindy (however, mostly all games have grind. At least you don't see here standart "I need eggs. Go kill hens and bring me eggs")
- No real point. You are free. You need to find what to do. 

 A pretty but overhyped game. Too high price for the current stage but maybe we'll get something more in the end.

Reviews.176868:
I watched the videos, i read the interviews but i held off on the hype.
The game sounded massive, like Minecraft meets Elite Dangerous, brilliant but let's wait until the NDA is lifted, lets see the game for what it is.

I bought the game on release day knowing what was and what wasn't included in the game.

I knew i'd never see any other players.
I knew the ending wasn't quite as satisfying as implied.
I knew there were a bunch of features absent/not as described.

However i also knew i'd be able to explore random generated planets, with random generated wildlife and upgrade my ship, suit and tool along the way.
I can mine resources, upgrade equipment and if i mine too much, or kill too many life forms then the Sentinels (robotic space police) will come to investigate or eventually try to kill me.

I'd meet aliens, learn their language, and trade with them.
I'd encounter Space Pirates who'd scan me for valuables and engage in combat if i was worth the effort.

And you know, that works for me.
However now they've gone and added some more features!

The new Foundation update adds 2 new game modes along with Base Building, and somewhere between the original release and now they've also updated minerals that can be used for refueling your life support system etc, which took a few minutes to get back up to speed.

Game modes are now:
Normal - Chilled out mode, Life Forms will still attack but are less of a threat and resource gathering is plentiful
Survival - Planets are harsher starting out, Life Forms are tougher and resources are much less frequent. Overall feels like a more rewarding survival experience rather than an exploration mode.
Creative - No resource cost for base building, unlimited cash, life, energy etc

Base Building
If you are familiar with Subnautica, the base building is almost copy and paste for style and use. Not a bad thing, but not original either.
It's interesting and helps to feel you're putting a mark on the planets you encounter.

Overall the game started off over-hyped by both fans and the developers but keeping expectations low i wasn't disappointed, though with the inclusion of the Foundation update i'll be keeping an eye on the game to see how it continues to progress.

Many of us have waited far longer for studios to follow through, *cough* Rockstar *cough*, with what they've said they'd do.  If you weren't suckered into boarding the faux hype train or you can pretend for a moment that you didn't read the internet in the months prior to NMS launching, and you're looking for a casual space exploration game that's very sandbox-y, NMS will be a decent fit.  

Don't expect anything we've seen before in terms of quality combat or super indepth story arcs like Eve or Elite, but it does offer some moderate trading (and getting better now that freighters are here), light combat (mostly against planetary drone forces or pirate ships attacking you for your precious cargo, or freighters in the system), a not-so-in-depth crafting system (I'm sure this will continue to develop into a more thoroughly and plentiful system in the future), and lots - and I mean LOTS - of exploration.  Players have the ability to discover new species of animals, planets, new systems, new planets and moons, and name them.  

Base building has now been introduced and offers players more ways to play the game.  Build a trade network of outposts and stations, or wage war on systems and attack trade vessels and other ships.   The game is fine for what it was meant to be, and Hello Games has kept their word in terms of providing additional content.  Yes, the hype train broke the damned internet.  Yes, I believe Hello Games could have received more support from their affilitates.  Do I think we should destroy what the game is because of bad PR?  No.  

The game is on sale at the time of this review.  If you've been curious, hesitant, or a basement dweller who's just now hearing about No Man's Sky, give it a shot.  It can be a little grindy, but rewarding.  I wish I could have paid $35.99 rather than full price as I totally feel like that's a great price for what the product is.  I look forward to seeing additional updates and mods release in the future.  o7

This game seems to be fun to hate, but after the 1.1 update, it is honestly not bad. Before, there wasn't much to do other than explore and collect resources while upgrading your supplies to collect more resources, and that did get boring after a while. However, with this new update, the game has added more to the loop that should have been included in the first place. Base building has been added, allowing you to create some pretty nice structures on planets to call home, while recruiting aliens and doing missions for them. The missions actually give you reason to go to other star systems, as certain resources can now be found only in certain colored star systems. While you're away on your missions, you can now purchase freighters that can act as a mobile base that you can customize on the inside. The developers added a survival mode which is actually a decent challenge now. For once, you have to actually watch your shields, use recharge canisters and charges, and every item feels valuable. Walking towards your ship for the first time felt like a real adventure and a challenge, and was a nice change from the much easier "normal" mode. Planets are decent, and so is the flora and fauna, but it can look a bit similar after a while, but in all honesty, its the same in real life. While there is room for improvment, this game has taken a step in the right direction. I hope one day a "true" multiplayer experience can be added, as survival mode with a friend would be fun, but in the meantime, I am satisfied with the progress that has been made with this game. 

I would recommend this game if you like exploring, or want a decently challenging survival game.

I don't usually review games unless I feel like there's a large distance between my impressions and the sentiment expressed by the majority of reviews. At the time of this reivew Steam lists the overall user reviews as "Mostly Negative." As my experience with NMS has not been "Mostly Negative" I wanted to offer my 2 cents. 

NMS is a really cool exploration crafting game. It is a super laid back experience that you can play for hours without getting fatigued or frustrated. Between bases and the Atlas "main quest" there's plenty to keep you on a track if you want, but you can jump off the main track and just do your own thing whenever you want. I like this sort of "opt in" gameplay. Sometimes I want to build up my base or discover more of the game lore, and sometimes I just want to explore. NMS can be a strcutured or free form as you want, and you can switch off freely.

I don't like sandbox survival games, and I don't really like crafting in games, so I was super skeptical going into NMS; I didn't expect to enjoy it. However, after a while I got into the groove and really enjoy it. Once I started to understand what types of resources I needed and generally how to find them I started to really like it. 

That said there are things I find aggrivating. Inventory space is really, really, really tight and the upgrades you craft must be equipped into inventory slots. That means that everything you equip reduces spots for materials. On top of this you have to keep a lot of basic materials on hand just for the core gameplay, such as fuel. Because of this I find that I'm rarely able to craft things. I've picked up dozens of recipies for upgrades, but in 30 hours I think I've crafted 2 upgrades. I really wish the game was more liberal in terms of the inventory space, or that equipped upgrades didn't eat up inventory space. Additionally, I wish there was some kind of resource locator or something. How do you find what you need? There's a scanner, but it doesn't work too well. There are upgrades for it, but I don't have the space to equip it and I can't find the materials to build it!

The above criticisms of the core crafting and collecting mechanic could have been enough for me to shelve the game after 10-12 hours. However, there's a lot here to keep me going. First, the base building in the Foundations upgrade holds out hope that resource space and resource availability will be easier with the base. Plus, the quests to build the base are fun and add some variety. Additionally, the exploration is just plain fun. When I get bored with a system, or if I don't like the planets in a system, I just take off to a new one. There's always new and exciting things to see. The planets varry quite a bit and no two are alike. A relaxing gameplay distraction I really love is scanning and cataloging animals and plats. When I don't feel like doing the resource grind I find a cool planet and go all National Geographic on it.

Finally, there is some really cool action. You'll get interdicted by pirates if you have valuable cargo and will have to dogfight. This was super aggrivating at first and I kep getting blown up. But after buing an upgraded ship this has gotten a lot better. Space battles are really fun. You'll also find freighters being attacked and can save them, so there's some variety in the space battles. You'll also find yourself fighting against the drones on the planets. The agressiveness of the drones varries from planet to planet, and planets with extremely valuable resources will often have very agressive drones. You'll find yourself fighting against them head on sometimes; other times you'll try to outwit and outrun them by hiding. The drones mix up the action on the planets, but they are also kind of weird fromn immersion perspective. Why are there these AI drones on EVERY planet and why do they all look and act the same? Where do they come from? Who mantains them? I have no idea. It seems pretty weird. Lastly there's the action and drama of dealing with hostile planets. Nothing will get your blood going like being out of fuel on a -230c planet during a storm!

There are definitely things I'd like to see in furture updates. A resource locator and some better balance for invetory would be nice. More quests and NPC interaction would great too. The ability to build temporary shelters on hostile planets would be helpful. Variety in the space station designs would be great too. Cities or towns on some planets would increase immersion. And a solar system map would be SUPER helpful. A more usable galaxy map would be nice too.

Overall this is a really great game. Two of my favorite games are Skyrim and Elite Dangerous. NMS feels a bit like a combination of the two. If you enjoy space games, exploration, free roaming, and a gameplay experience that can be as relaxed or as intense as you want then this is a great game.

Foundation Update: Simply put, 3 months are literally not enough to develop, implement, test and release an update of this magnitude, no matter how big your studio is. Anyone who has ever coded can understand this. This strengthens my suspicions that NMS 1.0 wasn't the game they planned to make in the first place, and they got pushed by Sony to an early release with everything that followed being a natural result. I believe many of these features were under development already when the game first launched. Even now, after 1.1, people still find more data files like the ground vehicles and the fourth alien race. After the tinfoil wars, HG have come out of their closet and the answer is good: These are good programmers and they love their game. For me this is good enough.

As for the content of the update: Survival Mode is probably the best thing that ever happened to the game. This is seriously difficult. The freighters and base building are a nice way to add more playtime and giving a way to build a full economy. Maybe for the Creative mode players it's all about the screenshots, but at Survival having a steady, safe income from your farm is VERY important. Other game changes like making buildings scarcer, auto miners, beacons and craftable save points help a lot with both immersion and cartography of an endless galaxy. Planets are now more diverse than ever, with varying biomes per regions. Mountains and valleys are way more distinct, unrealistic animal anatomies have been very toned down, animal population, size and behaviour is much better. Space battles are much better now, skies are more populated and new interesting features like Bounties are the icing on a very well baked cake. Overall, every single change in this update has been very good. Granted the initial ground was on the low side as they basic game was very blunt. This is no longer the case though. The game is now lifted in a very good standard, and if HG continue working with the same passion we will see an amazing game pretty soon. As I was writing since the initial release, the immense potential is still in the game.

Reviews.177092:
No Man's Sky is a decent game. Really, it is.

Yes, it's short on quests and content. This is probably the biggest fair criticism. But so do tons of modern sandbox/survival games out there. What is there to really "do" in Minecraft? You play for the sake of playing. Not every game makes you be the Savior of the Universe. 

Yes, the ending is dumb. So was Mass Effect 3's, doesn't mean it was a bad game overall.

Yes, it's short on variability. Game has 18 quintillion planets but they look like variations of 10 different planets. But Starbound is the exactly same in that regard (and was criticized early on for that exact reason, until they built enough content to make it fun.)

Yes, the universe feels sterile. So does the one in Elite Dangerous (which incidentally, also promised nearly unlimited planets and stars, except they also all feel the same).

Yes, the developers overpromised and underdelivered, and at times misled. Many other developers do the same thing. It doesn't make it OK, and the criticism is fair, but what's not fair is singling out this game among all others that didn't live up to their promise. We forgive when an AAA company screws over customers because we're used to the big studios doing this, but then outpour all our rage on an indie dev.

Yes, $60 was a bad value at start, and honestly it still is. But at least you get a whole game with free updates. Compare to other AAA studios which charge $70 + $100 worth of piecemeal DLC. Compare to ARK which released a *paid* DLC to compensate for flaws in the base game while the base game is still Early Access. Compare to Deus Ex: Mankind Divided which sells experience booster packs for money. Compare to Star Citizen which sells in-game ships for tens of thousands of real dollars.

Nonwidthstanding all the lack of content, the game isn't objectively bad. Sure, it's shallow. But as a light-hearted exploration game, it's not bad. If you don't put too much meaning into it, and just enjoy travelling through a vast universe, visit different planets, enjoy the scenery, upgrade your ship, and just enjoy yourself while at it, this was a decent game even at launch. 

And, of course, the game pushed technology boundaries. An indie team built something which nobody else even attempted before on that scale. Of course they'd make mistakes along the way.

So - nonwithstanding gameplay, lack of variety, ending, and overpromising (all those are valid reasons, but they aren't the main reason) - why do people *actually* pan this game? What makes it deserve a 30% positive score - lower than AAA releases which are unplayable on day 1, have intrusive DRM, or have a huge P2W scheme?

It's our own expectations. Things no developer can ever live up to. The moment we jumped on the hype train, we substituted our own hopes and dreams of what would make this "perfect", open-universe, "go out there and make your destiny", for what the game was actually supposed like. Even if the game was released with 100% features delivered, we'd still find something we hoped would be there, and be upset about that. You can't ship a dream.

It's also our worst fear that after shipping the game in its current state, the developers would close shop and jump ship. So long, and thanks for all the fish. Leaving our hopes and dreams forever shattered.

But amidst all the doom and gloom, Hello Games released a major content patch. It didn't address all the problems. Hell, it didn't even address the most important missing issue - lack of adventure and quest content. If anything, it released more of what it released on launch - game mechanics, which can be the basis for the ever-elusive "fun", but which require more building-up. In terms of concrete content, the November patch added a solid foundation in terms of base-building and owing freighters (which act like a mobile base). It addresses the core problem of you feeling of having no impact from exploration. It allows you to set up your own base (both on a planet and in space), and build it up, adding a lot of what makes games like Minecraft or Terraria fun. It's not nearly near its full potential, but it's a very solid start. The patch also enhanced space battles and alien interactions - slowly beginning the address the feeling of "sterile" universe.

And beyond concrete content, the patch also sent a strong message - that the developers are here to stay, that they will continue releasing major patches, and that the patches will be free for those who purchased the game and are still willing to give it a chance.

If you expect a game that lives up AAA expectations (and its price tag), don't buy this just yet. The game is still not ready. Perhaps wait a few more patches. Currently, it’s “OK” - no more, no less.

But if you've been following this game since the beginning, if you've been living the dream which then slowly became a nightmare, hold on to your hope. I still do. The game is not only "OK", but it can - and I truly believe that - can be made a great game, with enough content patching and support. And with the latest patch, we may just see the beginning of the journey to make No Man's Sky a game that lives up to its true potential.
Reviews.177093:
They've turned the corner. 

The most important thing the 1.1 Foundation update did was ramp up the difficulty in the new Survival mode. Kit that was meaningless has become vital, and colourful content that paled through ubiquity now has to be earned. It's gone from a walk in a garish park to a respirator-straining struggle up a martian cliff. And mainly in a good way.

It's no [i]Long Dark[/i], but you do find yourself balancing multiple survival strategies and resource decisions on the fly in a satisfying way. It's such a far cry from the 'my only problem is storage' dynamic of the clunky launch. Some balancing may be in order (aspects like shield recharge times feel too blunt a limitation on progress), but it's taken a leap in the right direction. It's still on the simplistic end, but it feels like its own intriguing beast in the survival game landscape now. 

Add in the base building, which is surprisingly solid, and you've got a reason to bed into a planet and appreciate it (and with the freezing winds and carnivorous kangaroos, a reason to appreciate a home too).  

The crafting etc still isn't the most profound, the grind is real, the thinness of the story's pull still remains... In short many things that were underwhelming about the launch game are still essentially the same. But the progress they've made in these 3 months is flat out impressive (from technical improvements like improved landscapes to actually presenting a proper game frame to hang your story on). The gameplay problems that remain now feel increasingly fixable... 
 
It's definitely not for everyone, but if you like the art style of these worlds, and don't mind directing your own grind, you'll find surviving and thriving on your favourite toxic planet can be a transporting experience. 

And in theory it should only get better...

While there's been a lot of negative reviews, I've enjoyed NMS from the start. Then again, I expected an introspective, exploratory game, with minimal combat and trade (you can easily ignore trade if you like and usually get to pick your own battles too), AND I didn't spend $60 on a game I knew was made by a mostly unknown indie group (of only 15 developers too!). I went and played a copy for exactly what they're released for: to get my own feeling without any sense of monetary loss. I felt it was a great indie game (worth about $20), and would've been fine buying it for that price. 

Two things have happened recently that lead me to being very happy to pay and support this game and it's deveolpers. First off, with all the harshness directed at them, these guys buckled down and got to work. Honestly, I'm sure they knew they weren't finished the game yet (and it definitely should've been an early access title), but when you have a big company beathing a deadline down your neck, I'm sure the pressure to release whatever you have is a heavy one. Secondly, the foundation update is a great start and shows how much Hello Games are paying attention to the public (even if they are being insanely silent in general hahaha). Normal mode is now harder in that there's less stuff to harvest and you can't just quickly find crash sites (thereby making ship slot growth slower). It also seems to be taking much longer to find some upgrades. Survival mode is a beast, just go read the stories on Reddit hahaha. Creative mode is a fun run around. Basically, you're an immortal money/resource wizard ;) Get creative and build or do a speed run to the center of the galaxy (I've never even gotten close in my normal game, so maybe one day lol)

To sum up, If you want a quasi zen-like game of chillin and wandering about, grab this one. If you're hesitent, wait for more updates, or buy it on sale (like right now it's 41% off here in China which means it's less than $20!). While I think Star Citizen will be more popular (as it's a more "normal" style game), I'm sure I'll still enjoy NMS more. For me, it's more similar to playing something like The Talos Principle or The Witness: almost like a mild meditative experience (at least the way I play it). One of those games that usually would've been overlooked and then gotten praise if it hadn't been hyped and displayed like a AAA title.

***Potential Spoilers***

I was recently asked, "How was Survival mode?"  The following was my response:

Wonderfully humbling.  At the end of two hours play, I found myself in a hollowed out chunk of Iridium, watching as the last 5% of my life support ticked away - praying that my toxic protection recharged fast enough to book it back to my broken ship (which, by the way, I started a 14 minute hike away from), hoping that a bug/crab wouldn't notice me and continue to eat my face.  I managed to get to the hunk-of-junk with one piece of health, no supplies (if you die you lose all materials AND some piece of equipment breaks), no toxic protection, and no life support (you can sit in your cockpit and you don't need life support, but it doesn't recharge either). I finally decided I couldn't leave, repair my ship, or repair an equipment - so I popped the hatch and let the acid rain corrode my suit, falling to the ground and towards the waiting crab-a**holes.

It was the most fun I've had in NMS since the first few hours after unboxing it. One mistake can cost you dearly and every choice matters.  I found myself leaving or ignoring Gold/Iridium/Emeril for desperate searches of Thamium9 (grab every piece you can!). Lastly, with the latest patch my PC went from being able to run the game on middling graphic settings and cranking out the heat, to all settings maxed out (excluding AA) and having my laptop purr.  Great update, beautiful game, good work HG.  At $60 I was happy with NMS - which met my $1/hour gameplay ratio and being one of the few games I could play with all members of the family.  At the current price point(s) its hard not to recommend this game. 

P.s. With three modes it gives our family multiple "profiles" for people to play:  my eldest - Normal, me - Survival, and my middle child - Creative.  Thank you again to the Hello Games team!

I'm a developer myself, and it was clear to me that they removed several features before release (quite a few were shown in live gameplay). I'm sure many due to bugs and performance - a few probably due to editing. But beyond that, they just were no where near done. Like they rabbit holed on the proc gen and programmed themselves into a corner or two. Nobody wants to release what they released. And nobody spends so much time on a damn niche aesthetic for an intentional scam. 

The Foundation update makes that clear - this isn't something you just throw together for a seasonal sale. The game has a ton of potential and they're still working on it. A lot of the scaffolding is there.

I'm enjoying the new survival mode since the original game had zero challenge. It could use some tweaking, but it feels like the right direction. You need to be selective about landing and careful with resources. I died five times in a few hours, and had several narrow escapes. Animals are dangerous if you walk into a herd of predators without a quick escape route. Upgrades are harder to come by. Settlements can be really SPARSE. Landing can be a real gamble on some planets - I won't land on a new planet until I can see a cave and plutonium in jumping distance. I'm harvesting things I've never cared to harvest before. 

On the other hand, I don't know if a new player would enjoy the difficulty if they didn't know what they needed already. Stumbling around on a harsh planet is tough if you don't know how to sprint/melee/jump, for example.

The default flight model still sucks (get a mod). I haven't even bothered trying to get a gamepad or joystick to work since combat sucks. I'd love to see this addressed in the next update.

Anyway, you're going to hate the game if you were expecting a multiplayer swashbuckler. It's closer to that scene in 2001 where Bowman goes through the stargate than Star Wars. 

It's different and in progress and probably doesn't deserve all the hate.

Despite the popular opinion, I enjoy No Man's Sky. Prior to a few days before release, I had no intentions on playing the game. So, I was able to avoid all the hype surrounding it.

While I don't believe the game is the exact same as the one marketed to the public, I do believe that it is still a good experience. I don't honestly think it is worth the full price, due to so many features shown not being present at launch, but it would be a solid buy if you can find it on sale. You can find a full list of features and resources that are not present on Reddit.

For those of you who do not know; the player will bounce from planet to planet, mining materials to create various items to assist them on their journey to the galactic center, or the atlas. During that voyage, the player will interact with various alien races, which requires them to learn their language via artifacts and monoliths. The player will also gather a copious amount of blueprints for new tools and technologies that aid them on their excursion. That's pretty much it. Yes, it does get repetitive, but it has kept me playing for over 60+ hours, so I can't really complain.

A lot of planets that I visited are barren wastelands; wastelands that are hazardous to the players health. You will not find life or water, and very limited foliage. That makes finding a planet exploding with life even more of a beautiful thing. Some of the most memorable planets had waving grass, thick areas of trees, oceans, beaches, and various creatures.

With the recent Foundation update, Hello Games are definitely making progress to make the game more enjoyable. The base building is a great addition. Even the slight adjustments to graphics and planetary composition has made a solid impact. I look forward to seeing what they have to offer with future updates.

If you're looking for a multiplayer space experience, heavy NPC interactions, or anything involving missions, look elsewhere. If you're looking for a solid, single player, exploratory experience, it's worth a buy.

As someone who was onboard with this game from the onset, I never jumped on the hype train. Did Sean Murray choose poor phrasing/lie about a couple features in the game? Technically yes, given what was released. But as a developer who has worked with a number of publishers, what does and doesn't get cut when time becomes a factor is usually out of the developers hands. Maybe Murray blatantly lied, but why would you lie and then try to right your wrongs, when you already have the money??? Because everyting he stated was probably on the laundry list of features planned for the game. Shit gets cut... thats a reality of game development. 

No Man's Sky is exactly what I expected it to be. An infinite universe that you will never be able to even come close to exploring even a single percentage of it. Is there a lot of repetitiveness to the gameplay? Sure there is. Did anyone expect every single planet to be a completely unique experience? Do you actually think that if you went out into the galaxy you wouldn't find some repetitiveness/likenesses the more you searched? I for one quite enjoy the (mostly) relaxing nature of this gameplay. Cruise around literally anywhere and discover another variation of procedurally generated animal X. It's fun. Is it $60 fun? That's an opinion only you can make for yourself.

The addition of the new features in 1.1 is a step towards fulfilling the unattainable expectations generated by the public. I hope Hello Games continues to build upon this truly unique and beautiful game.

Unforetunately not many folks will actually read this, but the sheer volume of negative reviews on this game are completely unjust. This is a feedback vaccuum where 95% of people read something and then just spew the same garbage rather than actually formulating their own opinion.

Buy it. Play it for a couple hours and decide for yourself, and then refund if you feel it's even 1/4 as terrible as all these reviews would have you believe.

I wanted to like this game, waited for sale before buying.  Even with the negative reviews and advice from other players I still was not convinced, something about the game seemed very alluring.  I can now honestly say that whether you want to believe everyone else or not, they're not exaggerating . . . much.

This game is very much a minecraft of sorts. . .at best.  It's got very little substance and overall it feels like the creators made the worlds but forgot to fill them with anything other than the generic stuff (night/day cycles, rough plants, hilarious animals) which gets old so fast.  I play this game about 2 hours a week as it does fill a sort of niche.  It's my relaxing-dont-make-me-think-just-veg-out game.  Podcast and chill.

My biggest grumbles are lack of auto saves, or, more appropriately: inconvenient save mechanics (I'd rather be able to save on the go).  Also the animals, while different in appearance, never really seem to make me excited as they all act one of two ways (fight or flight).  Would be cool if some hid and pounced, or others were more like wolves hunting in packs.  Instead, all animals either run on sight, or attack on sight.  

My favorite parts: The landscapes can be amazing.  The different appearances of the worlds varies a lot.  Water planets, green, orange, pink, red, brown, etc.  Some are barren, some not so much.  Very cool.  

Overall, 1.1 and beyond are probably going to be too little too late for most people and thats ok.  Save your money, look elsewhere and only ever buy if its a killer sale and you're like me (not trusting people. . . remember though, 75k people aren't wrong in this case).

After 10 - 15 hours of post patch play, I wanted to share my opinion about this game as I feel a lot of the reviews on here are just hating for the sake of it. Why the hate? Yes the launch was a disaster and there's a LOT about the game in its launch state that just felt broken or even missing, but that's done now and it's time to move on. Anyone is free to bear a grudge but I have a strong feeling most of the negative post patch reviewers have not even been in the game long enough to write an honest view of it in its current state. 

First off - this game is not for everyone. If you want an action packed adrenaline inducing game, dont look here. 

Instead, if you want something more relaxing and chilled with elements of base building and exploration, then this is where you want to be. 

Don't get me wrong, the game is still by no means perfect - there's a lot about it right now that could be done in better ways but I find it promising that Hello Games is still working on it and has clearly stated thier intentions to keep doing so. Given time, there's a lot of potential here and in the meantime I'm quite happy spending a few hours at a time wandering about gathering and building my own base. 

Best advice I could give potential buyers, ignore the reviews section for this game and just go and watch some gameplay footage (make sure it's after the recent patch) as this will give you a better idea if this is your cup of tea or not instead of reading 50 hate reviews from angry virgins.
