No Man's Sky is visually spectacular and endlessly, if subtly, inventive. However, there's no pretending it's not a niche game.  It is, at its heart, a repetitive time-sink, in which you must carefully manage resources in order to wander around and look at things that are slightly different from each other.

And yet . . . if that's your sort of thing, if you're the sort of gamer who plays Assassins Creed mainly to look at the 3D-rendered historical buildings and thinks all that action-stealth nonsense is a distraction, then No Man's Sky is an unparalled virtual tourism experience. It's an endless, procedurally generated nature walk with science fiction trappings and the occasional laser battle.

I bought it for full price on day one and I don't regret it, but it's definitely the kind of game you want to go into with eyes open. Buy it only if the thought of collecting minerals in order to earn the privilege of hopping from one vintage sci-fi book cover to another is one that really gets your heart pumping.

This game has copped a lot of flak. The optimistic goals of its creator, mentioned in a variety of interviews years before release became gospel and when they were not met at launch a lot of people got upset. Much of this criticism is valid, but much of it is not. 

The month before release, the community was clearly advised this was a single player game yet many people raised exception to the lack of multiplayer. The majority of 'broken promises' were made over 12-18 months prior to release, just like larger games, and when it failed to meet expecations it was significantly critcised.

In short, I loved this game when it came out. I played nearly 70 hours on the PS4, much more than other games that cost similar amounts. It was simple, but just what I was looking for at the time. I also bought it on PC but didnt jump into a second sitting.

Now that the foundation update has been released, I am going to jump back into this on the PC. The update brings many features that were NOT promised before release, but are welcomed none the less. It also makes space a much more dynamic place to explore.

Is the game perfect? No. But it is a worth-while experience to get lost in for hours on end. The added features do add to the longevity and warrant a try for new players and old ones alike.

Now, I'm playing the 'Survival' mode of the most recent patch and am having more fun than before.  I feel like there is risk in those plains between caves or indoor areas.  And there are less indoor areas!  I actually fear the voice telling me my shields are low, and the reduction of resource availability is a welcome change.

I played the broken product at launch for 35 hours and had fun, if not as much as I had hoped.  I'm playing the survival mode now and am enjoying the challenge.  I care more about the dangers.  I care more about the terrain.  It's harder and I like that.  

I'm only a small way in to the patched release on the 'experimental' branch as I write this, so take this with a grain of salt, but I'm enjoying my experience.  Yes, I understand about the failure to meet expectations, and that's on Hello Games to a large extent, but this latest patch is something this gamer is enjoying.  I'm glad I kept my copy, and I hope further updates extend the playability even more.

Reviews.177472:
PRO TIP: there is a game in here, it's just hard to find amidst all the sightseeing.  If you're looking for the game, here's the deal: go to planets with "frenzied" sentinels, empty your inventory, and collect Gravitinio balls.  Don't try to fight the enemies you'll aggro, you'll end up killing them and spoiling the fun; instead, use long jumps to run from them, keeping the pace up as you collect more Gravitinio balls and lose yourself in the planet you're visiting.  It's actually a decently fun bit; you just have to seek it out on your own, and therein lies No Man's Sky's greatest weakness.

Apart from finding the (relatively rare) activities within the game that are either challenging or exciting, there is little to do in No Man's Sky that fits the traditional definitions of a game.  Rather, No Man's Sky is a tech demo, and it demos some very impressive tech.  I knew it was a tech demo when I bought it, so I was not dismayed to discover that the veneer of gameplay was paper thin throughout most of the experience.

If you go into the purchase knowing that you're buying an exhibition, not a game, then I doubt you'll be disappointed.  However, if you go in hoping for a good story, polished gameplay, elegant controls, interesting characters, or anything else other than a "space bumbling simulator," then you will likely end up among the many others in these reviews who were tricked by a rampant hype machine into purchasing a "game" that is fascinating to think about, but often very dull to play.

[h1] Post Patch 1.1 [/h1]

The update brings the [i] foundations [/i] for a decent game we were promised years ago. It adds the following things:

• Base Building (modular, different types of objects and items)
• Multiple Game Modes (Standard, Hardcore and Creative)
• Improves Animal and Plant Life Algorithms
• Farming (Plants can be planted and harvested)
• Equipment (e.g mining machines)
• Frieghters (large ships that are actually larger than space stations and contain many NPC's, rooms and other terminals / objects)
• Graphical improvements (TAA [u][b]WHOO HOO![/b][/u] Motion Blur [u][b]NICE ;D[/b][/u] AND NO MORE F*CKING 720p UPSCALE [u][b] PRAISE THE LORD CUTHULU HIMSELF :DDDD[/b][/u])

All of this makes the game actually half decent and playable BUT we should have had all of this and more on release day. If HG can produce another update like this one in a month or so (rather than three...) I think we'll be on the clear path to a good game.

This was my review prior to the 1.1 update
________________________________________________________________________________
"This game has failed miserably, I am VERY annoyed that I am stuck with this garbage in my game library because it is completely terrible and I will most likely never play it again. When the game first came out it had over 200,000 players on at one point, now there is a mear 800. If that doesn't prove this game is the biggest scam of 2016 I don't know what does. The devs completely lied about countless features that were meant to be in this game."
________________________________________________________________________________

I clearly had very strong feeling about the game after playing for about 40 or so hours, but now that Hello Games have released the new update I decided I needed to revist the game in order to see what sort of improvements were made.

Obviously the update doesn't add all the features we were told about before the game was launched, but it does add content that we had all hoped to receive and that's awesome. It shows that Hello Games have started taking a step in the right direction in hopes to fix their game. I really did enjoy the game when it first was released, but did quickly realize how much content was actually not in the game. It's very nice to see the developers going back to try fixing this by adding content many players were excited about.

Thoughts about the 1.1 update
______________________

Game Modes
--------------
- The additon of game modes is very nice, I think it's a great way to allow different kinds of players to enjoy the game. 
The three modes are

Normal - this is what most players who revisit the game will know, it's basically the same as before 1.1 but with the new content such as base building

Survival - Practically the same as normal, but with a very steep learning curve. I personally really loved the challenge, you start in a random location on a planet (from my multiple games I noticed all the planets had some sort of harsh environment), and in order to get your ship you have to gather materials and reach you ship (the ship seemed to be anywhere from 8-15 minutes away from your spawn location)

Creative - Much like creative mode in minecraft. You have god mode, and unlimited materials. It's a great mode for building up a base if you want to see what all you can do with it.

Base Building
__________

- The base building is fun and simple. Being able to set up a planet as a "home base" was something I was excited about from the start of the game, it's very simple and I can already tell how useful the bases will actually be. They will not be something you spend time on and then forget about within an hour.

- Hiring people from the different races is an interesting way to liven up the bases.

- As you hire people to work at your base they will give you missions to go gather materials in order to advance or learn how to make a new building, the "base researches" is a great way to add somwhat of a "questing system".

- Within the bases it seems like you have you own personally space stations, which is very nice. No more flying back and forth once you fill up your ship with materials.

- Having a teleporter that can transport you from the space station to your base is actually very cool, I always hated having to fly to the space station just to buy some material I couldn't find on the planets easily.

Materials
_______ 

- The new materials are interesting, I like the idea of needing to research certain equipment in order to harvest new materials.

- Some of the new materials require you to have sort of gauntlet in order to harvest, I think it's great that you now need more than just your multi-tool in order to fully harvest a planet for all of its worth.


As I said above I really enjoyed experiencing the new content and found it very simple yet enjoyable. I think it's great to see Hello Games finally make a comeback after letting down so many people, it's obvious they spent a lot of time on the new content in order to make it up to the older players and to make sure they gave quality content to their players.

I preordered No Man's Sky, and to be honest, I have not been disappointed. It has been everything I expected and more. I'm quite glad we can't actually run in to other players, or we all know what this would turn into - another EVE pew-pew fest of advanced players endlessly slaughtering new players because it makes them feel better about themselves. No thanks.

I've never figured out what all the negativity is about, except for perhaps this, and for me that's just another plus here. I find NMS to be a very relaxing, soothing and introspective adventure, not just through space, but through one's own psyche.

Now this isn't to say it doesn't have it's faults either - everything does when you look. For me the biggest issues I've run into so far have been frame rate drops. Prior to the Foundations update it was something that just happened after a period of time. A quick save/quit/restart was all it took to remedy this, usually for several hours.

After Foundations, however, this frame rate drop seems to happen every time I get back in my ship, and nothing seems to have helped so far - though I'm sure it will be addressed in the next patch. I've written Hello Games support more than once, and I've always gotten a reply, usually within a day or two.

All in all, this is easily one of my favorite games, though it's certainly not for everyone. If PvP is your thing, don't bother, you won't find it here. But if you like exploration, both of space and of self, than No Man's Sky is the colorful, Through-The-Looking-Glass adventure you've been searching for all this time.

I'm writing this review before I update, so I don't know if the update will change what I'm about to say, take it with a grain of salt.

I really really enjoy NMS.  
It is a game of exploration. 
It is a single player experience.
You will have gradual progress dotted with minor setbacks.

I was honestly quite excited for this game when it came out, but I quickly learned, like most, that this game was not as advertised. The idea of exploring vast unknown planets sounds appealing, but the game's randomly generated planets are not as beautiful and captivating as the trailers lead one to believe, and the controls feel just as droll as the planets themselves. I played the game a while back, so what I have to say may be outdated, but if the only thing they did was attempt to fix the FPS issues and add in houses, then the game will still be fundamentally flawed.

I understand that the infinite nature of the game means that RNG can create some lackluster planets, but I went to ten different planets and had no joy on any of them. It felt like a pointless grind rather than a bright exploration. The creatures randomly generated looked absurd rather than majestic or even interesting, and seeing as how the combat system is also very clunky, that was rather frustrating. Because there is no real objective, it's hard to gauge success, which is something we seek as gamers. We like "winning" or at least accomplishing something. In similar games like Minecraft, you can find something interesting or build a base to your liking or play with friends, but with NMS, you have no great customization, no multi-player (which I think this game could benefit greatly from), and no idea what you're looking for.

There's a lot of potential here, but as is, the game is not worth the price. I'd pay $20 for this game, but not the $60 price tag. Steer clear.

I completely understand why this game has a largely negative review score: it's most definitely not the game that many were expecting. Even so, I would still highly reccommend this game to anyone. When the game came out, it was a slow grind-fest of resource collection and practically baren planets. Many of the features Hello Games had said would be in the game were absent; what was given was pretty much an Early Access game for full price. Thus far this sounds really negative but hear me out. Many people that played the game had the sole intent of getting to the fabled "center of the galaxy" as quickly as they possibly could and realised that the game is actually not as long/rewarding/intersting as they had hoped. I will tell you right now: DON'T RUSH THROUGH THIS GAME. If anything, don't even journey towards the center. Take your time. Get to know a single star system for a large amount of time and you'll see what Hello Games was going for: a sprawling universe with almost endless posibilities. Personally, I found the game most rewarding when screenshot hunting. The game, although not graphically the most beautiful game (compared to something like The Witcher 3 or Battlefield 1), it has an almost breathtaking art design that, when captured at the right moment can make any sci-fi lover squeal. Adding on to that, as of today (11/27/2016), update 1.1, a.k.a the Foundation Update, has been released. The Foundation Update brings an extremely comprehensive refresh to the entire No Man's Sky, making the game feel almost completely different. In short, base building is finally introduced; a new, harsher survival mode is also available; many tweaks have been made to the game overall to make the experience much more enticing. That's the beauty of this "Early Access" structure this game has. As Polygon said, "No Man's Sky is the new Destiny," in the sense that Destiny, when released, was lacking in fulfilling package of content. However, look at the state of Destiny now: many still play the game and expansions have kept Destiny thriving years after it's initial release. The same is likely to happen with No Man's Sky. With the Foundation Update, this is the start of larger things to come.

Also, in defense of Hellow Games, they are quite literally a fifteen person team: many AAA games are developed with teams spanning up to 500 people. The fact that No Man's Sky is playable in any state right now is quite amazing. In other words, let this small team work their magic: the game is still evolving to become their vision.

No Man's Sky has been a weird experience. Seen by many as a promising game, it quickly got consumed by its own hype, pushing even the developers and Sony to promise heaven. This lead to many things; From the false marketing of maybe planned but finally undelivered promises over the radio silence and bad customer treatment, up to the outrageous triple A price tag on the 'unfinished' product upon release.

But aside of that history and in light of the new Foundation Update with which Hello Games delivers on their promise of ongoing free updates to see their promised game realized one day, we should look at the game itself. Not what it could be or might be in the future, but what it has become. And by no means is it a bad game.

No Man's Sky's Vanilla mode, which is still an option in the new Foundation Update, was easy. Once you got the rough ideas of the game down, you had no problems gathering resources or surviving. It was just an exploration game with a sandbox universe far too big for its content. Quickly one saw that each planet was just a small number of variants that decided to randomly litter the overworld with monoliths to learn the language, plants and especially structures. They had no coherence or sense to them. In space you often found the same cookie-cutter setting with the same aliens and only slightly changed price tags. Sometimes you even saw the same alien three times... not by design, but by actual identity. The cloning bug.
The achievements were generally easy to do, aside of the planet exploration of species or the survival achievement. The main reason was the tedious search for the last alien that spawns as a rarity or the fact you had to survive 30 Sol in ONE sitting on a dangerous planet. It was not accumulative.

The vanilla version of No Man's Sky stands as a warning. Too high expectations and the urge to be swept up in hype forced an indi studio to oversell their own game and vision and they paid a terrible PR price for it. While one can point the blame here solely on Sean Murray and Sony, one has to ask what the other developers thought. Today we see their work which not only introduces crews, building, diversity and an actual survivor mode, it also offers new variety to a previously stale game.

No Man's Sky was delayed prior to release to finish features. It was still released without them. Today we might actually see the original idea of NMS in its 1.0 juvenile version, just with the label of being 1.1. In truth this game never deserved the triple A price-tag. It might not even deserve it now. But NMS is not the villian that people have branded it recently, it is just another indi game that was overhyped.

If you see NMS at a reasonable discount or for below 30 bucks compared to its 60 at release, this game definetly deserves to be explored. And with many people coming before you, you might actually be able to trace their steps as they weathered the initial experience during the games initial downfall. Ingame stories, standing in their own right...

In light of the recent awards, I say give this 'villian' a well deserved hug. In the sea of survival and exploration games, NMS still remains a rarity to be enjoyed.

Boundless, in one word.

This is such a phenomenal game, for those few people (like myself) who wonder what might be over the next hill.  Or past that flickering star.  Or on the surface of just one more planet.  This game fulfills many a childhood dream, and more.

Over 150 hours later, and deep into my SECOND galaxy (after having reached the center of my first), I can say that this game remains awe-inspiring...for the right person.  I'm the type of player, in Morrowind, Fallout, and others, who wanders off over far-reaching hills, often ignoring quest lines, in favor of exploring far-reaching caves, treasures, and dangers to see just how far the world goes.  I swam to the far reaches of the Morrowind oceans, because they were there... tried to climb out of the boundaries of Tamriel in Oblivion, likewise in Skyrim, because there were mountrains.  I tried to exit the greater D.C. area of Fallout 3, chasing a notion that the desolate wastelands might not extend to Philadelphia, or New York.  If for not other reason that to explore the farthest reaches, and push the boundaries, of those worlds. For the sake of it.

This game is built for that very select audience. Those whom struggle to push beyond boundaries. And for those of you who enjoy getting lost, alone, in a nearly infinite galaxy to explore, with no boundaries to limit that exploration...THIS is your game. Ignore the negative reviews, and reach into the endless void of space to find just how incredible, and gorgeous, boundless journeying can be.

Old review:

NMS, oh you little rascal.

By now you all know about this game, I suppose, the lofty promises, the more than bumpy start and the lack of any information since then.

I'm probably one of the only people left still playing and, surprise surprise, still enjoying No Man's Sky.
given, I do not have a lot of time to play it nor do I have a rig that supports it.

Pros:

- looks really nice on a good machine
- eerie and peaceful
- lots and lots of alone time
- discovering a new and funny looking species is quite entertaining

Cons:

- nearly no diversity with the planets; you get barren rocky worlds, populated rocky worlds, "islandy" kinda worlds, some greenish worlds with a bit of vegetation (I have yet to find a pure water or forrest planet)
- nearly no diversity with the creatures (I've found several creatures in youtube videos I have discovered myself as well as run into multiple similiar looking species on different planets in different systems)
- alien interaction is very bland and there's only one in a building besides from the Atlas stuff
- nothing to do on planets or moons. you walk around to find the same stuff on each planet.
- no end game
- system requirements are ridiculous. my laptop can easily run most games on 1080 on low settings. NMS runs on 600x900 with everything low at an astonishing 5-10 fps.
it does not work at all on a friends medium rig.
it runs decently on my gf's high end rig
- that long ♥♥♥ intro every time
- any change in graphics settings needs a restart of the game
- overpriced
- ship combat suuuuuuuucks
- controls are just aweful
- the UI is atrocious 

Verdict:

As much as I like and enjoy "playing" NMS, I can in no way recommend it to any one.
With the empty promises from Hello Games and Sean Murray, the terrible overall performance of the game on several PCs and the lack of any content and diversity, NMS is indeed a failure as a AAA "indie" title.
For me it delivered on what I expected, minus the dinosaurs/forrests/diversity, especially in the exploration and feeling relatively alone in a large "universe". but that is by far not enough for a thumbs up

don't pick this up if you're not totally obsessed with resource collection, aimlessly wandering around empty planets and every now and again zipping to a new one.
and even then: only heavily reduced.

Reviews.178045:
INTRO
This review covers a lot of the political repercussions of the poor launch reception but also discusses some key game features and their improvements. The nature of this review can cause quite a controversy so read at your own risk.

IMPORTANT NOTE FOR IMPROVEMENT
The game is much more likely to achive a greater improvement if the development team is motivated to improve it. Negative reinforcement alone is not a good motivator at all and in fact can leave the person or people in question unmotivated to do anything. I feel that if we want to see good improvements on this game we should give more support to the good features of the game but in so we must not forget the bad ones either.

GRINDING
Well the game has a lot of grinding as do other games and the grinding can be fun, but if you are just playing the game to complete it, then the grinding becomes the main objective and it can become very boring, if you take your time to explore and scan creatures and appreciate some of the good ones then you can expect to have a nice evened out experience.

SIZE OF THE GAME
The game is big, very big. The game consists of more planets than you will ever be able to set foot on so there is that but at the same time this is just kind of an illusion as you are going around from planet to planet, eventually you will realise that there is not a huge amount of variation amoungst the plannets. But, there is enough to give you that illusion if you let it, of course you can nit pick and look really closely and break the illusion but you are only doing that to yourself, take it like a picture best viewed from a certain distance.

EXPLORATION
It is no lie that No Man's Sky has a veriety of means to produce novel situations to the player, this is wonderful and really helps drive your onwards, the creatures that you discover can be very different from one another. However, you need to take this with a pinch of salt, it can't be easy trying to populate a game with all kinds of new creatures when the game is as big as No Man's Sky. There is a wonderful video that explains how the creatures in No Man's Sky are made up, I recommend taking a look at it if you are interested.

STORY
The game has an objective but also has freedom, the "main" objective (if you want to call it that) is to get to the center of the universe, yes you can do that but you can also take your time in doing so, that is how I have played it and I am enjoying myself doing so, you can really immerse yourself along the way and enjoy the game as an exploration.

SPACE TRAVEL
Who does not love space travel, and no mans sky does it wonderfully, I can fly down to a planet and blast off from one with no loading screen and I can explore a vast collection of star systems and fly wherever I want, the game does this brillinatly. The only drawback from this is the inavbillity to fly close to structures and terrain with your space craft, this really breaks the illusion of flight and makes it feel like you are being bubble wrapped and your hand is being held, maybe I want to crash into the ground!!

GROUND COMBAT
The combat in the game is some of the weakest combat I have experienced in gaming. However, the combat is there, it exists and I am happy that they put it in the game, the ground combat at least gives me some sense of danger whilst you are roaming around on the ground doing your thing. However the ground combat is really easy and does not pose much of a threat, this could really do with a tweak.

SHIP COMBAT
Well, the ship combat in the game is a different story, I personally like the ship combat with a pinch of salt but yet again, the inabillity to fly close to objects and terrain ruin it so much, I want to fear the ground and other objects as I battle it out in my ship, I want to use them to my advantage as I take risks by flying close to the ground so that my enemy struggles to keep up. Besides this immersion breaker, the ship combat is awesome and does what it says on the tin. However, it is few and far between, you are not going to be finding a lot of combat unless you go out looking for it and even when you do it can take a while to find it.

CRAFTING & INVENTORY
Of lord of lord, the crafting and inventory system needed a lot of work and work has been done. The inventory system was lacking to say the least and the crafting was simply combing two objects to make one, It felt very tacked on in the game. I am sorry Hello Games but this is one of the things that I couldn't stand in No Man's Sky and it needs an overhaul. I will however give it props that it does work and it does what it says on the tin so I can't complain too much, it is not somthing that will ruin your time playing No Man's Sky but sheesh, it could do with a little touch up.

VALUE
A lot of people critise the game for its price and I completely get that, I do see how the game could be a bit too pricey, yes it is pretty costly but I am keeping my hopes up that with more and more updates the game will become worth the original money that I payed for it. The first update marks a great step towords a great game and I have faith that the updates will keep on rolling out

NOTE ON SUPPORT
I know that the advertisement was really missleading and I know that the game was over hyped by a lot of people but if we keep throwing insults at the game just for the sake of it and just falling into confirmation bias, then all we will see is a crap game. Try not to be driven like a sheep with horse blinders on and make your own oppinion of the GAME and not the ADVERTISEMENT or POLOTICS that run with it. What we have here is a good game, its not the best game by any means but it is not a bad game at all. I have really enjoyed my time in No Man's Sky and will continue to play the game. Be unique and make your own oppinion of the game and don't follow the mass of people that are slandering the game for political reasons alone.

NOTE ON NEGATIVE REVIEWS
The majority of negative reviews are unfortunatly the product of something called "groupthink" (look it up) Where a large mass has come together and followed majority view and slandered the game without any real thought, in fact a lot of the reviews you will see have only reviewed this game, so you can see by this that they are just jumping on the band wagon and giving it a negative review. HOWEVER! before you go crazy on me, some of the negative reviews, in fact a LOT of the negative reviews highlight a lot of really helpful things that the development team can take action on, these are constructive reviews and well explained personal oppinion and I respect them.

NOTE ON POSOTIVE REVIEWS
The positive reviews on No Man's Sky are lacking and I am making an inference based on the key points I have discussed that this is a product of "The bystander effect" (look it up). Yet again, I erge you to make your own oppinions.

Overall I will recommend No Man's Sky not only to people that are new to it but also those that have purchased it before the update, give it another go and please make your own oppinion of the game, don't fall into "groupthink"

P.S
I value all others oppinions and I am open to constructive criticism of my review. Respect people and people respect you.

From one of the worst launches in history to endless performance problems, No Man's Sky takes the cake for biggest disappointment of all time. It is a perfect example of an indie darling that got carried away with all the attention it was receiving, headed by a designer who clearly has no idea how to keep his mouth shut in front of a camera. There have been many games that promosed more than they could deliverbut never one so publicly as this.

Despite all that, No Man's Sky presents us an awesome idea of what games could be and an aesthetic that many will seek to replicate for years to come. Maybe one day we'll actually get to play a game like it that actually lives up to the hype. For now though we only have a dream of what could have been.

So at what price point should you pick this game up at? Launching at $60 for a clearly incomplete and falsly advertised game was a huge mistake, even half that is asking too much. I would recommend waiting until it's at $15 on a sale. It has similar depth and playability of your typical Early Access title (and all the bugs that come with them), and I wouldn't pay a penny more than that.

No Man's Sky was a game I ignored for a very long time. It just didn't seem like my type of game at the moment. That is until a friend of mine was talking about a new game coming out soon and all the cool new stuff they were doing, etc.

I was intrigued and went to take a look on the steampage, after reading everything on there, I was excited, so much so that i went to look at all the videos, interview, redditpages, in short ALL THE THINGS! to find out everything there was to know about the game. I soon discovered all the hype around it and made sure I didn't fall prey to it.

One day after release on PC i chose to buy it. I knew it had some bad press and some stability issues, but i just wanted to see for myself. Luckely, I never really experienced performance issues and I genuinly enjoyed to game for about 30 hours. I explored all the planets in each system i visited, I found all the animals on each planet, went to as much of the POI's as humanly possible and I had fun!
But then it became less and less exciting. Planets didn't have as much variation as i would've hoped. Animals didn't feel really unique and more like different breeds of the same species. And then i just moved on. The game couldn't hold my attention any longer.

Based on my experience, I wouldn't recommend this game to any of my friends. It can be quite cool to start, but it starts getting repetitive really fast. I also know a lot of the reviews before (and probably after as well) will rage about all the lies that were told, missing features, etc. but I tried ignoring those and just focusing on the game as is. In that sense it is not a complete failure and it does some cool things, but it falls short in a lot of areas.

Plan was to evaluate NMS for less than the 2 hours refund window, but that proved impossible. 
The initial startup shows a planet surface with a defective space ship nearby, and remarkably few instructions or clues as to how to make progress.  Even with the copious startup tips on the web, often outdated due to updates, it still took around 30 mins play time just to get running and oriented with some of the controls, and I doubt 2 hours is long enough to fix the space ship and move off the first planet into space. Much of NMS is focussed on the exploration of space using warp drives to travel to distant systems, which is simply not possible in two hours.

I fixed my spaceship and went into space after around 4 hours on my startup planet. Space can be OK, blasting asteroids for some resources, and so much easier than on the planet surface, which can be a grind depending on how resource limited your planet is. It's still great being the first explorer of a planet, and being able to choose the next from effectively unlimited planets. I've found that it's worth spending time on resource rich planets, particularly when the scanner frequently helps to show where exosuit upgrades, crashed ships, or resources are.  It seems a bit of a lottery just how much help the scanner gives, being almost no use on some planets.

I understand upgrading the space ship can be done using crashed ships, but after maybe 10 planets, and upgrading my exosuit to 28 slots, I've found only one crashed ship, and it had one less slot than mine already, so no upgrade. Better space ships were arriving frequently at Space Stations, so I decided to use the Units acquired from exploring, trading, and mining to buy one. Can take a while, but seems more reliable than the crashed ship lottery.

There's lots more to NMS than these brief beginners comments get near to, but I'd certainly recommend the experience. I would have paid full price earlier if I'd known it was such a great exploration platform.  Instead I waited and paid the £23.99 sale price, which is still maybe a bit excessive for a game with more advertised content missing than present, but the truth is it works well for single player planetary exploration and space, and I play it more than any other game at present. I'm sure I'll go back to Elite Dangerous sometimes, but No Man's Sky is great for a more laid back visual experience of exploring new planets.

I'm now at 323 hours, and it's been excellent entertainment. I've maxed out my Exosuit at 48 slots, Ship at 48, and multi-tool at 24. Have a Home Base, with a hydroponics farm growing stuff to sell, so no longer much need for mining, and no looking for crashed ships to repair. Still lots to do, as not tried Freighters yet, nor joined many large space battles, nor escaped often when the space sentinals attack. No other space oriented simulation / game has provided anywhere near the fun, and for just a few pence an hour it's been fantastic value.

Reviews.179792:
If you have a sense of wanderlust, and want to just get away from it all, No Man's Sky is your ticket. At the start of any classic Star Trek episode, the objective is the same: To boldly go where no man has gone before. That's sort of what No Man's Sky is about, and in a really beautiful way.

Every single planet and moon is already old news to ancient alien races, and the mysterious sentinels, but it's new to you. You're most likely the first human to be there, but maybe, just maybe, someone beat you to it. Along the way, you'll find these monoliths, subtly varying from system to system, but they are everywhere. Touch them, and you'll learn about those three ancient races, and the sentinels. The more you find, the more you will learn.

Scattered in shelters throughout the galaxy, you will find the log of a dead traveler. It gets more interesting as you go.

So, there is a story in No Man's Sky, but it's not just about reading. There is also a survival element, which, for the most part, is pretty tame until the environment catches you off guard. Still, that isn't what really shines about the game.

It's the sight seeing. Even the desolate, wind swept worlds deserve a few screen shots. Some creatures are intimidating, and some are amusing. Ships, multitools, ruins, and monoliths all vary. Reports that they don't are from people who didn't explore. You have to travel to see something new. That's what the game is about.

UPDATE/MARCH 2017

The game has been modified with the Foundations update. It lets you own freighters, and build bases that you can teleport to through stations. The bases and freighters don't do much except for expanding inventory, and providing some missions. The designers said that it's more of a prelude for something else that they have in mind. 

It also provides a survival mode that ups the difficulty by a huge amount. I haven't died once in my first run through of NMS, but I died dozens of times in the survival mode. It might be due to a harsh start location.

I may give survival mode more of a chance, but I still think the main value of NMS is exploring new worlds, and piecing together the histories of the various races. One word of advice, unless you're hunting for a particular element, if a world looks dull, leave. Check out another planet, or better yet, another system. The further you go, the more likely it is that you'll see something different.

Before the Foundation update I had recommended this game for those that just enjoy exploring planets and going into space in their own space ships.  I said I wouldn't recommend based on the $60 price point. Luckily, the game dropped in price by 40%, and I believe $35.99 is a fair price for a decent-looking game, so I'd recommend it now. Many will disagree and ask for free handouts. So it goes.

[list]
[*]Since the Foundation update, they've added the ability to not only visit those freighters, but OWN them and gain extra inventory slots for your resources from them.

[*]Docks and space stations now have more aliens seated at them which I was happy about because I believe it makes these places feel a little more lively.

[*]You can have your own base on your favorite world, and move shop if you find a better one. 

[*]You can hire aliens to tend to your house and get you resources while you're away in the galaxy. 

[*]Space battles are more chaotic and you can actually see the freighters getting destroyed as the pirates take out their cargo. 

[*]Resources have been altered in such a way that you end up carefully considering how you'll use them. There have also been many other unique resources added for you to find.
[/list]

The developers have been listening to people's feedback and making changes as fast as a smaller studio can, and in less than 6 months have managed to make many changes and include entirely new features. Having your own freighters and bases is a fun addition that gives players something to strive for in their journeys through the universe, and new modes add more challenge (or less) to how you travel and the decisions you'll make.

Right now 30% found my original review helpful, and that's telling, as only about 30% of people like the game. The developers have stated this game was for a niche audience, and they were right. They didn't go in trying to make a game with killstreaks and meet-ups with your buddy in Dookie System VI. It's a solo experience with rare moments where you encounter things found by others, and in a game with a gorillion planets, you're bound to see something you haven't seen before.

I said before this game could possibly be a 6. Now I'm giving it 6.5/10

[b][Pre-Foundation Review below.][/b]
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Here are my previous pros and cons which still stand with a few tweaks to the cons as the developers have added some of them.

[b]Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*]Lots of planets. After exploring over 30 different planets, so far all of them have been unique in their own way. In a game with so many planets, it's entirely possible you could start out somewhere where the worlds around you all look the same. Maybe I just got lucky.

[*]Relaxing. After a long day at work, it's nice to come home and jump in a spaceship and warp into a new system, or land on a new world. I like seeing a cave and wandering into it to find that it's a deep network of tunnels running through a large area of the planet. I like island-hopping on an ocean world, or running from the sentinels as I steal precious albumen pearls. I like exiting a world and seeing freighters and frigates warp in from another system, regardless if it happens pretty much all the time. It adds to the experience.

[*]Great soundtrack. The music really adds to the atmosphere of this game.

[*]Great sense of scale. Some mountains, and some rock formations, really make you feel puny on some worlds. There are also tiny moons that take a couple minutes to fly around, and planets that would take you a while day to fly around if you're flying at surface level.

[*]Flying in your spaceship is pretty cool. Occasionally you'll get into dogfights in space. I've ran from a fight down to the surface of a world for a few hours, and then gone back into space and the pirates were still waiting for me, that was pretty neat.

[*]Art direction. I like the attention to detail in the different alien races, the buildings, the different ruins, the little touches on certain plants or animals. Ship designs are also pretty cool.

[*]Puzzles. I like the math puzzles that appear for some of the buildings you go into. Some of them you start to recognize after doing them a few times, but it's a nice touch and I hope they add more elaborate ones in the future.

[*]No multiplayer. I don't need some brat following me world to world and trying to shoot me down and won't leave me alone.

[*]Runs smoothly. I heard there were a lot of issues getting the game to work properly for lots of people. I have a GTX 950, 16 GB RAM, and 500 PSU. Haven't had one single issue with this game. Again, maybe I'm just lucky. Or maybe people thought they could play this on their Famicom.
[/list]

[b]Cons (suggestions really)[/b]
[list]
[*][strike]Can't board freighters and frigates.[/strike]

[*][strike]I want to see the frigates and freighters get destroyed slowly by space pirates if I do nothing. I'd like to see the big ships fight back against the pirates. Which brings me to my main issue.[/strike]

[*][PARTIALLY UPDATED]I'd like to see more life instilled into the game. I like exploring a world and getting that desolate feeling that I'm the only one there exploring it. But I don't like going to a space port where ships are arriving constantly, but no one gets out. [strike]The chairs in the lobby are empty.[/strike] No one else walks in and makes small talk with the Gek at the front desk of a outpost. There are no aliens sleeping at one of the camps you'll find. The ships coming and going is a nice touch, as are the bigger ships warping in, or small ships flying overhead while you're exploring, but it doesn't go that extra mile that you'd find in a polished product, I believe.

[*]More alien variety. This goes for the races you can talk to, and the ones you scan. Every once in a while you'll spot something unique, but usually they tend to follow a similar bone structure. This game could be any 3D modeler or texture artist's dream! But it doesn't push it enough.

[*]No fights with the locals. Let me stir something up with the Gek that tries to pull a fast one on me with selling some cheap piece of junk. I don't care if the sentinels come in and torch me, but I would like more challenge. It's fun when you arrive on a high security world and get attacked for messing with anything or simply breathing in the vicinity of a sentinel.  I'd like to see better AI and more versions of the sentinels. I'd like to see the alien races get up out of their chairs and pull out a gun and get into a fight with you, and maybe they have shields of their own.

[*][PARTIALLY UPDATED][strike]More treasures and things you can sell[/strike], and maybe create some sort of hub where players can upload really rare artifacts they found while exploring that other players can look at when they access the trade network. You emphasize showing off discovered worlds and species, but how about the other things we find like trinkets, or camps or ruins even?

[*]More technologies. Again, sky is the limit! A gun that sprays lasers in all directions, or shoots electricity, or turns into an underwater scooter that lets you swim faster, I don't know.

[*]Learning the language should help you communicate with locals that are sitting around the trade port and maybe they point you in the direction of something interesting on the world you're on.
[/list]

In the end, it doesn't feel finished. I wouldn't recommend it for $60 right now. I don't disagree with the 5/10 score, though I might rate it a 6 just because I find myself enjoying what's there so far. I do recommend it if you enjoy space games and flying around in your own ship and just landing on a new world to see what's there. Not every world will be a winner, but landing on the ones that are make the journey worth it.

TL;DR; I change my original review to a 'yes', because the recent update is one large step towards what the game could be/should have been at launch, and importantly, addresses a lot of the concerns I wrote about before.

Previous review is below.  In it, I wrote about unimpressive procedural generation which seemed more like rolling a bunch of dice to pick the atmosphere/ground colour, ore types and little else. As with all trivialistic random generators of that kind, everything feels samey - because it does average out over time. What's the point of a planet, when wherever you go, it's a uniform distribution of bump maps and terrain texture?

So compare older screenshots with the current version.  You'll immediately see what I mean.  Now we have the occasional huuuuuge monster/animal.  We have cliffs, nay, crevasses! We have fun/weird blue dirt.  We have base building. We have more than one alien in a room at the same time. More aliens that speak english and actually do things.  More ship variations.  More things to DO. 

So now, the car you ordered that wasn't the right colour, is not only closer to the right colour, you find out when you get inside it that you can bloody change the colour of it.  Doesn't affect the drive, that needs work still, but the fact they patched it, made it cooler, and listened gives you hope for the future.

It's still early access-ish, but I'm now confident it is/will be worth the money.

Previous review below:

TL;DR; Buying this game is like buying a flying car that can't yet fly.  Without the promise of a future update that'll make it fly.  And it's not the colour you ordered.  But you have to sit in it until the refund period expired before you can see if it's any good.

It's a tech demo, and an unimpressive one. Procedural generation is used, but... it's more like someone made a PRNG cough up 10-20 values that determine planet atmosphere, primary terrain colour, vegetation level and a handful of animals rather than anything truly generative and complete with requisite geological singularities and points of interest. 

Want canyons?

Mountains?

Craters?

Hell. Rivers?

Play Minecraft instead.

I know the backlash is hard, Hello Games, and I know how it feels when users don't appreciate the man hours. Hell I know what it's like to have a financing partner pressure you into releasing a polished turd. 

The only logical next step for this game is a massive patch that makes it, well, a game. Without that, I foresee the company dying and dying hard.

For that reason alone, and with the expectation that Hello Games has also arrived at that conclusion I'll tentatively recommend this game in general, but as gamers we shouldn't have to "bet" our disposable income on an unconfirmed patch.

--UPDATED REVIEW--

So, here we are. Months down the road, with a new update that has brought the people back.

This review is as of 11/28/16, a few days after the 1.1 "Foundation" Update was implemented.

-----
PRE 1.1 REVIEW:
-----
Since release, I've always gotten exactly what I wanted out of this game. I wanted to explore a galaxy, bit by bit, and enjoy a tranquil experience listening to my own music and marching through the endless spaces of No Man's Sky. I followed the Atlas path at the start and got a few galaxies in, enjoying myself throughout. The exploration was fun, the planets were interesting. There was some repetetive feelings, but as an 'experience' the repetition actually brought the gameplay in line with what I wanted: a nearly-mindless, sprawling experience. 

I found my own fun, naming things in silly ways and doing silly things with my time in the game, walking around and exploring planets and learning alien languages and seeing what there was to offer. It was always something interesting. It was also not an experience for everyone. My ability to find my own fun and use the game as a medatation after a long day immensely improved my experience, but these were not intrinsic to the game itself, simply a quirk of my personality aligning with the developer's expectation, rather than the hype that it was blown up to be. I am that small percentage of player that wanted what this game offered as it was. It was a visually appealing walking simulator with some basic crafting and a simple story that it wanted me to follow. I did, happily, and found a lot of enjoyment in the game.

All that said, the developer's long silence and the lack of communication was troubling, and I understand all the backlash the game recieved. I didn't buy in: I had what I wanted. If the game had stayed as it was, I'd have happily continued to enjoy it.

As it stands, I give the game an 8/10. Not a perfect game - deeply flawed, by many estimates - but the game that I wanted.
-----
POST 1.1
-----
So, now we are at 1.1. The Foundation Update! Bases to build, new gameplay elements, a "creative" and a "survival" mode to go along with the "Normal" space-walking-simularor chillfest.

--SURVIVAL--

Survival is a totally different game. The difficulty that some wanted is absolutely there, and in spades. It is a test of endurance and tenacity. Death carries weight, the enemies are dangerous, and sentinels are all-too-happy to escalate their use of force. The deadly planets are deadlier, the resources are slim, and every victory feels earned, rather than simply given. 

I spawned on a radioactive planet, 10 minutes away from my crashed ship. What followed was two hours of the most intense, difficult experience I've ever had with No Man's Sky. Running from cave to cave to avoid being cooked alive by radiation, scrounging up resources to keep my life support going, harvesting the materials to repair the ship... it was incredible, and difficult, and very fun. Launching off that god-forsaken planet felt like I'd won the game.

And then space pirates spotted all my rare materials and blew me into the vacuum.

10/10, would sob into my keyboard again.

Survival can be a frusturating experience, but the emphasis on difficulty requires patience and careful planning on every action taken. I highly recommend it, especially if you are a fan of Dark Souls/Demon Souls/Bloodbourne.

--CREATIVE--

Creative is... well, a simple creative mode. No achievements, no need for resources. The planets are your plaything, and you can explore and enjoy as you will. It does exactly what it says on the tin. Relaxing and interesting, especially if you simply want to explore the new options for base building and freighter customization. No score, it is a sandbox mode an nothing more.

--FINAL THOUGHTS ON 1.1--

So, with the 1.1 update, No Man's Sky is finally on the road to becoming the game promised to the entire fanbase. I was content with the origional, but the update is welcome content. The planets look better, there are more variations on terrain, flora, and fauna, and there are many more things to experience and enjoy. Survival adds a difficult, new experience for those who enjoy a challenge, Creative is a fun sandbox to experience the new additions, and Normal mode is as it was... just with more things to do.

Updated Score: 8/10

Welcome back to No Man's Sky. It's going to be an interesting ride.

[EDITED FOR FOUNDATION UPDATE]

Yeah, I have over 60 hours and, somehow, I'm mostly enjoying my time.

However, you can't argue that this is kind of a broken, unfinished game and certainly not for everyone. Every planet that you visit makes you less impressed with the lack of variety. You soon realize that everything is repetitive and superficial. There's no consequences and no sense of progress. Technically, things are not good either. Frame rates are atrocious. The game still rarely crashes or get sluggish for no reason. Texture and geometry pop-ins left and right.

It's worth noting that some announced features never made into the game. For instance, there was never a solar system simulation in place. Clearly these planets were never intended to rotate or orbit on each other. There is a sky box with a fake sun rotating around each solar system and you can't travel seamlessly through the whole galaxy. Weather, temperature, terrain, life forms and pretty much everything is entirely random.

Some people spend dozens of hours in this game not because there's a lot to do. It's just that everything that you do takes a lot of your time.

Still, you might be surprised by the gorgeous visuals and the delicious sound design. The Atlas interfaces are awesome. The weather effects are scary and convincing. When I ride my spaceship I feel like I'm relying on a tin can going through a harsh environment. Exploring caves and underwater are an out-of-this-world experience. There's something about being able to travel freely from planet to planet and see what they have and how they look like. Is that what I enjoy? Really, I can't tell. There's a subconscious tickle that I can't really explain.

Nevertheless, I would recommend the game itself - on a sale - if the developer was completely straight about its shortcomings. But that was not the case. Don't send money to dishonest people.

[FOUNDATION UPDATE]

Base building: Now you can build a base to your heart's content, much like Subnautica. You can only build on some predefined spots that need to be located. The building process goes fine for large structures but becomes finicky when dealing with small objects. In a game about exploration, there seems to be little point in owning a fixed settlement (you can have only one at a time). You do get virtually infinite storage space and resource farming and you need to "hire" alien companions to research new items and blueprints for you. You can build your own trading terminal. Your new friends have the same models and animations found on the original game, but they speak english this time, for some reason. You can also "teleport" between your base and the last visited space station and your spaceship goes along with you somehow (but wouldn't spawn on your personal landing pad).

Freighters: The large static freighters found on the original game can now be purchased for large sums of money. They provide about the same storage capacity of any spaceship and you can land inside them. You need to be on its bridge to transfer goods between your spaceship and your freighter's inventory. You can magically spawn them on the sky of your current planet (NPC spaceships travelling around will glitch through). And that's it.

Others: There were some marked improvements over the terrible texture and geometry that suddenly pops into view, but they are still there. Some models and textures got a remake, which isn't always a good thing. You can find out about a planet's main resource deposits before landing on them. You can deploy some gadgets to do a save point, a custom waypoint, to find nearby outposts or a new habitable base. Last but not least, there's a new quick access function to charge or repair your gadgets on the spot.

Conclusion: The core of the game remains largely the same, including its worse flaws. And I did not forget the developer's outright untruthfulness.

Short Edit: Changed to Yes to support Devs updating the game now, worth a look but only at a very low price point, perhaps $10 if you have a casual interest in a light exploration game, $20 if you love the concept and think you will get your moneys worth. Was never worth the initial asking price.

It's an attractive looking game, runs okay on an i7 4770 with an nvidia 760 card with medium graphic settings at 1080p.

Not much to do other than explore similar looking planets and systems, the scale of the galaxy is so large yet so similar that exploration is very limited in terms of encountering "different" things.

The whole procedural system generates very repetitive environments and creatures, yet perhaps worst of all the experiences are very similar.

Could of been better designed, seems like a small studio designed game that took an engine that can produce a limited amount of variation then scaled it up massively.

Wouldn't recommend at this price point, though worth getting on sale at $10 or so.

Would consider changing my review if new content patches are released in the future, would very much like to see changes in the scale and distribution of the playable universe to add more detail and less "bloat". Some ideas that would make this game much better (imo) follow:

- Not every planet should be covered in life, life bearing worlds should be few and far between to make their discovery more interesting.

- The planets in this game have no significant climate variations across their surface, no polar caps, no glacial regions, no mountain regions, no deserts or significant ocean features, they have very little "variation" - which makes them very "gamey" and less real.

- PG content should be based on reality to add depth and variation and reduce blandness

- Moons are very much the same as planets with no significant variations

- PG system produces very samey planets and moons

- PG system in general is very repetitive 

- Mountain ranges are insignificant and not really discernable

- Cave complexes are everywhere but very similar

- Oceans are like scattered lakes, the distribution of land and water reminds me of fractal landscapes in the early civ games, the PG algorithm just can't generate "variation" or anything that is "real"

- No really extreme landscapes, like active volcanism, or whiteout conditions, 

- The weather system is very meh, the occasional storms are a hint that the weather systems could of been so much better, more variated, more adverse weather, more windstorms or duststorms, the existing engine is close to this but it never gets it.

- Planets are all the same, no gas giants, dead worlds, desert worlds, words with just an ocean, or just a glacier, no extreme worlds or tiny moons and asteroids.

- Asteroids or rubble in space is everywhere, can't see space for all the rocks, really stupid idea as it makes the game more gamey

- Asteroids are all the same size, no real variations like the variations in space enginners, different shapes and sizes etc.

- Approach to a planet, and flight is very simplified, like child's play, there is no challenge here, no re-entry effects or differing approach angles etc. A simple overlay of reality, like gravitational accelerations or optimum approach angles, lift effects etc could of made the game much better. Can't even fly into terrain, everything sort of hovers.

- Hovering rocks are stupid, no real rock formations of any interest.

- No "significant" canyons on any of the worlds I explored, no massive caves or craters, no real "features" that would define a world by its topography. 

- Altitude maps are very "average" no valleys, no gorges, no highlands and lowlands, oceanic crust regions etc. Just a averaged map with little differences.

- Animals are probably the best bits of the game, but the PG system seems very constrained in its generation of animals, just bland animals with restrictions on size and body shape. They could of "gone to town" here, with no limits and really created terrifiying creatures that could tear you apart! But the animals all conform to a limited series (good within these limitations, just restricts diversity)

- PG plants are also very limited, they have good variations within their tight restrictions but there is no "wow" moment for different plants.

- PG system in general is very reigned in.

I could go on and on, I feel the PG system could of been so much more in this game, as it is it just doesn't generate that diversity of content that makes it worth exploring, this coupled with the terrible universe layout, and absurdly coloured skyboxes makes it very offputing to invest time in exploring. 

I was mostly let down by the lack of attention to the core of the game, the PG system, I feel it has been solidly designed, but it has been designed by a developer that hasn't consulted with, for example, a sci-fi writer or someone with lots of imagination. It generates "content" but it doesn't generate a universe to explore. 

Overall should of been released at a lower price tag with early access, so that revisions could of been made before release to keep people playing, and so that it could of been tested and perhaps more importantly "played" before release.

Perhaps a successful financial release, but the game itself was (in it's current state) a flop.

I've been enjoying this game.  
The variety of planets and animals, some more diverse than others, has kept my attention and kept the experience varied.  I am a sucker for collecting resources and upgrading, which is a core mechanic of this game. There is a variety of resources that need to be collected in order to: stay alive, keep exploring, and make upgrades. The game does a good job of putting something interesting "just around the corner". I've gotten lost in caves by chasing the next cache of Aluminum, or walked several miles from my ship to see what's over the mountain or to bypass the police. And landscapes are gorgeous. I've had to stop and admire the roses on several occasions. Upgrading your suit/ship/weapon is satisfying with noticeable changes and decisions of balancing space, resources and playstyle. Learning the alien languages is a neat idea and some understanding of it help with certain parts of the game. To max out your suit/ship/weapon will take a fair bit of time and exploration. I an just approaching this point at 50 hours and expect to have many more filling out the storyline, languages and milestones. A satisfying game for completionists.

I've been disappointed with the complaints I've heard about this game, so here's my take:
[b]Why I'm ok with most of this game's "problems":[/b]
[list]
[*][b]Lack of animal type and AI[/b] - Animals are part of the background for me. They are there, sometimes they look the same, sometimes different. Enough for me to say, "look at that guy. Neat!" or "is that gonna attack me?"
[*][b]Flying Low[/b] - They put a ground "buffer" to keep your ship from hitting the planet. This ensures that I don't crash my ship into the planet. I'll take that.
[*][b]Space battles[/b] - You can fight pirates in space, or attack freighters. Not super frantic, but reasonable encouters. I'm not here to play freespace, I'm here to explore.
[*][b]Ship controls[/b] - Yes, you aim with your mouse, not hard to get the hang of. You don't play racing games with a keyboard, why would you steer a ship with one?
[*][b]Multi player[/b] - Listed on Steam as single player. Know what you're buying before you buy.
[*][b]No tutorial[/b] - Goals in this game are whatever you set for yourself.  It will not hold your hand and you'll need to set your own agenda or learn through experimentation. I respect and enjoy that design choice.
[*][b]Repedative/grindy[/b] - Game are allowed to to do this. It makes the accomplishments more meaningful.
[*][b]It is hard to die[/b] - Some planets will be more of a pain to explore, keeping your suit running will be a task, and space pirates can be annoying, but this is not a survival game. It's an exploration game with survival elements.
[*][b]Orbits[/b] - Orbits of plants around a star would be really slow. Literally a year. don't know what they would add at the timescale
[*][b]Poor storyline[/b] - The story has not been gripping, but there is a vague history slowly revealed through exploration.  An ok, background narrative, but that's not why I'm here. Haven't finished it, so no comment on the "ending".
[*][b]HypeTrain[/b] - I was not on it. Taking "beta" features or dev discussions as promises as to what will be in the game on day one is ridiculous. Kickstarting is backing an idea, not a version of a product. Per-buying comes with risks. Be an informed consumer. I looked at this completed game from the Steam pics and descriptions and RPS. areas of cities from orbit. This has a devastating effect on the local population, because the terrifying noise of the beam cutting through the atmosphere can be heard for hundreds of kilometres, and will deafen anyone unprotected in the vicinity"

Right I thought, I need to get me some of that.  Thus began what was probably my first game grind, running missions, earning bountys, doing cargo runs and saving my credits until I could buy a ship large enough to mount this weapon of mass destruction.  And I have to admit, I had a blast doing it.

Then the time came, I had my Panther Clipper, I had my Large plasma accelerator, I even managed to earn the rank of "Deadly" (One short of Elite).  I was in the Sol System with my ship of death and I was about to conquer an empire.  I launched my ship, took up position above one of Earths more famous cities, took aim...........and fired.

What did I get?  I lousy pew pew and some grief from the local police.  So I flew closer and tried again, still nothing, no destroyed city, no atmosphere torn appart by my death ray, no ear splitting boom.  I actually ended up hovering a few feet above the city hammering at buildings with my now very underwhelming uber weapon without the desired result.

So I quit the game and never played it again.

Lesson learnt, Game mechanics can't keep up with my imagination.

And here I am today, I've played No Mans Sky for over 80 hours and while I've really enjoyed my time playing it I've also realised there is no hidden depth beyond the core game play and the things I thought I would be doing I'm not............. because I can't.

People have already listed all the missing features which no doubt resulted in the game feeling shallow and empty.  Aliens do nothing, planets while looking different are in reality very samey resource wise when you get down to it and the whole galaxy feels homogeneous.  I was able to find all the resources I need in every system I've been to.  Ship fuel is so common it fills the void between planets in the form of asteroids that are EVERYWHERE.

I really REALLY wish there was more variety, we were given four different star colours (yellow red, green and blue) that don't have a significant impact on the planets that orbit them.   Why not change that to four different types (red dwarf, yellow main sequence, blue giants and super giants) each  with different habital zones, rocky airless planets near to stars that are mineral rich but dangerous to mine.  Gas giants further out that ships can fly into and cloud scoop from the upper atmosphere (another thing Elite II did)  Ship upgrades would be more relevant and more dynamic when you have to survive in different conditions.  How cool would it be to watch sunrise on a mercury type planet with a star that fills the sky and sends you rushing for the nearest crater to hide in lest you fry.  Life should be rare, there should be pockets of civilisation not a even spread, we need variety and mystery.

I see a game with lots of potential but not much substance to keep a person playing for very long.  I like that the game is simple to pickup and play without having to have the training of a fighter pilot or the trigger finger and reflexes of the best COD players.  

I wish there was a "maybe" option for do I recomend because I paid £40 for this game and I enjoyed playing it and feel I got my moneys worth.  However I know exactly why so many people are unhappy with it and I share their frustrations.  I hope future updates will solve some of these issues because I truely believe this game could be one of the greats.

FOUNDATION UPDATE: 
You can read my review from launch down below and know that I still stick by my original review remarks. This is my review of the new Foundation Update that just released.
 Having already invested nearly 200hrs into NMS, I was getting pretty bored. The wow factor started to wear off after a while. Once you max out your ship, multitool and your suit... there is really nothing to do but explore and harvest resources to keep going forward from desolate planet to desolate planet. My biggest gripe was that there was no easy way to return to a point of interest or previous planet that you liked. You woud be forced to continue forward into the unknown; gathering and naming and so on and so on. The game had become a bore fest to me. 

Hello Games has just now release their first true expansion update; The Foundation update!
This update rebuilds the game's framework up from the ground (get it? Like a Foundation.) Now allowing more features to be added in the future that will align with what was shown off at that E3 those many years ago. 

Now you can find a planet you like, scan for a suitable base of operations location and build yourself a home/base. A much appreciated and what I felt was an overlooked feature was the addition to scan for resources from orbit in your ship. Thank goodness for this addition. But what's even more cooler is that you can hire NPCs from space stations to inhabit your home/base. So you won't feel so alone now while you're planetside. They can be set forth to research new techs for you or additions to your base/home. There are warp portal between your multiple bases (if you have more than one) that allow you to establish a travel network between your favorite home/base planets. Very cool.

 Freighters are now dockable and purchaseble, allowing you to store 1000 item stacks in it. But be warned, it will take gobs of credits to work your way up to the coveted maxed out freighter. I'm seeing a number like 300-400 million credits to get up to that 48 storage slot freighter. 
 But in the meantime, you can summon your freighter to anywhere you're currently exploring or harvesting in space. System to system, planet to planet, it will warp to you. 
 Be warned again that your freighter will get attacked and I mean A LOT by Pirates wherever you take it with you, so brush up on those dog fighting skills. I do wish Hello Games will add actual combat roled craft to be stored in the hangar bays of our freighter to be used in defense. Or even a manable turret defense system would be a really cool addition. 
The first time I fended off a pirate attack I totally got this BSG or the opening space battle sequence from Revenge of the Sith rush as I dove, rolled and skimmed over my freighter hull trying to get a pip over a pirate ship. It was actually cool and I gasped that NMS is moving towards actual combat mechanics. If Hello Games were to add actual capitol ship fighting against larger pirate ships that would probably be the creme de la creme for me in NMS. The mechanics and damage modeling is already in game for epic space battles so hopefully that day will come.
Planetside combat could use some sprucing up too, like adding actual combat missions. And why arent't there established system worlds populated with towns and maybe even capitol cities of the ruling alien presence? Fingers crossed!
  
The Foundation Update also refines the game graphically and technically with some much needed optimizations. I've yet to experience a crash since the new update. And I swear the clouds viewed from space look much much much betterl. I don't remember low orbit vistas being so gosh darn beautiful over cloud covered worlds.
 
I truly hope Hello Games continues to update NMS... the game is just oozing with potential.
 In conclusion, if you've beem soured by the fallout of NMS post launch... then your mind is already made up and no review is gonna change your opinion. However, if you're like me and you are a scifi/space nut then DEFINETELY check out NMS with it's new Foundation Update.
 I hope the game gets better and better from this point moving forward.
 If SquareEnix can ressurect Final Fantasy XIV from the ashes then I have faith that HelloGames can do so with No Man's Sky.


ORIGINAL REVIEW:
If you're looking for a Star Citizen killer, stay away from NMS. However, f you're looking for a open galaxy to explore and get lost in then NMS is for you. Players feel betrayed over what Sean Murray conveyed in a pre release interviews. However, I personally never got the incling that NMS was somehow this end all be all space sim; even as far back as it's E3 unveil. HelloGames never once showed space PvP dogfighting, or planet side squad based assault missions, base building, faction shaping or two or more players playing the game in some form of co-op. IGN had a lengthy hands on with the game several weeks before it's release and they streamed their gameplay. No where was it shown thet the above mentioned game modes were in the game.
I personally find NMS to be a relaxing journey through space. I've logged in just shy of 120hrs into the game and there is more depth to the game than what people who've not given the game a decent play through. In fact, it seems that some players installed the game and made a staright beeline to the center of the galaxy. Then complained the game had no content or how pirates were too powerful to take on in space combat.
 I didn't leave my origin planet until I had mastered the governing alien's language which made selecting the right responses so much easier. I can't even fathom how any players were able to progress by just guessing at the npc responses. You need certain quests to receive rare blueprints for your suit, multitool and ship. 
 I then fully maxed out and synergized my multi-tool, which in turn made resource gathering and self defense a breeze.
 I mined and traded my way to a nice chunk of money and went from the dlc ship to a mini hauler (30slots). This in turn gave me the ship space to max out the systems and weapons.
 I then went into space and started exploring my origin system. Now very much like real space, mosty planets are barren, enviromentally hostile and desolate of life. However, when you do come across that tropical ocean planet, or jungle planet, Highlands of Scotland-esque and even a nearly comple sandy dune like planet... the game just makes me smile.
 I can only imagine this course would be very similar to real space exploration. Not every world would be this lush Garden off Eden. In fact, a planet like that would be far a few between all of the rocky in-hospitable planets/moons that made up the galaxy.
 Also, I have absolutely no problems with pirates in space or hostile life forms planetside; of course my current ship has a storage of 35 slots, fully maxxed out and is armed/shielded to the teeth.
 So in conclusion... I may be in the minority but I absolutely love NMS and it's sense of exploration. I have taken so many screenshots and my travel album will continue to grow lol.
 I'm in no hurry to get to the center of the galaxy even though I've already know what happens when you do get there.
 I'm more on my five year mission to seek out new worlds and civilizations... to bodly go where no one has gone before lol.
 Stay put on your origin world and build up your arsenal before you go galavanting out into the cosmos. Space can be a very dangerous and lonely place if you try to rush rush.

OBTW- I have a 4790k(OC'd) , MSI Golden Edition GTX980Ti, 16Gigs of ram, Windows 10 and I've NEVER had NMS crash or lock up. My game settings are totally maxed out and I'm locked at a constant 60fps at 1080p. 
I have had this weird bug where it appears too many things happen at once in the game and the game engine goes full decrepit (like FPS drops to 10) forcing a restart. But even then... that bug has occured only 3 or 4 times in 120hours of gameplay.
