Reviews.194982:
If you've stumbled upon this review after all the negativity, good for you!
Now don't go just yet, hear this out:

tl;dr
No Man's Sky screwed their advertisement up and sold the game like it was a AAA title, whilst it could have better followed normal INDIE game development. The Foundation Update does bring new fun to the game, both on the ground as in the air. Tedious glitches still reside in the game from time to time, like impossible to manouvre spacecrafts. The new update is certainly a step in the good direction. Sadly it still deviates greatly from what original advertisement claimed it to be.

Full Review:
The history
We've all witnessed the community go highwire over this game, partly unfair. The simple task of adressing runaway expectations were to late on HelloGames' their part. And the community saw way to much in the game, as I did. But remaining silent on the hype and throwing the game out in the wild with a AAA pricetag made sure of the situation it was in for a very long time. The pricetag simply gave the community the expectation that we'd be receiving a full blown game, whilst it turned out rather bland after release, more a grindfest than anything.
But we've all known this, so nothing new there.

Performance
The game ran pretty smooth on my PC originally, this was before the updates came. I have not encountered the gamebreaking elements other people in the community talked about. It was glitchy at times, where terrain would not generate properly, with more than often ending up being stuck half way through a mountain and the like. Also moving in and out of an atmosphere was tedious, as you'd be watching a slideshow for a couple of seconds, really unhandy if you're stuck in a sub-orbital dogfight with the poor handling the NMS's ships have. Also the popping in of textures was really noticable.
In the new update they adressed the terrain at least. Havn't found a weirdly located station or things like that, and most elements seem to spawn in decently. Now when travelling from space to surface, the slideshow persists, but popping in of textures appears to be a tad more smooth. 

Gameplay
Oh, the gameplay... The original game was devoid of content that would make it worth the 60 Euro's that would've been paid for it. Just after 3-4 hours you'd start to see the copy-paste elements throughout different worlds. Animals all behaved very simplisticly, being either scared or angry at you, or just not giving a crap. Same went for the Sentinals.

Most landscapes seemed to have the same overall structures (with the veiny mountains popping up on just about every planet) The tedious grindfest persisted with you grinding your way through inventory expansions on both your backpack and your ship, with costs greatly increasing with each new addition. Let alone that you'd waste your money on a ship, only to just lose that ship when buying a new one. 

Its both enginious and annoying that inventory slots are required for the use of upgrades (aside from your multitool, the both gun and mining apparatus of the game) It would've been nice if your upgrades had a few slots of their own, so you could maximise the use of your inventory. 

Then there's the ship... A couple of points on it are rather annoying, and havn't been adressed as of yet. 
- The great amount of fuel required for your launch thrusters (which you'll use each time you lift off) It makes little sense.
- the same handling on just about every ship
- manually having to refuel your shield, even when you're dogfighting
- spaceguns not needing to refuel? (whilst everything else does)
- half the ship becomes automated (approaching bays of a freighter or space station, trying to get nearer to the surface)
- not being able to use the mining options the ship has for use on surface mining (would be handy)
- handling being so much better with controller than with mouce+keyboard, whilst it is the other way around when outside of your ship (but possibly personal preferance) The ship could use a better layout for manouvring it. (at least a button that lets you look around with the mouse or something like that)


In the new update the use of your multitool and ship remains the same, although even more powerful upgrades have become available to you, leaving you to scavenge again. No more slots have been added. The procedural generation in both space and surface seems to work more coherent. Planets now seem to vary a bit more as well, with some mostly barren, and others filled with life. And the last also has the plus of rendering a tad easier, so it looks good, and looks to keep the framerate up.

Then there's the element of basebuilding, freighters, research and extra tools:

- Basebuilding
It's fun, its fluid, it's useful for the game, and they made a nice workaround to help you get back to that said base. BUT, an basebuilding feature would've been nice when the game got out, and should not have become such a core part of the game, which it now appears to have become. It is rather nice that it adresses the inventory issue by giving you the option to place extra inventory boxes where you can store huge amounts of a few items, as you can do inside the freighter as well.

- Freighters
Once purchased they can be called upon from anywhere in any galaxy, and become readily available. You're also allowed to build a base inside of the freighter, giving its internals custamisability. This has been done very nicely, with the mostly intuitive basebuilding features lending themselves for easy construction from inside the base, and not being forced to stay outside to make sure things snap correctly. The freighters also have their own inventory slots. (which you can add to with building storage containers, but up to 10 MAX, combined over the base and freighter!!)
Unfortunately the freighter has a major downside, which is also its most important task: keeping inventory. It's rather convoluted getting your inventory from either yourself or your ship to the freighter, let alone the other way around... 
Also freighters work like normal ships, where buying one will make more expensive ones appear nearby, but far from always an upgrade. (I've found freighters costing 30% more whilst missing 3 or more slots of my current vessel)
They now spawn in massive fleets as well, which is really nice to see!


- Research
In your base you can plant various research desks, which allow you to craft more and different items. It's rather fun, as it sends you on quests to find certain elements or people to get the place up and running. This way you'll be taught how it all works and what their uses are. Usually the elements for progress can be found within one or two system jumps. 

-Extra tools
You'll be able to set extra elements down in the game. Like notes for people to find, waypoints to keep your bearings and mobile savepoints, just in case you get into a sticky situation. A very welcome addition which the game could have used on release.

They have also added new materials in game, and new tiers to go through before they can be harvested. The game now presents more goals, which is really nice to see.

Conclusion/my advice
Overall, steps in the right direction, but I think the community was hoping for different things to be adressed. Even with all the additions it still makes it far from being a worthy AAA priced title. So get it cheap, or wait untill there's more clarity on the future updates. This update alone does not make it worth that kind of money yet. If future updates make it even better, this review might go positive.

Reviews.195528:
49h in and nothing more 2 do. Everything maxed out, even the multi-tool and spaceship "styles" I liked most in a nice color scheme. The two things I can do from now on are 1. hoarding money and 2. getting to the galaxy center (y I know what’s there -_- ).

My journey started unbiased. I just watched some YT content of ppl starting out in this game and thought ... I want to explore it too. So I bought it, played it and here is my review.

[b][u]1. GraFX[/u][/b]


[b]1.1 Planets[/b]

I hated the Style in the beginning. I'm not a big fan of pastel colors but came along some planets which were pretty dark with red "vines", barren ice worlds and really nice looking greenish toxic/radiated ones. So, there's obviously diversity here. 
What really broke the immersion for me here were the "load-ins" of landscapes when you fly to and on a planet. It counted 5 detail levels loading in depending on how far away you are from the landscape.
I understand from a programmer’s pov that you have to do the LOD trick to optimize the overall game performance but in this dimension, it's just stupid.

[b]1.2 Space ships, stations / Ground Structures / Aliens[/b]

You have 3 Races with their own style of Structures and stations which are nicely designed. I like the styles.

[b]1.3 Star map[/b]

1st of all I really like the design of the star map just looking from a graphical view. "Color-Coded" planet systems, the feeling of getting lost fast and be a small thing somewhere between the huge amounts of stars. What I didn't like is the way-point system and that you have no option to retrace your steps and revisit (e.g.) your starter planet. It also lacks an overview (like in spore) where you can see the whole galaxy you're in. 


[b]2. UI[/b]

Yeah, not my cup'o'tea. I play exclusively on PC and hate these console constructed UI's but can also understand why game studios struggle to find the sweetspot between m&k and controller. In this case it’s rather scaling towards console controls and that’s annoying as hell to me. Also the waiting time for clicking on intractables, npcs, etc. is way too long. It doesn't feel fluent in any way. Also that there's no option to skip duologue is a missing "quality of life" feature. 


[b]3. Procedural everything[/b]

Love the concept! Execution -> meh.

[b]3.1 Spaceships / Aliens[/b]

The Spaceships are procedurally generated but to a point where there isn't much diversity. You have "body 1" with "wings 4" and "vanity 4" in the color scheme "body 4" and "decals 2". What may look like diverse possibilities is way downscaled "irl" because there are restrictions on how many of these possibilities can occur in a station.
Aliens = same.

[b]3.2 Planets[/b]

The biggest problem I had with the generation was that it overlaps way too often. I saw the same viney structure on ~ 6-8 planets throughout my journey (have been to ~20 systems 17-20 Planets). Creatures are the same deal. I had a streak of 5 planets where I found creatures with the same pig-head only differ in body size and vanity.

[b]3.3 Structures[/b]

Now for the most annoying and not thought through placement of structures.

It doesn't make any sense like it is at the moment. Look at it like a chessboard. 

On square:

A3 -> Command center
A5 -> Resource
A8 -> Manufacturing Facility
C4 -> Alien Artifact (Plaque)
etc.

There are way too many structures on a planet’s surface. Why scattering out so much when a sentient species would have basic logistics down. And what are the Command Centers for? No story background whatsoever. Why are some of them abandoned? We're left in the dark.

It would make sense to have big outposts, like max 4-6 per planet rather than 200 small ones.
And where do the Alien Artifacts come from? And again, why are there so many scattered around the planet?
This concept makes sense for the shipwrecks, debris and resources but other than that it's not conclusive.
I dig the exploration thing, but I'd rather explore an ancient city or temple with like 5-10 words to learn from then this. 
Structure diversity is also abundant. They only vary from race to race always looking the same. After Command Center, plaque, etc. 10 it gets very old and you have to find hundreds for the languages, blueprints, etc.

[b][u]4. Gameplay[/b][/u]

[b]4.1 Spaceship handling[/b]

To someone who has never or rarely played space sims before the "help" you get controlling your ship is really nice. But I started playing space sims in '93 with "Star Wars: Rebel Assault" so give me more freedom please!!! 

[b]4.2 Mining[/b]

Really fun but not enough resources that matter for your upgrades or trading purposes. I figured out the resonator trading on my own btw and that’s what broke the mining game for me.

[b]4.3 Space Stations[/b]

They look really cool! But again not diverse enough to be special in any kind. And waaaay too small.
What about a cantina, a market place for the traders coming in, a red light district, different styles of stations like pirate / trading / religious / etc.? They feel empty!

[b]4.3 "Survival"[/b]

Nonexistent! 
Even the harsher planets are easily exploreable without any of the hazard protection. 
No hunger or thirst.
The only thing is to fill up your life support with materials you find more than enough of on ANY planet out there. Ah and a shitton of plutonium for your landing thrusters which are not upgradeable to be more effective. Really annoying!
Also the Sentinel-Drones are a joke! The time for them to call for reinforcements is ridiculous. You can literally melee them to death long before they send their signals out.
The "aggressive" creatures are no threat at all.

[b]4.4 Languages[/b]

Nice side concept. To learn words and understand a species little by little. Love it! But the way you learn the words is just tedious.
I also liked the puzzles at the monoliths! But, like the number game in Command Centers and Manufacturing Facilities, they repeat too often.

[b]4.5 Atlas Passes[/b]
Like the finger in the center, I had the same feeling when getting my Atlas pass 2&3.
Pass 1 was nice, to find essential resources for your hyper drive fuel!

[b]5. Story[/b]

? What story ?

3 races: Vy'keen = warriors ; Gek=Traders ; Korvax=Explorers/Science
ATLAS "Religious/Philosophic" blah
Get to Galaxy Center to get the finger!
 
That’s literally it!


[b][u]6. Technical[/u][/b]

I had "memory-leaks" after 1-2h making it impossible to play with massive frame-drops (from ~50-60 fps to 7-12 fps). Also tried the experimental version, but no difference. And yeah, my drivers are all up to date.
Other than that I had 1 CTD. 

[b]7. Sound[/b]

Just awesome! All of it!

[b][u]8. Conclusion[/u][/b]

I had fun in the game for about 35h of gameplay. After you max out all your stuff, get the desired styles of your ship and tool and can understand most of the languages there is no more progression to make Also the scanning of flora and fauna of a planet gets very old very soon, mostly because you can’t scan for something "new" and can’t complete the planet in a reasonable time. 
After I played the game to this extent, I watched some reviews (Angry Joe for example) and felt a bit gob smacked.
I can see that many people out there are on the warpath right now, because what we have here feels to me like an alpha. With many balancing issues, missing "quality of life" features, and cut content.

I think the problem for Hello Games was, they ran out of money too quick for finishing their product. They had to hype the crap out of the game to continue working on it. And in the end they got more than a few angry customers because of missing, promised features.
"Procedural generated" doesn't implicate a huge diversity. You can have a black and white plane and a plane, procedural generated from these 2. The result will still only be black and white.

Would I recommend buying this game? For 60 bucks ... rather not. In its current state, 20-30 would be a fair price.
Cheers, Sunny

Reviews.196787:
TL;DR I liked the game when it came out, despite the many flaws and blatant misrepresentation. With the 1.1 patch I'm loving the brutal difficulty in survival mode, and the careful planning it requires. This game won't be worth your money unless you have a healthy dose of imagination, but the systems are incrementally improving. If you want to make your own fun in a space-themed sandbox this is worth $30-$40 (especially if they keep the updates coming). If not, wait for a steep discount to satisfy your curiosity, because for more than $10 you will be disappointed.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Watching the promotional trailers, etc. it's disappointing how much was inexplicably left out. As much as I want to believe that some of those features will be added in as patched content, I wouldn't count on it (just to be realistic). That being said, I've logged about 50 hours on the PC and what's here has been captivating.

That feeling of slowly improving my gear and touching down on a new planet to roll the dice and see what the game has to offer has kept me hooked. Even this many hours in there are planets, vistas, animals, etc. that make me stop and go "cool" or capture my imagination. I'm also enjoying the lore they've created for each alien race (though it's presented in bite-sized walls of text and not as part of any sort of immediate plot).

The actual systems in place are grindy and repetitive. The simulation leaves a lot to be desired that was supposed to be in the game (planets rotating on their axis, planets orbiting their sun, animals interacting with one another and their environment, meaningful alien factions and reputations, flying low to the ground). It's frustrating because with such a vast universe and so many parts in play it feels like this should all add up to more. But they're not [b]moving[/b] parts.

When it's just me, the planet, and the flora/fauna this is the best Spaceman Spiff simulator I'll likely ever play. When I walk into my 1,000th "outpost" to chat up my 1,000th alien (who just stands there waiting for me), it feels like a lifeless theme park. If you don't have Calvin's imagination, and/or you're looking for more game in your game then I'd recommend a pass.

Me, I'll still be exploring (if they update the game, for christ's sake).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

1.1 Foundation Update

A long time coming, but a welcome addition to the game. The base "research" adds a much-needed questing element that introduces the new systems well. Some tweaks to the resource economy also make the various resources feel more unique (not just "red" "yellow" "other"). Exploring the new content will take no more than a few hours so it's not a new lease on life, but it adds (hopefully) a sign of things to come and personally I think it's a big step in the right direction in terms of game design (the new additions are just more FUN than the systems in place at the start).


Personally, the best parts of this update are the three game modes, including "vanilla", "creative", and "survival". I appreciate that they left the standard gameplay more or less as-is for those that enjoy it, rather than radically changing that (and I'm still chasing that final elusive achievement there). Creative mode doesn't do much for me, but it's an easy way to explore the new systems and build a base to your heart's content. Survival mode is my jam--it is brutally difficult compared to vanilla mode, but in ways that make sense. The first few hours of constant death and frustration punished me for trying to approach it like I did the original game. Once you adapt to the brutal curve, it makes No Man's Sky a more thoughtful, tense experience where juggling your systems and inventory feels like making meaningful decisions rather than a pointless slog. For the first time I find myself grateful to see a building in the distance, worried that I'll end up stranded on a hostile planet for lack of fuel, fighting for my life when I get jumped by the wildlife, and feeling genuinely immersed in the game for the first time (after 50+ hours of gameplay in the vanilla version).

Reviews.197903:
I would really like to give this game a thumbs up, but I can't.

The Good
This game is massive. There are beautiful and terrifying planets and systems and a gazillion different animal and plant species that you get to discover and name. There are various schematics, you can acquire that will aid you on your journey. There are mysterious ruins and monoliths and plaques and caves and space stations. There are also aliens that you can interact with.

The Bad
The game is very shallow. There is very little you can do with all of the things I described above. The only group of people this game caters so far are sight seers. For everyone else this game is just a skeleton of a framework. Every place is empty. NPCs just sit or stand in their cubby holes. There are no meaningful conversations, no interesting quests, no Machu Piccu, no Egyptian Pyramids, no Skyscrapers. For all their wonderful variety, all of the planets are somehow turned plain by the same-looking monoliths, ruins and tiny one-room buildings. When you ask "what do you do in this game?" the answer is only "sight-see".

The Ugly
In a nutshell the game is a very poorly ported console game. You can see where it was castrated to have it fit the console-style casual gameplay. You can see where the controls were altered to be usable with a joystick. This game is a marathon runner athlete that had it's legs cut off, and was then thrown onto a wheelchair called PS4. It may still win something in the Paralympics, but it'll never run a real marathon.

Bottom Line
Unless you're a sight-seer, do not buy this game.
Hello Games needs to roll out many many free updates and gameplay fixes before this "game" actually becomes a game. Right now it's just a generator of pretty screenshots.

Post Foundation Update:
As someone who bought at launch without knowing of the hype, this update makes the game worthwhile if you like exporing and building.

The update heavily removes a lot of the spamming warning and constant need for recharges (these are moved to Survival Mode for those who liked them, as well as increased enemy difficulty). You gain a X menu for quick recharging of items, both on foot and in your ship. You gain a Z menu for building, which starts you with a "Note" objects to leave behind for other players, a savepoint, and a scanner deployable, which replaces the randomly placed scanner before.

Destroying deployables grants 100% of the resources back. To begin base building scan the planet for a "Habitable Base," upon claiming it and the planet you can expand it and start recrutiing staff (the section I'm currently at). These staff send you to find stuff to further improve your base and tech, and after three warps, you can teleport back to base from any spacestation. One of the first techs given is a placeable beacon for finding locations later. Your homebase itself is permantly marked on the map. Base parts can also be rotated and colored out of a list of choices. 

Freights appear to be mobile bases, but the one I found cost 15 million units, so I have yet to purchase one.
Water movement seems to have improved.
If you were hoping for the hype, I can't say if you'll like this now. If you liked it already or found it not bad, but lacking, give it another try. If you don't own and are looking to buy, the choice is yours.

Right to this moment (18.08.2016 7:20PM CEST, just marking if they maybe decide to change that) the shown videos and pictures are not only outdated, but far from the truth. 
Taking the first video: We can see a dinosaur-like creature going on a rampage and scare the heck out of the smaller creatures. You cant find this level of interaction between NPC's. There are some creatures that attack others, but not anywhere near this. They attack, kill, and then just sit there.. 
After the 'player' flew into space, you can see a huge fleet warping into this starsystem right in front of him. Not only are there no such fleeds, but also no moving freighters. They are static. And i have yet to encounter a fight between freighters and other NPC's.
The second video shows a desert planet at the end. And this is also something, that the game does not have.

This is just the part, we can see now. The part that players, who didnt follow the games advertisment or development, will see.
But there is also the side i just namend. WE, the ones that followed the game from early on.
Besides the fact that we were promised the noted fleets and fights, we were also promised that there will be more different factions and that affilations with one or the other will have an impact on the game. For the players who want to kill, a military focused faction would be better suited, then a trading heavy faction. And the other way around. But there are literally just two factions. And you can befriend them both without any impact at all.
The next big lie is the dependency of the distance to the sun and the influence of environmental factors while generating the resources of a planet. Not only can you find nearly every ore on every planet, except that there are some that are not on planet X but on Planet Y that is maybe 30 seconds of flight away. 
Speaking of resources: we were promised a wide varity of resources and a Minecraft-like crafting system. The current crafting system is just a 'farm and click.' You get the stuff you need, and press a button. You need to learn the recepies from the NPC's and cant find them by accident. And the even bigger factor: Most of the resources are just good for selling. Not many things you can craft with them. It mostly comes down to the basic three or four types of ores. 

The four big pillars, as adverted, are ' Exploring, fighting, trading and surviving.' I cant say anything against the first one, you do explore. I cant say anything aganst the second either, i did not fight (at least not with my ship). BUT: I can tell you, that the third one is not what you think it is. You can trade. You can sell your stuff, and you can buy stuff, but you cant buy in a quantity that allows you to trade with a profit big enough to make it worth your while.
The last one 'Surviving' is just a joke. The only thing that can kill you, is your own fault: not seeing that you have run out of energy, or protection. You cant consider the fights with the sentinals as a threat, as long as you are carefull not to get a full wanted level. And even then, you can deal with them easily.

If you want to play this game so bad, than speak with your friends; Everyone will give a bit of money, one purchases the game, and you all play it via Steam family sharing. 

But DO NOT buy this game for its full price. 
IT IS JUST NOT WORTH IT!

Post-Foundation Update Review

The foundation update has added much that this game needed to encourage deep exploration of planetary systems.  

In general, resources are more rare and harder to come by, and the requirement to pick up biome-specific resources to finish of base-building quests and to create a more interesting base means that players must spend time exploring planets to get what they need.

Changes to the planet generation algorithms also result in a much more varied experience, cutting down on the "I've seen this before" feeling one gets after having seen a great many planets.

And base-building/ freigher customization also provide goals that players can work towards -- gathering the right materials to leave one's mark on a planet!

In addition, this update makes the game look more beautiful, and also improves some of the aesthetic issues that used to come up when dropping into a planet or flying around a surface -- pop-in is much less noticeable and smoother now.

The update was a great step in the right direction and definitely leaves me salivating for more updates from Hello Games.

Below is my post-launch review (August 2016)
----------------------------------------------
This game is not for everyone.

It is a resource gathering, gear upgrading slog with admittedly ungainly menu and unimaginative combat.  Its NPCs are static and the story is told through pages in a "Choose your own Adventure" book.  Very little of the experience you saw in trailers is handed to you on a platter: some of it isn't there, but other things may have you scouring the galaxy for ages before you find it.

That said, this game delivers wonderfully on a planet exploring, small rewards feedback loop - and while sometimes I find myself asking why I continue, the next moment along will come some new creature or new sight or experience that fills me with wonder or awe or curiosity.

Did the game deliver everything that excited fans were hoping for? Perhaps not.  But the mystery and loneliness, and the feeling of awe and wonder at finding something new that perhaps no one else will ever see again is enough to keep me coming back again and again.

I have had no issues with performance using maxed out settings on the following rig:

GPU: GTX-970
i7 2600K 3.4GHz
16GB RAM

(Hovering around 60FPS with rare stutters on dropping into a system. It's true that pop-in can be a bit of a problem when cruising around a planet....)

There's a lot of controversy over No Man's Sky currently around release. All in all, what matters most is what it actually is in its current state. So I'll talk and review it for what it is, not what it *should* or *could* or *might* be in the future.

I've loved discovering new weird creatures and flora and trying to think up clever names for them. My particular favorite so far was a very red planet I named Blood Gate. On Blood Gate there are all sorts of things that looked like they crawled straight out of the gates of Oblivion. Giant Blood Leaves, Hydrogen Lickers that dangle their tongues upwards to the sky, Blood Plumes smoking in the distance, Amber eyes and Toeshells scattering the ground. I love naming discoveries and making that planet something my own.

The actual "game" systems can be a bit shallow. Finding upgrades and gathering resources can feel tedious and repetitive at times. Especially if they become your primary goals while playing. I actively try to break up my time doing those things so that they don't let me forget what I really enjoy about the game. Discovery, wandering a new planet's surface and scanning everything in sight. An acid rain storm blowing in and taking a brief respite in a nearby cave to let my suit's systems recharge. The sound design in general really helps the immersive experience. And the game is gorgeous to boot. Perhaps not gorgeous in a "these textures are super high res" sort of way. It's just that structures and color palettes come together to create very visually interesting vistas. 

It's almost always a gorgeous game no matter what planet I set foot on. There are a couple of ugly ducklings here and there, but every planet I've been to seems to have a redeeming factor in one way or another... if you look hard enough. And I think all of that goes back to my overall impressions of the game. If you want a game where you can pop it open and have a chill walk around a planet's surface, admiring the strange rock formations and stuff the game generates... this is your game. The game's systems won't necessarily encourage you to see the best parts of those experiences, so if you aren't the type to set your own goals and run over those hills without a waypoint to lead you to them... it might not be what you're looking for. 

This is a fault in the design to me, that the best parts of the game can go unseen because the systems encourage you to grind your way to a better ship inside space stations. Many people will dislike the game for being too grindy, and to an extent they're totally right. If you can't get past those systems you won't enjoy the game. But for those few seekers and adventurers content to see this universe for what it is rather than what it isn't... then this may be one of the more impressive video games you've seen in a while.

I think I've played NMS long enough to have a good feel for the game (49 hrs at this writing) so here goes.  First the the disclaimers: NMS is not a fast paced high action FPS space sim.  It is also NOT a multiplayer game where you can meet up with your friends and declare war on everyone else in the game.  I think these two facts are the reason for a lot of the negative reviews.  As for complaints about it being repetive, every game I have ever played as been repetive in some way.  I think it's the nature of video games.

What NMS is first and foremost is an exploration game with some survival components.  The survival part may get larger as the player nears the center of the galaxies/universe.  I don't know yet since i'm in no hurry to do that.  The player has to explore for pretty much everything, minerals, component recipes, equipment blueprints, and sometimes even ships.  And there are obstacles that provide varying degrees of difficulty.  In most cases the game is more of a laid back methodical exploration of the game world.  If that is the kind of game you like ( I do ) then definitely give it a try.

Some things that were pleasantly suprising for me:
The crafting was pretty much glossed over in all the prerelease hype.  I was expecting a very shallow crafting component to the game but it is surprisingly more in depth than I expected.  While not extremely extensive it provides enough variety to keep it somewhat interesting and I'm hoping that as I progress it will become more extensive with more components, more upgrades and more equipment.

The game lore/language component has been providing more enjoyment than I expected.  I started learning languages to help get some of the blueprints and component recipes and found myself trying to learn as much language as possible.  Learning the language results in getting bits and pieces of the game lore and now it's like reading a good book.  I want to know how it ends. 

In short, if you're looking for a fast paced shoot 'em up space sime give it a pass.  But if you like games that require some thought and patience definitely give it a go.

UPDATE WITH FOUNDATION EXPANSION

When first launched I enjoyed the game quite a bit but it did get rather boring after a while.  The increased difficulty and crafting was not there as I had hoped.  The recent expansion is a big step in addressing that.  I now play mostly in survival mode.  Survival mode is not for the weak hearted and is very challenging.  You will die.  You can restart at the most recent save point which occurs every time you leave your ship.  I have imposed a personal permadeath on myself and start over when I die.  That may change as I die a LOT.

[h1]Longer, Maybe More Precise Version[/h1]
I've had more fun watching the god awful Sword Art Online 2 which is hard for me to say. I know I shouldn't compare one form of media such as Anime to a Game but I'm just pointing out that I enjoyed a series which killed itself in it's own second arc of the first season but then resurrected to turn it from a MMORPG about swords into guns and such. I'm sorry, I launching into a review of anime when I should be reviewing this piece of shit...

I have spent 12 hours atm in this game, have been to 9 celestial bodies, have several mid-point milestones, and over 1.3 million units (currency). I have seen this game for all it is because I have realized that there isn't shit to do. If someone more thoughtful had been in charge of developing this cheap chinese iphone that's actually just a piece of plastic than maybe it would've turned into a real piece of technology. I'm gonna come straight out with it, this game has nothing to do unless your interested in endless exploring of planets with the exact same reused assets and barely any distinctions between each planet. There are 2 parts to this game: Exploring monoliths/beacons/colonies/outposts/overrun buildings/abandoned buildings and mining the shit out of everything. Sure, this game "Infinite" seemingly as it would take any person more than their entire lifetime to explore every planet for just one second, but is that really an acomplishment? No, because the planets are procedurally generated which translates to "We made a code for how each planet is made using these assets", and if you don't understand what that means or why it's bad than you should watch an hours long gameplay video uncut and see how fresh the gameplay is. I'm sorry but I dont enjoy traveling to different planets that happen to have the exact same texture for the surface with different tints or the fact that every planet I go to has a breathable atmosphere, fuck it every planet has an atmopshere at all. IDK, maybe it's just my luck that I ran into planets full of life but I was hoping for some diversity.

I've compared it before to Stellaris and while, yes I know, Stellaris isn't spacefaring but a strategic game with stupid rules and the ability to control a procedurally generated galaxy with size and shape aswell as other lifeforms. Atleast Stellaris didn't pride itself on it's animations for tactical battles, because it has AMAZING animations if you ask me but thats not the point. No Man's Sky has based it's entire selling point off of an expansive galaxy that looks great for the first hours until you start piecing everything together. Neither great games Starbound and Stellaris that take settings in space [u]similiar[/u] to No Man's Sky succeeded in graphical achievement alone. No, they succeeded from the activities in the game besides sight seeing which I think is nice. I didn't spend $60 bucks to sight see reused assets, I came for the adventure but I get didn't shit. The reason I wanted to compare this to Starbound is because, there's diversity to the planets and star systems. Plus, at the end of the day you have something to do in Starbound, while it may not my cup of tea, it's still good. 

Anyways, if you actually made it to the end and read all this shit than congrats, I need to figure out how to perfect my reviews if I actually wanna put the rest of my unrefundable games to use so any feedback is appreciated (even negative) and I thank you. Oh right, 1/10 Walking simulators aren't my type of game and I came here for a spacefaring game

Reviews.207886:
The No Man's Sky features planetary exploration, deep oceans, space-based battles, predators and prey, and much more across various procedurally-generated worlds. Each world has its own ecosystems, rewards, and dangers, leading the player through the "Core" areas of the game: Explore, Fight, Trade, and Survive.


Pro's:

This game initially has a ton of depth, a very interesting universe to explore, and decent combat mechanics. I was surprised that the masses were as interested in this game as they were when it was announced, it seemed like a pretty niche game. I can't help but feel like a lot of the negative reviews are people who the game quite simply wasn't made for.  Also, the negative reviews are frequently coming from those that are "mad" that the game isnt running at 120 fps or that the PC version was delayed beyond the PS4 version.  

If you are an action game junkie or someone that only ever plays AAA games. It may not be your cup of tea. However, if exploring space and experiencing the scope of the universe while surviving in hostile environments and just enjoying the immersion of it all, sounds like your cup of tea, you should definitely pick it up. 

The game feels like a unique hybrid of MMO space game with a survival game like Minecraft or Ark. But I can imagine with the base building and other features the developer has coming and the other additions, it will become a truly engrossing experience. 

I can't stop thinking about going back to it. 4 hrs after release and I had to force myself to go to bed. It is like Elite in the sense you have to use your own imagination a bit while exploring and kind of narrate your own story. Has some issues but the sense of awe and enjoyment of discovery are still there for me. This is a love it or hate it game for sure.


The Con's:  

In the long run, I feel the game might become one dimensional and repetitive (without the Hello improvements mentioned earlier). Currently, it can be borderline frustrating at times (constant inventory and exo-suit management). No quests, no set character, no interesting aliens (NPCs lack meaningful personalities). Hello could have made the planets feel more alive. 

The complete lack of direction doesn't help pull in the masses,  Many will ask, What am I doing? Why am I doing it? Give me some motivation to keep playing it. 


Overall, I really like the game so far.   With some improvements and tweaks, this game could be come a real gem.

It's a BIg Chewy = 7/10

Notes on NMS Foundation Patch

As many moderated-non-hater users, I enjoy NMS from the very beginning, even if I realized that the game proposed for 59.90 euros in August was far of being finished. Patches became then fixing some majors and many minor issues the weeks after the release without actually solving the main problem of the game: it still remained clearly unfinished. After several weeks of absolute silence, Hello Game’ staff brings us a major patch and new forwarding promises: Foundation. These are my notes, thus subjective tips, on the patch after more of 50 hours of playing: 

1.	I really like the possibility of founding a homeworld in which I could build up my busyness with a fully functional landing base, store mining elements (great thing, even if I could not understand why the store boxes cannot have their access point into the base)  and culture exotic plant species of both high commercial and useful value. I also really appreciated to can use my previous-to-the-patch saved status (credits, ship, mined elements and last position into the galaxy). 

2.	Recruiting specialists to acquire new blueprints and technology is really funny and gives the game new life and sense to me. Even if the quests from each alien collaborator are more or less quickly achieved (and they are quite limited in number), interact with “someone” that speaks an unequivocally comprehensible language and learns you not quite few of things in this infinitely solitary Universe of fools is something of great comfort.

3.	Even if I could realize that new fauna forms where added, they still remain quite childish and most of them without any interest (if you need some new bioidea, call me: I’m a biologist open to a job design ;-) ).

4.	Flying land and space with my ship was what I enjoyed the most in NMS. Some info was included now on the board, it is ok even if reference direction is always missing (who can explore whatever and wherever without a visual crystal clear compass or something like?). But now, flying mode have a huge problem to me: slow rendering making the action impossible because the ship stalks. I have a good gaming machine, well updated and so on, and flying definitively doesn’t work with this patch as it happened at the release. Space battles are too simply horrible in my machine with this patch, without talking about entering the base planet in warp.  

5.	I liked the idea of having a freighter, call it wherever I am and evolve its capacity by buying new ones (as was for the ships: could we find abandoned and ruined freighters to claim them and repair?). And I definitively like to see the silhouette of the ship in the sky of my homeworld, but such a huge inner space in such a huge ship with at least four crew members where only the captain is available to interact and just for managing the location of the storage is not a dream. This is something added to the game that, to my eyes, is an unfinished concept with a good face. I felt the same thing when I discovered that rooms opened by the hard to obtain Atlas passes where a deceiving “waste of space”, just places to grab some carbon, plutonium or matter alike that can be found without any problem on every planet or moon. I must agree that I was expecting something more (shortly something) from this patch concerning Atlas passes and I felt actually a great disappointment.    

6.	The new patch, then, permit to us to found a base and explore from it the whole star system in which we established our base. Great! One of our alien collaborators strongly and comprehensibly asks to build a beacon “to not be lost during exploration”, obvious, said to myself. This beacon works well in the star system of our homeworld, but if we pretend to “explore” other systems in the galaxy, even in the neighborhood, and then come back to our base planet, we were definitively lost. I cannot understand this mistake, because to my eyes this is a big one. I want to jump out of my star system and explore all around, and then jump back to my system using the galaxy chart that shows me crystal clear the signal of my beacon. The galaxy chart is something that must to be globally and urgently reviewed by HG’s staff. We are talking about exploration, guys!!!

7.	When I saw that I could build an automatic mineral extractor, I said to myself: this is great! Once I get all the components and I understood how to use it, I put the gadget in a source of Heridium to test it. Great deception! The gadget mines in 10-15 minutes… just 20 units of mineral and it stops until you empty its poor load. What does it serve for, really, when you can mine with your gun extractor in its base configuration the whole source (800-1000 units) in half of this time? 

8.	Teleportation between the space station you landed in and your base is a good way to win time when you need to trade, store or employ an alien for your base wherever you are. Why not to add the same trait into the cargo, taking in mind that the only thing that we can make with freighters from outside it is just to send materials to theirs storing placements? 

9.	Alien bases and monoliths and alike are mostly absent in planets I could explore after installing Foundation patch, what made me think specially about portals and all the energy that some users put to understand their meaning. Their absence (at least in my exploration) suggests that this very interesting mystery of NMS is just other thing that users very wait of the game that the game is not able yet to deserve.

I will continue to play NSM even its unfinished scope (I hope not as infinite as the space HG says to have created for us) only if the flying mode is revised and works properly in my machine and galaxy chart be refund. Even if I’ve lost the way of the Atlas ‘cause I had have sold the pearls and when I visited the last Atlas station I couldn’t present the ten ones (and it was out of consideration for me to restart the game!). Even if I will not use again the automatic extractor and certain bugs keep me out of the immersion sometimes. To me, NMS still represents the possibility of a great voyage, the kudo of a unique place where to be settle and quiet and active, and in a moment to get out for exploring and get this pretty special thing that is unique: the discovering by itself. It is true that other games are deserving it quite well. HG’s people should be consider more seriously their competitors and the users so far to give the concept of NMS the place that it merits.   

For all this above I only recommend this game to people that accepts that nothing is perfect but perfectible (and are patient), that likes space crafting and mining single player but NOT multiplayer or collaborative games, that enjoys travelling without a clear sense nor direction but a full spirit of evasion. And, hey HG guys! I am looking forward to your new patches: The Atlas way obliges you. ;-)

I can't recommend this.  At 2.5 gigs, the only thing you're paying for is the planet-generating algorithm; the game on its own is MAYBE worth $30, but I wouldn't buy unless it was $15 or less.

The Foundation update has brought me back to this game after around 37 hours played on the original version and a massive and frustrated break. ORIGINAL REVIEW:
No Man's Sky was riddled with launch problems for me as with so many people. Some are resolved, some are still around, but in the 11 hours I've played as of writing this, I've had 1 crash and overall smooth frames.

In the first hour I experienced tons of stuttering caused by the shaders being built. Once that process was done the stuttering mostly stopped. I still experience it from time to time but not in any game breaking way.

I am a long time fan of the obscure video game series Noctis, all the work of a single man. Noctis was a procedurally generated galaxy, planets could be embarked upon, there was "life" on some of the planets (some basic vegetation and a hopping bunny... thing.) It was as bare bones as it could get, but I loved it for its ambition and scale. No Man's Sky to me represented a spiritual continuation of the concept of nearly endless galactic exploration, a shareable database of discoveries (Noctis had this too!) but with the added benefits of modern graphical capabilities and additional gameplay elements as it started creeping towards the 4X genre. Unlike many disappointed people, I never put too much weight on the 4X aspect. Nothing about the footage being shown gave any depth to those aspects of the game, so to me they were if nothing else just little bonuses.

I contemplated canceling my preorder twice. The curse of hype was making me fidgety and the delay (and micro delay for PC) were putting all sorts of worries into my mind. The community's rollercoaster of passion became so off-putting that I stopped participating in it as it was making me anxious over a game I just wanted to peacefully spend time with.

After an hour or so of tweaking, reading threads, reading Sean's Tweets, getting help from a friend, and just bumbling through some test gameplay, I finally got everything to work more or less as I figured it should (playable framerate, namely.) I started a new game and when nothing went terribly wrong after a few minutes of exploration, all of the panic faded. I set out exploring my starter planet and system, then chose to follow the guide to build a hyperdrive and leave the system. I quickly came back and spent over 7 hours straight exploring the entire first system. This is one system of a ludicrous number of them and the game subtly urges you onward towards the center of the galaxy (and then universe), but nothing is set in stone. Everything is up to you.

If you've long been a fan of hardcore 4X space games, this very well may not be your cup of tea. If you want an Elite Dangerous competitor, this is not it. If you want an early taste of Star Citizen, don't hold your breath. These aren't criticisms of the game, just distinctions. No Man's Sky is a colorful, casual game of solo exploration. It's a game for people who maybe just want to be left alone by the chaos of the increasingly online world of gaming. The thought might bother some, but it feels like a game for introverts whose youthful spark of curiosity never really found its way in the world.

I'm not doing a pros/cons list as some of it really is subjective, but I will point out some flaws other than what has been regurgitated in a million ways across the internet already.

Some of the flora is unremarkably restricted in its procedural generation, meaning variants from planet to planet and system to system of for instance a shell-like fungus (species supposedly being unique to each planet) are really almost clones. The fauna can at times start to feel repetitive, but there is enough variety that you can pick out differences and realize that you're recognizing perhaps the front end of one creature and the tail end of another that just happened to make up a third creature on a planet light years away. The colors are at times just way too much. There are scenes of true beauty tucked away, things you'll never see in another game, but often I find myself almost squinting through the candy colored worlds to find my next landing site.

Finally, and most importantly to me, is the concern I have that I am already at 11 hours nearing the mid-way point on maxing my stuff out. [EDIT at 13hrs: I just saw a 32 million unit ship someone posted on reddit, I'm definitely not half-way there.] I haven't been trying to, either. I've only upgraded ships twice (and one was the pre-order bonus ship) and I am already seeing that if I spent a not too unreasonable amount of time mining gold, I could have one of the best ships I've seen thus far in my hands. Furthermore, the ranking of upgrades makes it seem as though I'm already coming across some of the highest powered components, having only travelled between two star systems. It's possible that there's more out there (or in there, towards the center) than I'm aware of, but if I get everything upgraded within the next 10-20 hours, the gameplay would seemingly only leave me with a journey towards the center with no prospect of better items along the way.

But the reason I give this game a positive review whole-heartedly is because whether I ever make the voyage to the center of the universe or not, and whether I feel that voyage is necessary or not, there are 18 quintillion planets out there and I'd be happy to just fly around and screenshot as many of them as I could. I'm not everyone, certainly.

With the game now out, I feel pretty confident that despite its abyssmal reception, Hello Games has every opportunity to patch things up and start to introduce neat little additions. New ship types (already planned), base building (already planned) new algorithms to create bigger, more dangerous or more beautiful creatures. Enhancements to combat. Enhancements to trading. New races. The possibilties are as endless as the game's universe.

The game itself is creative from a programmer's point of view, but the player has no opportunity to be creative. The creatures are diverse, but this diversity is inconsequential for the gameplay. The planets look slightly different (uninhabited dead moons or gas giants don't seem to exist in this universe though), but the resource gathering is the same, with the same scanner icons, the same tool, the same unrealistic graphical effect for every element. The survival aspect is boring as hell - no shelter building, no cooking recipes, no search for clean water, just a few bars that indicate the state of decay for life-support and environmental protection. You cannot even see your equipment deteriorating, it is just the bars, which have to be refilled every few minutes using elements you grind. The repetitive voiced messages concerning equipment decay get annoying very quickly. The sentinels and static outpost NPCs (static meaning: They sit around in the same spot all the time and wait for you to talk to them, as if this was a 90s RPG) are all the same, with the exception of the NPC races, but this is only a skin without consequences for behaviour: They always say and do the same thing. You can craft upgrades after you collected the recipes for them, but you never really see the upgrade on your tool or ship, it is just an icon in the respective inventory. The major difference between all those cool-looking ships is - the number of inventory/equipment slots, making it worse than Elite: Dangerous in this respect. You use the same tool for gathering and combat the whole game, with a few skin and slot number upgrades, but no diversity in the sense of melee/distance, single target/AoE etc., no gameplay changing progression, no character customization, no bond between you and your toon.

The game is bland, and I regret that I bought it.

Update 1.0

Now having played the game for many hours, It's worth giving a more detailed responce to the game. Evidently many people are having issue with it, I'm not but that doesn't lessen the risk that maybe your machine won;t run it well. It seems very CPU heavy, your graphics card maybe a beast, but if your CPU isn't as fast, you find it will run badly.

The game play is much like ark or subnautica with more focus on moving forward, rather than setting up home. 

If this resourse gather style of game play doesn't suit you.. just walk away now. If however you like this kind of upgrading and searching for rare resources then this is one for you.

There is a good flow of game play, you're always doing something, and have 2-3 other things you're thinking about doing all the time.. this can mean you keep getting side tracked from what ever task you'd set yourself.. And set yourself is very much the way this game plays. If you're used to being told go here do this kill that, then while this game has much of that in it's waypoint system.. the real goals are ones you set yourself.. Will I upgrade this or that, buy a better gun, ship or just try and earn some money.. Will I try and get in many fights as I can, find the prettiest planet, or the most hostile.. will I charge toward the center, or just hang out in a few star systems.

Ultimatly I really really enjoy this game.. But I can also see its not going to be everyones cup of tea. so In general my persoanl score is 9/10.. but for a general score I think a 7/10 is fair.. if you have issues with it technically.. that will pretty much reduces it to zero.. so try it on your system.. if it doesn't work get a refund quick.

Update 2.0

After about 30-50 hours you will have pretty much got every upgrade to weapons, ship ect.. I still haven't got to the center after 150 hours but I havn;t been pushing for it as much as I could, and I haven't got the largest ship yet. But the game has now become something new.. after the inital upgrade cycle, of finding and upgrading weapons ship ect.. what you get in the later game, may not appeal to everyone. But I am still personally playing it a lot. 

Essentualy after you have everything upgraded,, and a fairly large ship, you know how the game works well ect, what you are left with is an exploration sim. I personally set my own goals to find cool looking planets and go for a stroll, find as many interesting creatures and landscapes as I can. This will NOT appeal to everyone.. so if you want more than 30ish hours out of the game, then this part of it may not appeal.. but for me, this now feels like I've reached the real game, the game where I just explore.

Update 3.0

New patch 1.1.. now opens the game up and give a great deal more challenge in survival mode, which I'm now playing.. this update really has made the game a real game now, and I whole heartly recomend it.. the 30hour gameplay I'd recon most players would have enjoyed in the vanilla game.. I'd say has now extened to over 60-100 hours.

For a general player I'll now give this a good 8/10 , I'm now feeling it's a 10/10 for me and I'm looking forward to further expansions.

Updated review following 1.1 release.

Well the changes are a tremendous positive and introduce some traditional gameplay elements, building and go fetch missions, into the NMS universe. Suddenly there are things to do. I can't pretend that I have got to grips with all the new stuff, and the game still cries out for a hand-holding tutorial. However, in Normal mode I now have a growing base, which gives a sense of ownership and purpose to my travels, and a freighter which so far I haven't got to grips with. I may soon suffer buyers remorse for parting with 7 million for a ship with only 13/24 inventory slots, but I was impatient to play around with it.

The difficulty seems ramped up even in normal mode and my previous gameplay method of plundering crashed ships for resources at the moment seems closed to me. I may have to focus on collecting resources which was something I thought was behind me. Still, I will take that hit as the changes are very much for the better. Certainly planets and wildlife seem richer and more engaging and I found myself removing my mods without feeling that I had lost anything in the process.

The new hardcore survival mode is a hell-pig. It is like a strategy game just figuring out how to make the journey to my ship. It is 15 minutes away and there are practically no resources between me and it, on a hazardous world that kills me within 2 or 3 minutes the moment I step out of cover. My first hour or two with it has been a complete failure but I shall return to it once I have learned everything in normal mode.

If you liked the game, even a little, 1.1 makes it worth your while visiting it once more.

What is missing still is a multiplayer option. Whilst I didn't care about that before, the new additions are crying out for the option of co-operative play. I hope that is something which can be added in future.

Meanwhile, give it another whirl.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Thoroughly enjoyed it so far. Very like Subnautica in terms of little to do but explore, but with no confines on how far you travel. My son hated it and insists it is a sightseeing simulator and then an unexciting and repetitive one. I found the exploration engrossing, relaxing and pretty much the equivalent of Red Dwarf's Better Than Life machine. In terms of atmosphere I am constantly reminded of the original Elite, LucasArts The Dig, the elements of Tabula Rasa whereby you learn about a lost race and as I already mentioned, Subnautica.

If you play Overwatch then this probably isn't for you. If you play Subnautica or remember being caught up in the mysterious atmosphere of The Dig, then this is just great. It constantly throws up moments where you think 'awesome', like the tree covered snow planet where the temperature drops to a hostile -75 at night and where there are frequent storms whipping the local flora about. It feels real, you forget that it is being created by a bunch of random numbers and an algorithm. That really is an extraordinary achievement of itself.

Sure it sometimes gets boring when you lose your focus, if you were dropped in your local wilderness the views would probably get samey after a while. But, take a short break and then head for pastures new, you'll soon be lost in the experience again. [EDIT] After almost 2 months playing I find that I want to play little and often rather than for long spells, setting myself an achievement or two and then calling it quits for the day. I try and find all fauna on every planet which can sometimes be a bit of a drag, especially with the big 2.4 mod on which makes flora look awesome but which provides a lot of hard to find hidey holes for small critters. I also play with the low flight mod on which makes flight much nicer.

Who knows whether the game has longevity, time and tastes will tell. But I have had better value from this game in a day than anything else I have bought in the last 12 months. [EDIT after playing 130 hours] Reading a review of Quantum Break today the reviewer seemed happy enough that the game provided 12-13 hours play-time. I think by comparison NMS has provided me with fantastic value for money. I hope there will be future updates to the game as have been promised, but the complete silence from the devs leaves me with no confidence that they will happen.

In terms of the whining and negative reviews based on disappointment that the game is not a different game, people need to get a grip. I was paying £40 per cartridge for the Atari VCS2600 in 1979. 37 years later a game is still £40 and you are moaning about it? You should be dancing with joy. And crying because the game isn't Fallout, Elite, Star Citizen, World of Warcraft in space. etc? Why aren't you spamming the forums of Overwatch moaning that it is far too shooty and not at all like Angry Birds?

Game works fine for me. Let's just get this out of the way first: I'm running a GTX 780 and get 40-60 frames on high settings, no AA, and 4x anisotropic filtering at 1920x1080.

The game itself is a very niche title that definitely will not appeal to every gamer out there. The main focus is on exploration. Other things like trading, fighting, and flying are like spices that accent the main entree. You wouldn't eat basil or paprika on its own and it's basically the same thing with this game.

What I mean is, don't go into No Man's Sky expecting a complex space combat title or an RPG with a compelling narrative. There are other games that do those things much better. No Man's Sky is an exploration game first and foremost.

For me, this game is everything I've ever wanted. I've been able to kick back and explore the world at my own pace and decide on my own objectives. Nothing ever feels forced and there's plenty to do. Small point-of-interest markers dot the landscape and serve as little breadcrumbs that beckon you to keep exploring. The planets and creatures are always interesting to observe, and the overall look of the game perfectly captures 70s sci-fi aesthetic.

I'd recommend No Man's Sky to those who just want to relax and enjoy its many worlds. If the screenshots and videos don't immediately excite you then you may find yourself getting bored within a few hours.

================== New Review for 1.1 ===================

I love this game. I liked it before the 1.1 update. I love it since then. Lots of people were angry when the game came out. I guess they wanted a space mmorpg. Which I knew it wasn't. Granted, the PR wasn't all that great. They didn't clearly said what the game was. And many people misundertood what was said. I watched every interview and I never thought that this would be a multiplayer game. I never thought that you could meet your friends in the game. Just looking at the scale of how many stars there is, it's pretty obvious they don't want player to see each other. Just implementing that on a universe this scale would be pretty stupid. It's a single player game that is played in a shared persistent universe. That's all.

Now, I player a lot of this game when it came out, and I agree that it is a pretty repetitive game. You will encounter a lot of planet that look alike, animals that look alike and plants that look alike. But that's just the limit of procedural generation. If you don't mind repetitiveness (I don't, I like repetitive came actually) then it was an awesome game when it came out.

Now there is the 1.1 updates which adds a whole new dimension to the game. Now you can build a base, hire specialist which gives you missions, buy a freigther ship, build a base in that ship, etc. So that's a lot of fun. And knowing now that they release such a big update is a sign that they want to continue releasing big updates like those and the game will just become better and better. Right now the game is much more worth it to buy at the price it is.

A lot of the recent negative reviews are from people who didn't give the game a second chance and are stuck in their own  opinion because that's the cool thing to do right now. 

=================== Previous Review ===========================

So there's a lot of negative review in here about the low fps. Most of the people complaining say they have a good graphic card and this should not happen. First, you need to understand that this is a game mostly based on procedural generation. The problem is not the graphic card but the CPU. You need a very good CPU to run this game since it is the component that will have the most work to do. If the CPU is not good enough, the game will lag a lot, like 10 fps lagging and lower. For my part I have a beast computer and the game is awesome. I love it and have being lost in this game for now 3 hours and I haven't seing the time pass.

 Now, the cpu heavy operations making the game lag is not really an excuse since most of the people don't have a powerful pc. There's some solution that the developers can create to solve this problem but it will impact the beauty of the game. Like for example, a distance fog that hides what is far from the player which means no loading and no generation where it's hidden. There's some other possible solution but I hope the developers find a solution since the game is actually fantastic and everybody should be able to play it.

I'll give you some of my computer's spec so you can evaluate if your computer can run the game at the moment.
My CPU is a intel i7-2600 3.4Ghz and my graphic card a Nvidia GTX 970. I run the game at medium graphics without problem.

When I first launched no man's sky I was thrust straight into the game.  No intro, no guide, nothing.  Just thrust right in.  Sometimes I like the challenge but not always.  Controls at first seemed straightforward with the standard WASD movement with press E or click to interact.  I spent the first minute or so just pressing all my buttons on my keyboard to figure out what to do.  

Rember to read tooltips!  They help.

But my review has to be not recommended.  NMS is the never ending quest for inventory slots.  You will NEVER have enough inventory slots.  

The second reason I do not recommend this game at present is PC preformance.  The game can be a bit stuttery sometimes.
